problems.title: Superacids
problems.problem:
Problem 1. Superacids

The acids which are stronger than pure sulfuric acid are called superacids. Superacids are very strong proton donors being capable of protonating even weak Lewis acids such as Xe, $\ce{H2}$, $\ce{Cl2}$, $\ce{Br2}$, and $\ce{CO2}$. Cations, which never exist in other media, have been observed in superacid solutions. George Olah received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1994 for the discovery of carbocation generation by using superacids. The enhanced acidity is due to the formation of a solvated proton. One of the most common superacids can be obtained by mixing $\ce{SbF5}$ and HF. When liquid $\ce{SbF5}$ is dissolved in liquid HF (in molar ratio of $\ce{SbF5}$/HF greater than 0.5) the $\ce{SbF6-}$ and $\ce{Sb2F11-}$ anions are formed, and the proton released is solvated by HF.

a) Write balanced chemical equations to show the species formed when HF and $\ce{SbF5}$ are mixed.

b) Draw the structures of $\ce{SbF6-}$ and $\ce{Sb2F11-}$ (in both ions the coordination number of antimony is 6 and in $\ce{Sb2F11-}$ there is a bridging fluorine atom).

c) Write the chemical equations for the protonation of $\ce{H2}$ and $\ce{CO2}$ in HF/$\ce{SbF5}$ superacid solution.

d) Draw the Lewis structure of $\ce{HCO2+}$ including the resonance forms and estimate the H–O–C bond angle in each resonance form.

problems.title: Stabilization of high-valent transition metal ions
problems.problem:
Problem 2. Stabilization of high-valent transition metal ions

Relatively few high-valent transition metal oxide fluoride cations are known. $\ce{OsO3F+}$, $\ce{OsO2F3+}$ and $\mu$-$\ce{F(OsO2F3)2+}$ are some of these, where $\mu$-F indicates the $\ce{F-}$ ion bridging the two Os units. In a recent study (Inorg. Chem. 2010, 49, 271) the $\ce{[OsO2F3][Sb2F11]}$ salt has been synthesized by dissolving solid cis-$\ce{OsO2F4}$ in liquid $\ce{SbF5}$, which is a strong Lewis acid, at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, followed by removal of excess $\ce{SbF5}$ under vacuum at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The crystal structure of $\ce{[OsO2F3][Sb2F11]}$ determined by XRD reveals the existence of $\ce{OsO2F3+}$ cation and fluoride bridged $\ce{Sb2F11-}$ anion. Under dynamic vacuum at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the orange, crystalline $\ce{[OsO2F3][Sb2F11]}$ loses $\ce{SbF5}$, yielding [$\mu$-$\ce{F(OsO2F3)2}$][$\ce{Sb2F11}$] salt. In both salts osmium is six-coordinate in solid state, but in liquid $\ce{SbF5}$ solution, both $^{19}$F-NMR and Raman data are consistent with the presence of five-coordinate osmium in the trigonal bipyramidal $\ce{OsO2F3+}$ cation.

a) Write balanced chemical equations for the formation of $\ce{[OsO2F3][Sb2F11]}$ and [$\mu$-$\ce{F(OsO2F3)2}$] [$\ce{Sb2F11}$].

b) Draw all the possible geometrical isomers of trigonal bipyramidal $\ce{OsO2F3+}$ cation.

c) What is the oxidation number of Os in the $\ce{OsO2F3+}$ and $\mu$-$\ce{F(OsO2F3)2+}$ cations?

d) When we assume a free rotation around Os-F(bridging) bond, $\mu$-$\ce{F(OsO2F3)2+}$ cation complex can be represented as a mononuclear octahedral complex of osmium, $\ce{[OsO2F3X]+}$, where X = F-$\ce{OsO2F3}$. Assuming that X is a monodentate ligand, draw all possible geometrical isomers of $\ce{[OsO2F3X]+}$ complex ion. Is there any optical isomer of $\ce{[OsO2F3X]+}$?

problems.title: Colemanite mineral as boron source
problems.problem:
Problem 3. Colemanite mineral as boron source

Boron is an important element in the world from both strategic and industrial points of view. Although the element is not directly used, its compounds have a wide range of applications almost in all manufacturing areas, except food. Boron is oxophilic and, therefore, occurs primarily as oxide (borates) in nature. Borate minerals occur in a few locations in the world. The largest reserves of boron minerals are in the western part of Turkey. One of the most important borate minerals is colemanite with the formula $\ce{2CaO.3B2O3.5H2O}$. Boric acid ($\ce{H3BO3}$) is produced in Turkey and Europe mainly from the reaction of colemanite with sulfuric acid.

The reaction is carried out at temperatures above $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Calcium sulfate dihydrate (Gypsum, $\ce{CaSO4.2H2O}$) crystallizes from the reaction solution and the crystals are filtered out from the hot solution. Subsequently, boric acid crystallizes from the solution when it is cooled down to room temperature. Filtration of gypsum crystals from the reaction solution is a crucial process in the boric acid production for achieving high purity and high efficiency, as the subsequent crystallization of boric acid from the supernatant solution is substantially affected by contaminations. The reaction of sulfuric acid with colemanite takes place in two steps: In the first step colemanite is dissolved in sulfuric acid forming the calcium(II) ion and boric acid. In the second step, calcium sulfate, formed from $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\ce{SO4^{2-}}$ ions, precipitates as gypsum crystals. In an experiment, 184.6 g colemanite containing 37.71% wt. $\ce{B2O3}$ and 20.79% wt. CaO is dissolved in aqueous sulfuric acid yielding initially 1.554 M boric acid at $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The reaction is carried out in a closed system so that the volume of the solution remains essentially constant. The saturation concentration of calcium ion in this solution is $[\ce{Ca^{2+}}]_{sat} = 0.0310\,\mathrm{M}$ at $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

a) Write a balanced equation for the dissolution of colemanite in sulfuric acid.

b) Calculate the amount of gypsum obtained from the crystallization.

c) Calculate the mass of calcium ion remained in the solution.

d) Calculate the theoretical amount of boric acid that can be obtained in this experiment.

e) After hot filtration of gypsum crystals, boric acid is obtained by crystallization when the solution is cooled down to room temperature. The boric acid obtained is still contaminated by sulfate ions. The sulfur contamination is not desired in industrial use of boric acid, such as production of borosilicate glasses. Can recrystallization of boric acid in water remove the sulfate contamination of the product?

problems.title: Magnesium compounds
problems.problem:
Problem 4. Magnesium compounds

Magnesium is one of the important elements in human body. Hundreds of biochemical reactions that drive energy metabolism and DNA repair are fueled by magnesium. Over 300 different enzymes rely on magnesium to facilitate their catalytic action. Magnesium maintains blood pressure and relaxes blood vessels and arteries. Magnesium deficiency leads to physiological decline in cells setting the stage for cancer. Among the numerous available magnesium dietary supplements, magnesium citrate has been reported as more bioavailable than the most commonly used magnesium oxide. Magnesium is a highly flammable metal. Once ignited, it is difficult to extinguish as it is capable of burning in water, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen.

a) Write a balanced equation for the formation of magnesium oxide by reaction of magnesium with

i. oxygen, $\ce{O2}$

ii. carbon dioxide, $\ce{CO2}$

b) Magnesium hydroxide is formed by reaction of Mg or MgO with $\ce{H2O}$. Write a balanced equation for the formation of magnesium hydroxide from the reaction of $\ce{H2O}$ with

i. Mg

ii. MgO

c) When magnesium metal is heated in $\ce{N2}$ atmosphere the white-yellow compound $\mathbf{A}$ is formed. Hydrolysis of $\mathbf{A}$ yields the colorless gas $\mathbf{B}$ which has basic character when dissolved in water. The reaction of $\mathbf{B}$ with aqueous solution of hypochlorite ion generates chloride ion, water, and the molecular compound $\mathbf{C}$ which is soluble in water. The reaction of $\mathbf{B}$ with hydrogen peroxide also produces the compound $\mathbf{C}$ and water. When the colorless gas $\mathbf{B}$ is heated with sodium metal, a solid compound $\mathbf{D}$ and hydrogen gas are produced. The reaction of compound $\mathbf{D}$ with nitrous oxide produces gaseous ammonia, solid sodium hydroxide, and a solid compound $\mathbf{E}$. When the solid $\mathbf{E}$ is heated it decomposes to sodium metal and nitrogen gas. Write balanced equations for the formation of each compound $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, and $\mathbf{E}$.

d) Draw the Lewis structure of the anion present in compound $\mathbf{E}$. Choose the most stable resonance structure.

e) Compound $\mathbf{C}$ was first used as rocket fuel during World War II. Today, it is used as a low-power propellant in spacecrafts. In the presence of certain catalysts such as carbon nanofibers or molybdenum nitride supported on alumina, one of the decomposition reactions of $\mathbf{C}$ involves production of ammonia and nitrogen gas. Write a balanced equation for the decomposition reaction of compound $\mathbf{C}$ generating ammonia and nitrogen gas.

f) Estimate the energy associated with the decomposition of compound $\mathbf{C}$ into ammonia and nitrogen gas and standard enthalpy of formation of $\ce{NH3}$ at 298 K. Standard enthalpy of formation of liquid and gaseous $\mathbf{C}$ are 50.6 and $95.4\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively, at 298 K. Average bond energies of N≡N, N=N, N-N and N-H are 946, 418, 163, and $389\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively, at 298 K.

g) In an experiment, 2.00 mL of $\mathbf{C}$ is placed in a 1.00 L evacuated reaction vessel containing a suitable catalyst at 298 K. After decomposition, the reaction vessel is cooled down to 298 K. Calculate the final pressure inside the vessel (density of liquid $\mathbf{C}$ is $1.0045\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$).

h) Calculate the work done if isothermal expansion of the reaction vessel discussed in part (g) occurs against the atmospheric pressure of 1 atm.

problems.title: Nitrogen oxides and oxoanions
problems.problem:
Problem 5. Nitrogen oxides and oxoanions

Nitrogen occurs mainly in the atmosphere. Its abundance in Earth's Crust is only 0.002% by mass. The only important nitrogen containing minerals are sodium nitrate (Chile saltpeter) and potassium nitrate (saltpeter). Sodium nitrate, $\ce{NaNO3}$, and its close relative sodium nitrite, $\ce{NaNO2}$, are two food preservatives with very similar chemical formulae, but different chemical properties. Sodium nitrate helps to prevent bacterial colonization of food. Sodium nitrite is a strong oxidizing agent used as a meat preservative. As in the case of almost any food additive or preservative, sodium nitrate is linked to several adverse reactions in susceptible people. Consuming too much sodium nitrate can cause allergies. Excessive ingestion of the preservative can also cause headaches.

a) Draw the Lewis structures for the anions of these two salts including all possible resonance forms. Which one of these two anions has shorter N-O bond distance?

b) Zn reduces $\ce{NO3-}$ ions to $\ce{NH3}$ in basic solution forming tetrahydroxozincate(II) ion. Write a balanced equation for the reaction between zinc and ammonia in basic solution.

c) When a strong base is gradually added to a solution containing $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$ ions a white precipitate of $\ce{Zn(OH)2}$ first forms ($K_\mathrm{sp} = 1.2\times10^{-17}$ for $\ce{Zn(OH)2}$). To a 1.0 L solution of $5.0\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{mol}$ $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$ ions, 0.10 mol $\ce{OH-}$ is added. Calculate the pH of this solution.

d) When more base is added to the solution, the white precipitate of $\ce{Zn(OH)2}$ dissolves forming the complex ion $\ce{Zn(OH)4^{2-}}$. The formation constant for the complex ion is $4.6\times10^{17}$. Calculate the pH of the solution in part (c) when 0.10 mol $\ce{OH-}$ ion is added (assuming the total volume does not change).

e) A mixture containing only NaCl and $\ce{NaNO3}$ is to be analyzed for its $\ce{NaNO3}$ content. In an experiment, 5.00 g of this mixture is dissolved in water and solution is completed to 100 mL by addition of water; then a 10 mL aliquot of the resulting solution is treated with Zn under basic conditions. Ammonia produced during the reaction is passed into 50.0 mL of 0.150 M HCl solution. The excess HCl requires 32.10 mL of 0.100 M NaOH solution for its titration. Find the mass % of $\ce{NaNO3}$ in the solid sample.

f) Both NaCl and $\ce{NaNO3}$ are strong electrolytes. Their presence in solution lowers the vapor pressure of the solvent and as a result freezing point is depressed. The freezing point depression depends not only on the number of the solute particles but also on the solvent itself. The freezing point depression constant for water is $K_\mathrm{f} = 1.86\,^\circ\mathrm{C/molal}$. Calculate the freezing point of the solution prepared by dissolving 1.50 g of the mixture described in (d) consisting of NaCl and $\ce{NaNO3}$ in 100.0 mL solution. Density of this solution is $d = 0.985\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$.

g) $\ce{N2H4}$ is one of the nitrogen compounds which can be used as a fuel in hydrazine fuel cell. Calculate the standard free energy change for the fuel cell reaction given below.

$$\ce{N2H4(g) + O2(g) -> N2(g) + 2 H2O(l)}$$

The standard potentials are given below:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{O2(g) + 2H2O(l) + 4e- -> 4OH^-(aq)} & E^\circ = 1.23\,\mathrm{V} \\ \ce{N2(g) + 4H2O(l) + 4e- -> N2H4(g) + 4OH^-(aq)} & E^\circ = -0.33\,\mathrm{V} \end{array}$$

h) The free energy change is related to the maximum amount of electrical work that can be obtained from a system during a change at constant temperature and pressure, under reversible conditions. The relation is given as $-\Delta G = w_\mathrm{max}$. Calculate the maximum amount of work that can be obtained from the fuel cell which consumes 0.32 g $\ce{N2H4(g)}$ under standard conditions.

problems.title: Ferrochrome
problems.problem:
Problem 6. Ferrochrome

Chromium is one of the most abundant elements in Earth's Crust and it is mined as chromite mineral, $\ce{FeCr2O4}$. South Africa, Kazakhstan, India, Russia, and Turkey are substantial producers. For the production of pure chromium, the iron has to be separated from the mineral in a two step roasting and leaching process.

$$\ce{4 FeCr2O4(s) + 8 Na2CO3(s) + 7 O2(g) -> 8 Na2CrO4(s) + 2 Fe2O3(s) + 8 CO2(g)}$$

$$\ce{2 Na2CrO4(s) + H2SO4(aq) -> Na2Cr2O7(s) + Na2SO4(aq) + H2O(l)}$$

Dichromate is converted to chromium(III) oxide by reduction with carbon and then reduced in an aluminothermic reaction to chromium.

$$\ce{Na2Cr2O7(s) + 2 C(s) -> Cr2O3(s) + Na2CO3(s) + CO(g)}$$

$$\ce{Cr2O3(s) + 2 Al(s) -> Al2O3(s) + 2 Cr(s)}$$

a) Calculate the mass of Cr that can be theoretically obtained from 2.1 tons of ore which contains 72.0% $\ce{FeCr2O4}$ mineral.

b) Chromium, due to its strong corrosion resistance, is an important alloying material for steel. A sample of certain steel is to be analyzed for its Mn and Cr content. Mn and Cr in a 5.00 g steel sample are oxidized to $\ce{MnO4-}$ and $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}$, respectively, via a suitable treatment to yield 100.0 mL solution. A 50.0 mL portion of this solution is added to $\ce{BaCl2}$ and by adjusting pH, chromium is completely precipitated as 5.82 g $\ce{BaCrO4}$. A second 50.0 mL portion of the solution requires exactly 43.5 mL of 1.60 M $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ for its titration in acidic solution. The unbalanced equations for the titration reactions are given below.

$$\ce{MnO4^-(aq) + Fe^{2+}(aq) + H+(aq) -> Mn^{2+}(aq) + Fe^{3+}(aq)}$$

$$\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}(aq) + Fe^{2+}(aq) + H+(aq) -> Cr^{3+}(aq) + Fe^{3+}(aq)}$$

Balance the equations for the titration reactions.

c) Calculate the % Mn and % Cr in the steel sample.

problems.title: Xenon compounds
problems.problem:
Problem 7. Xenon compounds

Xenon, although present in the earth atmosphere in trace level, has several applications. It is used in the field of illumination and optics in flash and arc lamps. Xenon is employed as a propellant for ion thrusters in spacecraft. In addition, it has several medical applications. Some of xenon isotopes are used in imaging the soft tissues such as heart, lung, and brain. It is used as a general anesthetic and recently its considerable potential in treating brain injuries, including stroke has been demonstrated.

Xenon being a member of noble gases has extremely low reactivity. Yet, several xenon compounds with highly electronegative atoms such as fluorine and oxygen are known. Xenon reacts with fluorine to form three different xenon fluorides, $\ce{XeF2}$, $\ce{XeF4}$ and $\ce{XeF6}$. All these fluorides readily react with water, releasing pure Xe gas, hydrogen fluoride and molecular oxygen. The oxide and oxofluorides of xenon are obtained by partial or complete hydrolysis of xenon fluorides. Xenon trioxide can be obtained by the hydrolysis of $\ce{XeF4}$ or $\ce{XeF6}$. The hydrolysis of $\ce{XeF4}$ yields $\ce{XeO3}$, Xe, HF, and $\ce{F2}$. However, hydrolysis of $\ce{XeF6}$ produces only $\ce{XeO3}$ and HF. When partially hydrolyzed, $\ce{XeF4}$ and $\ce{XeF6}$ yield $\ce{XeOF2}$ and $\ce{XeOF4}$, respectively, in addition to HF.

a) Write balanced equations for the generation of

i. $\ce{XeO3}$ by hydrolysis of $\ce{XeF4}$

ii. $\ce{XeO3}$ by hydrolysis of $\ce{XeF6}$

iii. $\ce{XeOF2}$ by partial hydrolysis of $\ce{XeF4}$

iv. $\ce{XeOF4}$ by partial hydrolysis of $\ce{XeF6}$

b) Draw the Lewis structures and give the hybridization at the central atom of

i. $\ce{XeF2}$

ii. $\ce{XeF4}$

iii. $\ce{XeO3}$

iv. $\ce{XeOF2}$

v. $\ce{XeOF4}$

problems.title: Structure of phosphorus compounds
problems.problem:
Problem 8. Structure of phosphorus compounds

Phosphorus is very reactive and, therefore, never found in the native elemental form in the Earth's Crust. Phosphorus is an essential element for all living organisms. It is the major structural component of bone in the form of calcium phosphate and cell membranes in the form of phospholipids. Furthermore, it is also a component of DNA, RNA, and ATP. All energy production and storage, activation of some enzymes, hormones and cell signaling molecules are dependent on phosphorylated compounds and phosphorylation. Compounds of phosphorus act as a buffer to maintain pH of blood and bind to hemoglobin in red blood cells and affect oxygen delivery.

Phosphorus has five valence electrons as nitrogen, but being an element of the third period, it has empty d orbitals available to form compounds up to six coordination number. One allotrope of phosphorus is the white phosphorus which is a waxy solid consisting of tetrahedral $\ce{P4}$ molecules. White phosphorus is very reactive and bursts into flame in air to yield the phosphorus(V) oxide $\ce{P4O10}$. Its partial oxidation in less oxygen yields the phosphorus(III) oxide $\ce{P4O6}$. Disproportionation of white phosphorus in basic solution yields the gaseous phosphine, $\ce{PH3}$ and hypophosphite ion, $\ce{H2PO2-}$. Phosphorous acid, $\ce{H3PO3}$ and phosphoric acid, $\ce{H3PO4}$ can be produced by the reaction of $\ce{P4O6}$ or $\ce{P4O10}$ with water, respectively. White phosphorus reacts with halogens to yield halides with general formulae $\ce{PX3}$ and $\ce{PX5}$. Oxidation of $\ce{PCl3}$ forms phosphoryl trichloride, $\ce{POCl3}$. Reaction of $\ce{PCl5}$ with LiF yields $\ce{LiPF6}$ which is used as an electrolyte in lithium-ion batteries.

a) Write balanced equations for the preparation of

i. $\ce{PH3}$

ii. $\ce{PCl3}$

iii. $\ce{PCl5}$

iv. $\ce{P4O6}$

v. $\ce{P4O10}$

vi. $\ce{H3PO3}$

vii. $\ce{H3PO4}$

viii. $\ce{POCl3}$

ix. $\ce{LiPF6}$

b) Draw the Lewis structures of the following molecules or ions, including the resonance forms if any.

i. $\ce{PCl3}$

ii. $\ce{PCl5}$

iii. $\ce{PO4^{3-}}$

iv. $\ce{POCl3}$

v. $\ce{PF6-}$

c) Draw the structures of the phosphorus oxides $\ce{P4O6}$ and $\ce{P4O10}$, starting with tetrahedral $\ce{P4}$ skeleton. Each of six oxygen atom will be bridging two phosphorus atoms on an edge. An additional oxygen atom will be bonded to each phosphorus atom as terminal oxo-group in the case of $\ce{P4O10}$.

d) Using the Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion model determine the geometry of the following molecules or ions.

i. $\ce{PCl3}$

ii. $\ce{POCl3}$

iii. $\ce{PCl5}$

iv. $\ce{PF6-}$

e) What is the hybridization at phosphorus atom in the following molecules or ions?

i. $\ce{PCl3}$

ii. $\ce{POCl3}$

iii. $\ce{PCl5}$

iv. $\ce{PF6-}$

problems.title: Arsenic in water
problems.problem:
Problem 9. Arsenic in water

Arsenic is known as a pollutant in environment and a toxic element. However, in December 2010 researchers of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) of USA reported a species of bacterium in Mono Lake, California, that can use arsenic instead of phosphorus in biological molecule structures. It seems that monitoring concentration and identities of arsenic species in water will become even more important in near future.

In natural waters, arsenic is present in the form of oxoacids: Arsenous or arsenic acid with oxidation states of +3 and +5, respectively. The source of arsenic in natural waters is often of geological origin. Arsenous acid and arsenic acid have the following dissociation constants.

$$\begin{array}{llll} \ce{H3AsO3} & K_\mathrm{a1} = 5.1\times10^{-10} & & \\ \ce{H3AsO4} & K_\mathrm{a1} = 5.8\times10^{-3} & K_\mathrm{a2} = 1.1\times10^{-7} & K_\mathrm{a3} = 3.2\times10^{-12} \end{array}$$

In aqueous systems, oxidation state of arsenic is dependent on the presence of oxidants and reductants, dissolved oxygen plays an important role. World Health Organization (WHO) has established a maximum total arsenic concentration of $10\,\mathrm{\mu g/L}$ in drinking water; this value has been adapted by many countries.

In a water sample obtained from a river as a potential source of drinking water, pH value is found to be 6.50. Using atomic absorption spectrometry, speciation analysis is also performed and arsenic(III) and arsenic(V) concentrations are found to be $10.8\,\mathrm{\mu g/L}$ and $4.3\,\mathrm{\mu g/L}$, respectively.

a) Calculate the total molar concentration for arsenic(III) and arsenic(V) inorganic species in the system, assuming that these are the only arsenic species present.

b) What will be the predominant molecular or ionic species for arsenic(III) at pH = 6.50? Write the formula(s).

c) What will be the predominant molecular or ionic species for arsenic(V) at pH = 6.50? Write the formula(s).

d) Calculate the molar concentration(s) of arsenic(III) species suggested in (b).

e) Calculate the molar concentration(s) of predominant arsenic(V) species suggested in (c).

f) arsenic(III) is known to be significantly more toxic to human as compared to arsenic(V). Is it advantageous or disadvantageous to have oxidizing agents such as dissolved oxygen in water?

problems.title: Amphoteric lead oxide
problems.problem:
Problem 10. Amphoteric lead oxide

In aqueous media, $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ ions form a precipitate, PbO, which is an amphoteric oxide. In acidic medium, only $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ species is present; with increasing pH, PbO and $\ce{Pb(OH)3-}$ are formed in appreciable quantities. The important equilibria for lead species in aqueous medium are given below:

$$\begin{array}{lll} \text{Reaction 1} & \ce{PbO(s) + H2O(l) <=> Pb^{2+}(aq) + 2 OH^-(aq)} & K_\mathrm{sp} = 8.0\times10^{-16} \\ \text{Reaction 2} & \ce{PbO(s) + 3H2O(l) <=> Pb(OH)3^-(aq) + H3O+(aq)} & K_\mathrm{a} = 1.0\times10^{-15} \end{array}$$

a) The amphoteric PbO completely dissolves when pH is sufficiently low. When initial concentration of $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ is $1.00\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$, what is the pH at which PbO starts to precipitate?

b) Starting from the value in (b), when pH is increased to a certain value, precipitate is redissolved. At what pH value does the precipitate dissolve completely?

c) Write a general expression for molar solubility, s, of PbO.

d) Theoretically, the minimum solubility is achieved when pH is 9.40. Calculate the molar concentration of all the species and the molar solubility at this pH.

e) Calculate the pH range where the solubility is $1.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$ or lower.

problems.title: Analyzing a mixture of calcium salts
problems.problem:
Problem 11. Analyzing a mixture of calcium salts

When a 5.000 g mixture of $\ce{CaCO3}$, $\ce{Ca(HCO3)2}$, $\ce{CaCl2}$ and $\ce{Ca(ClO3)2}$ is heated at elevated temperature gaseous $\ce{CO2}$, $\ce{H2O}$, and $\ce{O2}$ are evolved. The gases evolved exert a pressure of 1.312 atm in an evacuated 1.000 L cylinder at 400.0 K. When the temperature inside the cylinder is decreased to 300.0 K, the pressure drops to 0.897 atm. The vapor pressure of water at this temperature is 27.0 torr. The gas in the cylinder is used to combust an unknown amount of acetylene $\ce{C2H2}$. The enthalpy change during the combustion process is determined as $-7.796\,\mathrm{kJ}$ with the use of a calorimeter.

$\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\ce{C2H2(g)}) = 226.8\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$; $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\ce{CO2(g)}) = -393.5\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$;

$\Delta_\mathrm{f}H^\circ(\ce{H2O(g)}) = -241.8\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$; $\Delta_\mathrm{vap}H^\circ_{298\,\mathrm{K}}(\ce{H2O(l)}) = 44.0\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

a) Write balanced equations for the possible decomposition reactions generating gases.

b) Write a balanced equation for the combustion of $\ce{C2H2}$.

c) Calculate the total number of moles of gases produced in the cylinder.

d) Calculate the number of moles of $\ce{O2}$ that was present in the cyclinder.

e) Calculate number of moles of $\ce{CO2}$ and $\ce{H2O}$ produced.

f) Calculate the weight percentage of $\ce{CaCO3}$ and $\ce{CaCl2}$ in the original mixture.

problems.title: Breath analysis
problems.problem:
Problem 12. Breath analysis

Ethanol is dissolved in blood and distributed to organs in the body. As a volatile compound, ethanol can be vaporized quite easily. In lungs, ethanol can change its phase from liquid to gaseous and, hence, it can be exhaled with air. Since the concentration of alcohol vapor in lungs is directly related to its concentration in blood, blood alcohol concentration can be measured using a device called a breathalyzer. In one of the older versions of breathalyzer, a suspect breathes into the device and exhaled air is allowed to pass through a solution of potassium dichromate which oxidizes ethanol to acetic acid. This oxidation is accompanied by a color change from orange to green and a detector records the change in intensity, hence, the change in color, which is used to calculate the percentage of alcohol in breath. When the oxidation of alcohol by potassium dichromate is carried out in an electrochemical cell, either the electrical current generated by this reaction or the change in the electromotive force can be measured and used for the estimation of alcohol content of blood.

a) Write a balanced equation for the oxidation of ethanol by the dichromate ion in acidic solution.

b) If the standard potential for the reduction of $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}$ to $\ce{Cr^{3+}}$ is 1.330 V and reduction of acetic acid to ethanol is 0.058 V, calculate the standard electromotive force $E^\circ$ for the overall reaction and show that overall reaction is spontaneous at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and 1.0 bar.

c) In a breathalyzer which uses oxidation of ethanol, the volume of solution is 10.0 mL. When a suspect breathes into the device, 0.10 A of current flow is recorded for 60 s. Calculate the mass of alcohol per volume of exhaled breath.

d) In calculating the alcohol content of blood from the amount of alcohol in a breath, the "2100:1 partition ratio" needs to be considered. The ratio states that 2100 mL of expired air (breath) contains the same amount of ethanol as 1 mL of blood. Alternatively, each milliliter of blood has 2100 times the amount of ethanol as each milliliter of expired air. If the volume of expired air described in part (c) is 60.0 mL, calculate the amount of alcohol per mL of blood.

e) $\ce{Cr^{3+}}$ precipitates in basic solution as $\ce{Cr(OH)3}$. The solubility product of chromium(III) hydroxide is $6.3\times10^{-31}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Calculate the standard potential for the reduction of $\ce{Cr(OH)3}$ to Cr. Standard potential for the reduction of $\ce{Cr^{3+}}$ to Cr is $-0.74\,\mathrm{V}$.

problems.title: Decomposition kinetics of sulfuryl dichloride
problems.problem:
Problem 13. Decomposition kinetics of sulfuryl dichloride

Sulfuryl dichloride ($\ce{SO2Cl2}$) is a compound of industrial, environmental and scientific interest and widely used as chlorinating/sulfonating agent or as component of the catholyte system in batteries. At room temperature, $\ce{SO2Cl2}$ is a colorless liquid with a pungent odor; its boiling point is $70\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. It decomposes to $\ce{SO2}$ and $\ce{Cl2}$ when heated to or above $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

$$\ce{SO2Cl2(g) -> SO2(g) + Cl2(g)}$$

An empty container is filled with $\ce{SO2Cl2}$. Its decomposition to $\ce{SO2}$ and $\ce{Cl2}$ is followed by monitoring the change in total pressure at 375 K. The following data are obtained.

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|l|} \hline \text{Time (s)} & 0 & 2500 & 5000 & 7500 & 10000 \\ \hline P_\text{total}\ \text{(atm)} & 1.000 & 1.053 & 1.105 & 1.152 & 1.197 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

a) By graphical approach, show that the decomposition is a first order reaction and calculate the rate constant at 375 K.

b) When the same decomposition reaction is carried out at 385 K, the total pressure is found to be 1.55 atm after 1 h. Calculate the activation energy for the decomposition reaction.

c) There will be a negligible amount of $\ce{SO2Cl2(g)}$ in the reaction vessel after a long period of time. Therefore, the content of the vessel might be considered to be a mixture of $\ce{SO2}$ and $\ce{Cl2}$ gases. $\ce{SO2(g)}$ is separated from $\ce{Cl2(g)}$ as $\ce{H2SO4}$ and $\ce{Cl2(g)}$ is used to construct a $\ce{Cl2}$/$\ce{Cl-}$ electrode. This electrode is combined with a $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$/Cu electrode to make a Galvanic cell. Which electrode is the cathode? $E^\circ(\ce{Cu^{2+}}/\ce{Cu}) = +0.36\,\mathrm{V}$ and $E^\circ(\ce{Pt}/\ce{Cl2}, \ce{Cl-}) = +1.36\,\mathrm{V}$

d) Calculate the $\Delta G^\circ$ for the cell reaction given in (c).

e) A possible way for separating $\ce{SO2}$ and $\ce{Cl2}$ from each other is to pass the mixture over solid CaO which will convert all $\ce{SO2}$ to $\ce{CaSO3}$, a strong electrolyte. Calculate the pH of a 0.020 M $\ce{CaSO3}$ solution. For $\ce{H2SO3}$ $K_\mathrm{a1} = 1.7\times10^{-2}$ and $K_\mathrm{a2} = 6.4\times10^{-8}$.

problems.title: Clock reaction
problems.problem:
Problem 14. Clock reaction

The iodine clock reaction is a classical chemical clock demonstration experiment to display chemical kinetics in action. In this reaction two clear solutions are mixed and after a short time delay, the colorless liquid suddenly turns to a shade of dark blue. The iodine clock reaction has several variations. One of them involves the reaction between peroxydisulfate(VI) and iodide ions:

$$\text{Reaction }\mathbf{A}\text{:}\quad \ce{S2O8^{2-}(aq) + 3 I^-(aq) -> 2 SO4^{2-}(aq) + I3^-(aq)}$$

The $\ce{I3-}$ ion formed in Reaction $\mathbf{A}$ reacts immediately with ascorbic acid ($\ce{C6H8O6}$) present originally in the solution to form $\ce{I-}$ ion (Reaction $\mathbf{B}$).

$$\text{Reaction }\mathbf{B}\text{:}\quad \ce{C6H8O6(aq) + I3^-(aq) -> C6H6O6(aq) + 3 I^-(aq) + 2 H+(aq)}$$

When all the ascorbic acid present in the solution is consumed, the $\ce{I3-}$ ion generated in Reaction $\mathbf{A}$ forms a blue colored complex with starch present in solution (Reaction $\mathbf{C}$).

$$\text{Reaction }\mathbf{C}\text{:}\quad \ce{I3^-(aq) + starch ->} \text{Blue-complex.}$$

Thus, the time $t$ elapsed between mixing the reactants and the appearance of the blue color depends on the amount of $\ce{I3-}$ ion formed. Therefore $1/t$ can be used as a measure of reaction rate.

At $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, 25.0 mL $\ce{(NH4)2S2O8}$, 25.0 mL KI, 5.0 mL 0.020 M $\ce{C6H8O6}$, and 5.0 mL starch solutions are mixed with different initial concentrations of $\ce{(NH4)2S2O8}$ and KI, and the elapsed time $t$ for the appearance of blue color is measured. All the data are tabulated below.

$$\begin{array}{cccc} \text{Experiment No} & [\ce{(NH4)2S2O8}]_\mathrm{o}\ \text{(mol/L)} & [\ce{KI}]_\mathrm{o}\ \text{(mol/L)} & t\ \text{(s)} \\ \hline 1 & 0.200 & 0.200 & 20.5 \\ 2 & 0.100 & 0.200 & 41.0 \\ 3 & 0.050 & 0.200 & 82.0 \\ 4 & 0.200 & 0.100 & 41.0 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

a) Find the rate law for Reaction $\mathbf{A}$ using the data given in Table.

b) Using the data for the experiment 1, find the initial rate of Reaction $\mathbf{A}$ in $\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$.

c) Calculate the rate constant for Reaction $\mathbf{A}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

d) The following mechanism is proposed for Reaction $\mathbf{A}$:

$$\begin{array}{l} \ce{I^-(aq) + S2O8^{2-}(aq) ->[$k_1$] IS2O8^{3-}(aq)} \\ \ce{IS2O8^{3-}(aq) ->[$k_2$] 2 SO4^{2-}(aq) + I+(aq)} \\ \ce{I+(aq) + I^-(aq) ->[$k_3$] I2(aq)} \\ \ce{I2(aq) + I^-(aq) ->[$k_4$] I3^-(aq)} \end{array}$$

Derive an equation for the rate of formation of $\ce{I3-}$(aq) assuming that the steady-state approximation can be applied to all intermediates. Is the given mechanism consistent with the rate law found in part (a)?

e) Ascorbic acid is a weak diprotic acid. In order to find its first acid dissociation constant, $K_\mathrm{a1}$, 50.0 mL of 0.100 M ascorbic acid solution is titrated with 0.200 M NaOH solution. The pH of solution is measured as 2.86 after addition of 1.00 mL NaOH solution. Calculate acid dissociation constant $K_\mathrm{a1}$ for ascorbic acid.

f) Give the predominant species present at pH = 7.82 if $K_\mathrm{a2}$ for ascorbic acid is $2.5\times10^{-12}$.

problems.title: Mixing ideal gases
problems.problem:
Problem 15. Mixing ideal gases

Two rigid containers in thermal equilibrium at 298 K connected by a valve are isolated from the surroundings. In one of the containers, 1.00 mol of He(g) and 0.50 mol of A(g) are present at 1.00 atm. In the other container, 2.00 mol of Ar(g) and 0.50 mol of $\ce{B2(g)}$ are present at 1.00 atm.

a) Predict whether the entropy will increase or decrease when the valve separating the two containers is opened assuming that no chemical reaction takes place.

b) Predict whether the entropy will increase or decrease, stating all factors that will have contribution, if a chemical reaction takes place according to the following equation when the valve separating the two containers is opened.

$$\ce{A(g) + 1/2 B2(g) -> BA(g)}\qquad \Delta H^\circ_{298} = -99.0\,\mathrm{kJ}$$

c) Assuming that all the gases present are ideal, calculate the final pressure at the end of the reaction. The total heat capacity of two containers is $547.0\,\mathrm{J/^\circ C}$.

problems.title: Kinetics in gas phase
problems.problem:
Problem 16. Kinetics in gas phase

The gas phase reaction

$$\ce{A2(g) + 2 B(g) -> 2 AB(g)}$$

is accelerated by catalyst C. The overall rate constant is found to increase linearly with the catalyst concentration. Following measurements are done at 400 K with $[\mathrm{C}] = 0.050\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$:

$$\begin{array}{cccc} \text{Experiment No} & [\ce{A2}]\ (\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}) & [\mathrm{B}]\ (\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}) & \text{Initial rate}\ (\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}) \\ \hline 1 & 0.010 & 0.10 & 1.600\times10^{-10} \\ 2 & 0.010 & 0.20 & 3.200\times10^{-10} \\ 3 & 0.100 & 0.20 & 1.012\times10^{-9} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

a) What is the rate law of this reaction?

b) Calculate the numerical value of $k_\mathrm{overall}$ at 400 K.

c) For this hypothetical reaction following mechanism was proposed.

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{A2(g) <=>[$k_1$][$k_{-1}$] 2 A(g)} & \text{fast equilibrium} \\ \ce{A(g) + B(g) + C(g) ->[$k_2$] ABC(g)} & \text{slow step} \\ \ce{ABC(g) ->[$k_3$] AB(g) + C(g)} & \end{array}$$

Check that the suggested mechanism gives the equation for the overall reaction.

d) Show that the suggested mechanism is consistent with the rate law determined experimentally.

e) Calculate the dissociation enthalpy of $\ce{A2}$ bond using the following information:

• At 400 K, when $[\ce{A2}]$ is $1.0\times10^{-1}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$, [A] is $4.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$.

• When the first experiment is repeated at 425 K, the initial reaction rate increases to a three-fold value.

• Activation energy of the slowest step is 45.0 kJ.

problems.title: Chemical Equilibrium
problems.problem:
Problem 17. Chemical Equilibrium

Iodine is an essential trace element for life and is the heaviest element commonly needed by living organisms. At high temperatures an equilibrium between $\ce{I2(g)}$ and $\ce{I(g)}$ takes place.

The following table summarizes the initial pressure of $\ce{I2(g)}$ and the total pressure when the equilibrium is reached at the given temperatures.

$$\begin{array}{ccc} T\ \text{(K)} & 1073 & 1173 \\ \hline P(\ce{I2})\ \text{(bar)} & 0.0631 & 0.0684 \\ P_\text{total}\ \text{(bar)} & 0.0750 & 0.0918 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

a) Calculate $\Delta H^\circ$, $\Delta G^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ at 1100 K. (Assume that $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ are independent of temperature in the temperature range given.)

b) Calculate the mole fraction of $\ce{I(g)}$ in the equilibrium mixture when the numerical value of $K_\mathrm{p}$ is the half of the total pressure.

c) Assuming ideal gas behavior for $\ce{I2(g)}$ and $\ce{I(g)}$, calculate the bond energy of $\ce{I2}$ at 298 K.

d) Calculate the wavelength of radiation that must be used to dissociate $\ce{I2(g)}$ at 298 K.

e) In an experiment, when a sample of $\ce{I2(g)}$ is irradiated by a laser beam of $\lambda = 825.8\,\mathrm{nm}$, at a rate of $20.0\,\mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$ for 10.0 s, $1.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mol}$ of $\ce{I(g)}$ is produced. Calculate the quantum yield for the dissociation process (i.e., the number of moles of $\ce{I2}$ dissociated per mole of photons absorbed by the system).

problems.title: Iodine equilibrium
problems.problem:
Problem 18. Iodine equilibrium

Drinking water may contain small amount of some contaminants that are harmful to living organisms. Iodine is used as a disinfectant for drinking water for the International Space Station Alpha. Aqueous $\ce{I2}$ forms a number of inorganic derivatives, such as hypoiodous acid, HOI; iodate, $\ce{IO3-}$; iodide, $\ce{I-}$ and triiodide, $\ce{I3-}$. An equilibrium reaction takes place involving $\ce{I2}$, $\ce{I-}$ and $\ce{I3-}$ in water according to the following equation;

$$\ce{I2(aq) + I^-(aq) <=> I3^-(aq)}$$

When dichloromethane, $\ce{CH2Cl2}$ is added to aqueous solution of iodine, $\ce{I2}$ is distributed in water and $\ce{CH2Cl2}$ phases according to the following equilibrium process. The equilibrium constant for the distribution is 150.

$$\ce{I2(aq) <=> I2(CH2Cl2)}$$

a) For the homogenous equilibrium reaction which species acts as a Lewis acid?

b) One method for determining the concentration of $\ce{I2}$ and $\ce{I3-}$ in a solution is the titration with a standard solution of $\ce{S2O3^{2-}}$. An oxidation-reduction reaction takes place when $\ce{I2}$ or $\ce{I3-}$ interacts with $\ce{S2O3^{2-}}$ yielding $\ce{I-}$ and $\ce{S4O6^{2-}}$. Write the balanced equations for chemical reactions that take place during the titration of $\ce{I2}$ and $\ce{I3-}$ with $\ce{S2O3^{2-}}$. Indicate the oxidant and the reductant in each reaction? Give the oxidation state of S in $\ce{Na2S2O3}$.

c) In order to determine the equilibrium constant of the reaction involving $\ce{I2}$, $\ce{I-}$ and $\ce{I3-}$ in water the following experiments are performed at 298 K. When 50.0 mL of 0.010 M KI aqueous solution is added to 25.0 mL solution of $\ce{I2}$ in $\ce{CH2Cl2}$, two separate phases, aqueous and organic, are formed. Assume that there is no volume change upon mixing. In order to determine concentrations of $\ce{I2}$ distributed in $\ce{CH2Cl2}$ and aqueous phases, a 5.00 mL aliquot of the $\ce{CH2Cl2}$ phase is diluted to 100.0 mL by addition of the solvent, $\ce{CH2Cl2}$. The visible spectrum of $\ce{I2}$ in the diluted solution, recorded in a 1.00 cm-cell, had a band with a maximum absorbance of 0.516 at 510.0 nm. The molar absorption coefficient, $\varepsilon$ of $\ce{I2}$ in $\ce{CH2Cl2}$ at 510 nm is $858\,\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$. Calculate equilibrium concentrations of $\ce{I2}$ in $\ce{CH2Cl2}$ and aqueous phases.

d) In order to determine the equilibrium concentrations of $\ce{I-}$ and $\ce{I3-}$, a 25.0 mL aliquot is taken from the aqueous phase. To this solution, an excess amount of KI, namely 10.0 mL of 0.100 M KI solution, is added to avoid evaporation of $\ce{I2}$. Then, the final solution is titrated with a 0.0100 M solution of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$. The end point is reached upon addition of 3.10 mL of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution. Calculate the equilibrium concentrations of $\ce{I-}$, and $\ce{I3-}$ in the aqueous phase and the equilibrium constant at 298 K.

e) Calculate $\Delta_\mathrm{f}G^\circ[\ce{I2(CH2Cl2)}]$, if $\Delta_\mathrm{f}G^\circ[\ce{I2(aq)}]$ is $16.4\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

problems.title: Molecular weight determination by osmometry
problems.problem:
Problem 19. Molecular weight determination by osmometry

Measurement of osmotic pressure is one of the techniques used to determine the molecular weight of large molecules, like polymers. The device, osmometer, used to measure the osmotic pressure, consists of a semipermeable membrane that separates pure solvent from a solution. The flow of solvent from pure solvent side to solution side, due to concentration gradient, across the semipermeable membrane is called osmosis.

Polyvinylchloride, PVC, is one of the most widely used plastics and can be prepared via chain polymerization. In chain polymerization monomers are added to a growing polymer chain. A typical chain polymerization involves three main steps named as initiation, propagation, and termination. In termination reaction two growing chains combine to form either one dead polymer chain (termination by combination) or two dead polymer chains (termination by disproportionation). In an attempt to determine the molecular weight of PVC via osmotic pressure measurement, a PVC solution is prepared by dissolving 7.0 g of PVC in cyclohexanone ($\ce{C6H10O}$) to make a 1.0 L solution at 295 K. One arm of the osmometer is filled with this solution of density $0.980\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ and the other arm is filled with pure solvent cyclohexanone to the same level. After a certain time, the height of liquid in the solution side arm increases and at equilibrium a 5.10 cm level difference between two arms is recorded.

a) Calculate the osmotic pressure and average molecular weight of PVC. (density of Hg = $13.6\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, $g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$).

b) The kinetic chain length $\nu$ is the ratio of the number of monomer units consumed per activated center produced in the initiation step and used to estimate the mode of termination. In the chain polymerization of vinyl chloride to produce PVC, the concentration of active centers produced in the initiation step and the change in the concentration of monomer is found to be $1.00\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{mol/L}$ and $2.85\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{mol/L}$, respectively. Calculate the kinetic chain length, $\nu$.

c) Predict whether the termination is by combination or by disproportionation.

d) The vapor pressure of pure solvent cyclohexanone is 4.33 torr at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Calculate the vapor pressure of the PVC solution.

e) For pure solvent cyclohexanone, normal freezing point is $-31.000\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. If the freezing point of the PVC solution is $-31.003\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, find the molal freezing point depression constant of cyclohexanone.

problems.title: Allowed energy levels and requirements for absorption of light
problems.problem:
Problem 20. Allowed energy levels and requirements for absorption of light

It is a well-established experimental fact that the internal energies of a given atom or a molecule M are confined to discrete values, so called "quantized energies". "Internal" energy is the total energy of M excluding its translational energy. Translational energy of M is equal to the kinetic energy of a free particle that has the mass of M, which is moving along a straight line with a constant speed. It is not quantized, and it does not play a role in absorption of light by M. Internal energy of an atom is the energy associated with the motion of its electrons around the nucleus. In molecules, there are additional contributions from rotational and vibrational motions. The "allowed" internal energies of M can be numbered as $E_1$, $E_2$, $E_3$, ... in increasing order of energy. These are called the "energy levels" of M. The lowest energy level, $E_1$, is called the "ground" level, and when M has this lowest possible energy, M is said to be in its ground state. All the other, higher energy levels are referred to as "excited" levels of M, and if M is in a state with one of these higher energies it is said to be in an excited state. There is one and only one ground level whereas there are infinitely many excited states of M. Each atom or molecule has its own characteristic set of energy levels.

When a sample of M molecules is exposed to a beam of monochromatic light with wavelength $\lambda$ there may be an energy exchange between the light and the M molecules. In its interaction with M, the monochromatic light beam is considered to consist of identical "photons", with all photons moving in parallel and along the direction of the beam with the speed of light. Each photon carries an energy given by $E_\mathrm{photon} = h\nu$, where h is Planck's constant and $\nu$ is the frequency of the light, related to its wavelength by: $\nu = c/\lambda$. Since $c$ is a constant, a given monochromatic light may be characterized by stating either $\lambda$ or $\nu$.

A molecule M may take energy from an external source such as light, thereby changing its initial energy level $E_\mathrm{initial}$ to a final level $E_\mathrm{final}$. For example, consider a case, where M is initially in its ground state with the lowest energy $E_1$. Its final energy ($E_\mathrm{final}$) can only be one of $E_2$, $E_3$, $E_4$, ... As a consequence, the amount of energy that M can accept from the external source is restricted to the values: $\Delta E = E_n - E_1$, where n=2, 3, ... Conservation of total energy requires that if M gains energy equal to one of these allowed $\Delta E$ values, the external source must provide precisely the same amount of energy.

When light is used as the energy source, a photon from the light beam may or may not be absorbed by an M molecule in the sample, depending on the frequency $\nu$ of light used. Only when the photon energy is exactly equal to one of the allowed $\Delta E$ values of M, the energy of the photon may be accepted by M. The fundamental condition for absorption of light by M is expressed as $h\nu = \Delta E$. This is a minimum requirement for absorption of light. Depending on whether M is an atom or molecule, and the nature of the energy levels involved in the transition, additional conditions called "selection rules" may have to be concurrently satisfied.

A closed test tube containing gaseous H atoms is irradiated by monochromatic light. Six experiments are done, differing from each other only by the wavelength, $\lambda$, of light employed.

$$\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|l|l|} \hline \text{Experiment No.} & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline \lambda\ \text{(nm)} & 129.6 & 121.6 & 101.6 & 97.25 & 94.97 & 94.11 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

Find out the experiments in which light will be absorbed by the H atoms in the sample, and describe the transitions involved.

Additional Data:

The allowed energy levels for the electron in a hydrogen atom are given (in SI units) by

$$E_\mathrm{n} = -\frac{R_\mathrm{H}}{\mathrm{n}^2},\qquad \mathrm{n} = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$$

where $R_\mathrm{H} = 2.1787\times10^{-18}\,\mathrm{J}$ is a constant; i.e. $R_\mathrm{H}$ is same for all values of the "n" quantum number. Assume that initially all of the hydrogen atoms in the sample are in their ground electronic states. Conservation of total energy is the only requirement for absorption of a photon by a H atom; i.e. there are no extra selection rules regarding the "n" quantum number.

problems.title: Rotational and vibrational energy levels of a diatomic molecule
problems.problem:
Problem 21. Rotational and vibrational energy levels of a diatomic molecule

Part A: Rotational Energies

Within the rigid-rotor approximation, the list of allowed rotational energies of a diatomic molecule, AB(g) in the gas phase, are given by:

$$E_\mathrm{rotation} = B\,J(J+1),\qquad J = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$

where $B = \dfrac{h^2}{8\pi^2 I}$ is a characteristic property of the molecule called the "rotational constant" of the molecule. The expression for $B$ is in SI units; $h$ is Planck's constant, and $I$ is the moment of inertia of the molecule defined by: $I = \mu R^2$, where R is the bond length, and $\mu$ is called the "reduced mass" of the diatomic molecule. The latter quantity is defined in terms of the masses, $m_A$ and $m_B$, of the atoms in the diatomic molecule AB.

$$\mu = \frac{m_A m_B}{m_A + m_B}$$

Theory indicates that the bond length, R, does not change when either A or B is replaced by other isotopes of the atoms A or B.

When a sample of gaseous molecules is exposed to microwave radiation, a molecule in the sample that is initially in a rotational energy level with $J = J_\mathrm{i}$ may absorb a photon, ending up in a higher energy level with $J = J_\mathrm{f}$. It may be shown that only those rotational transitions in which $J_\mathrm{f} = J_\mathrm{i} + 1$ can occur in absorption of light that changes the rotational state.

The rotational constant of the $\ce{^{12}C^{16}O}$ molecule has been experimentally determined as $B = 23.115\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The isotopic masses of the two atoms in this molecule are known: mass of $\ce{^{12}C}$ = 12 amu by definition, and that of $\ce{^{16}O}$ = 15.994915 amu. The longest wavelength of electromagnetic radiation that causes a transition between the rotational levels of $\ce{^{12}C^{16}O}$ molecule in a sample has been observed to be $\lambda = 0.25876\,\mathrm{cm}$.

a) What are the values of $J_\mathrm{i}$ and $J_\mathrm{f}$ for a molecule that absorbs a photon with a wavelength of 0.25876 cm?

b) Calculate the moment of inertia and the bond length of the carbon monoxide molecule.

c) Predict the values of the rotational constants, B, for each of the following three molecules: $\ce{^{12}C^{18}O}$, $\ce{^{13}C^{18}O}$, and $\ce{^{13}C^{16}O}$. (Additional data: masses of $\ce{^{18}O}$ = 17.999159 and $\ce{^{13}C}$ = 13.003355 amu.)

d) Calculate the longest wavelengths of microwave radiation that may be absorbed by each of $\ce{^{12}C^{18}O}$, $\ce{^{13}C^{18}O}$, and $\ce{^{13}C^{16}O}$ molecules.

Part B: Rotational plus Vibrational Energies

Within the harmonic oscillator approximation, the list of allowed vibrational energies of a diatomic molecule, AB(g) in the gas phase, are given by:

$$E_\mathrm{vibration} = \left(\mathrm{v} + \frac{1}{2}\right)\varepsilon,\qquad \mathrm{v} = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$

where $\varepsilon$ is a characteristic vibrational property of the molecule defined by

$$\varepsilon = \frac{h}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}}$$

In this expression $h$ is Planck's constant, $k$ is called the "force constant" of the molecule, and $\mu$ is the reduced mass of the diatomic molecule. In SI units, $\varepsilon$ is in joules, $k$ in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, and $\mu$ in kg. Theory shows that the force constant $k$ is independent of isotopic substitution in the molecule. When a sample of gas molecules is exposed to infrared (IR) radiation, a molecule in the sample that is initially in a vibrational energy level with $\mathrm{v} = \mathrm{v}_\mathrm{i}$ may absorb a photon, ending up in a higher energy vibrational level with $\mathrm{v} = \mathrm{v}_\mathrm{f}$. It may be shown that only those transitions in which $\mathrm{v}_\mathrm{f} = \mathrm{v}_\mathrm{i} + 1$ can occur in absorption of light that changes the vibrational state.

Absorption of light in the IR region changes not only the vibrational state, but also the rotational state; i.e., a simultaneous change in v and J is involved now. This is because the allowed vibrational plus rotational energies of a molecule are given by

$$E_\mathrm{rot.+vib.} = E_\mathrm{rotation} + E_\mathrm{vibration}$$

a) The force constant of the carbon monoxide molecule is $1901.9\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$. Find $\varepsilon$ in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ (to 4 significant figures) for each of the following isotopically related CO molecules:

i. $\ce{^{12}C^{16}O}$

ii. $\ce{^{12}C^{18}O}$

iii. $\ce{^{13}C^{18}O}$

iv. $\ce{^{13}C^{16}O}$

b) Find the wavelengths (to 4 significant figures) of IR radiation that may be absorbed by a molecule in making a transition from an initial state with (v,J) = (0,0) to a final state with (v,J) = (1,1) for each of the following isotopically related CO molecules:

i. $\ce{^{12}C^{16}O}$

ii. $\ce{^{12}C^{18}O}$

iii. $\ce{^{13}C^{18}O}$

iv. $\ce{^{13}C^{16}O}$

problems.title: Particle in a box: Cyanine dyes and polyenes
problems.problem:
Problem 22. Particle in a box: Cyanine dyes and polyenes

In quantum mechanics, particle in a one dimensional box model describes a particle moving between two impenetrable walls separated by a distance L. The allowed energies for a particle in one dimensional box are

$$E_\mathrm{n} = \frac{n^2 h^2}{8 m L^2}\qquad \text{for n = 1, 2, 3, ....}$$

where h is Plank's constant, m is the mass of the particle, and L is the box length.

The electronic absorption spectra of conjugated linear molecules can be simulated by the one dimensional particle in a box model. The delocalized $\pi$ electrons are treated as free electrons and they are distributed into the allowed energy levels obeying the Pauli Exclusion Principle. If the molecule contains N delocalized $\pi$ electrons, then the levels from n = 1 to n = N/2 are occupied in the ground state. Figure given below exhibits the energy levels for a conjugated molecule with N = 8.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2011-22-fig1.png

The energy levels for a system with 8 free electrons, N=8

The lowest energy electronic transition for such a system involves the excitation of one of the electrons in level n = 4 (N/2) to the level n = 5 (N/2 + 1). For this transition to be affected by light absorption, the wavelength $\lambda$ of light must be such that

$$\Delta E = \frac{hc}{\lambda},\qquad \Delta E = \frac{h^2}{8mL^2}\left[\left(\frac{N}{2}+1\right)^2 - \left(\frac{N}{2}\right)^2\right] = \frac{h^2}{8mL^2}(N+1)$$

Cyanine, pinacyanol, and dicarbocyanine shown below, are dye molecules that have a conjugated chain between the two ends.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2011-22-fig2.png

a) Draw the resonance forms of these three molecules.

b) The delocalized electrons can move freely along the central chain of the molecule, between the two terminal nitrogen atoms but not more than one bond length beyond the nitrogen atom. Particle in a box model can be applied to calculate the quantized energy levels of these delocalized electrons. The box length can be taken as the distance between the two nitrogen atoms, measured along the carbon-carbon bonds, plus one bond length on either side of each nitrogen atom. Determine the number N of delocalized electrons in each dye molecule.

c) Experimentally, the electronic absorption band maxima of these molecules, $\lambda_\mathrm{max}$, are recorded at 525, 605 and 705 nm for cyanine, pinacyanol and dicarbocyanine, respectively. Calculate $\Delta E$ for cyanine, pinacyanol and dicarbocyanine.

d) Predict the chain length where the electrons can move freely in these molecules.

e) As the conjugated $\pi$ electrons are free to move along the polyene carbon backbone, but not allowed to leave the molecule, they can be viewed as particles in a box defined by the carbon backbone of a linear polyene. The average carbon-carbon bond length in a hydrocarbon chain of alternating single and double bonds can be approximated to 140 pm. The length of carbon chain, the box length, is approximately $L = 2j\times140\,\mathrm{pm}$, where j is the number of double bonds in the polyene chain. Determine the number N of delocalized electrons and the box length L for 1,3-butadiene and 1,3,5-hexatriene.

f) Estimate the frequencies and wavelengths of the lowest electronic transition for 1,3-butadiene and 1,3,5-hexatriene.

problems.title: Radioactive decay
problems.problem:
Problem 23. Radioactive decay

Although twenty three isotopes of phosphorus are known (all the possible isotopes from $\ce{^{24}P}$ up to $\ce{^{46}P}$), only $\ce{^{31}P}$, with spin 1/2, is stable and is therefore present at 100% abundance. The half-integer spin and high abundance of $\ce{^{31}P}$ make it useful for nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopic studies of biomolecules, particularly DNA. Two radioactive isotopes of phosphorus have half-lives that make them useful for scientific experiments. $\ce{^{32}P}$ has a half-life of 14.3 days and $\ce{^{33}P}$ has a half-life of 25.3 days. Both radioisotopes of phosphorous, $\ce{^{32}P}$ and $\ce{^{33}P}$, are beta emitters and they decay as shown in the following nuclear reactions;

$$\ce{^{32}_{15}P -> ^{32}_{16}S} + \beta \qquad\qquad \ce{^{33}_{15}P -> ^{33}_{16}S} + \beta$$

$$\begin{array}{ll} \text{Isotope} & \text{isotopic masses (amu)} \\ \hline \ce{^{32}P} & 31.97390727 \\ \ce{^{33}P} & 32.9717255 \\ \ce{^{32}S} & 31.97207100 \\ \ce{^{33}S} & 32.97145876 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

a) Calculate the energy of $\beta$ particles emitted in the decay reactions of $\ce{^{32}P}$ and $\ce{^{33}P}$.

b) To shield beta radiation usually lead is used. However, secondary emission of X-rays takes place via a process known as Bremsstrahlung in the case of high energy $\beta$-emission, Therefore shielding must be accomplished with low density materials, e.g. Plexiglas, Lucite, plastic, wood, or water. During shielding of $\beta$-emission from $\ce{^{32}P}$, X-ray photons of $\lambda = 0.1175\,\mathrm{nm}$ are produced. Calculate the energy of X-ray photons in eV.

c) Find the mass of $\ce{^{32}P}$ which has activity of 0.10 Ci (1 Ci = $3.7\times10^{10}$ disintegration/s).

d) A sample containing both radioisotopes $\ce{^{32}P}$ and $\ce{^{33}P}$ has an initial activity of 9136.2 Ci. If the activity decreases to 4569.7 Ci after 14.3 days, calculate the $\ce{^{32}P}$/$\ce{^{33}P}$ ratio initially present in the sample.

problems.title: Enzyme-substrate interaction
problems.problem:
Problem 24. Enzyme-substrate interaction

In biological systems, it is very common for proteins such as enzymes or receptors to bind to multiple ligands or substrates at the same time. Binding of the first ligand usually affects the binding of the second ligand either positively or negatively. In this question, imagine that there is a protein $\mathbf{P}$ which can bind to two different ligands $\mathbf{L}$ and $\mathbf{MH^+}$ as shown in the figure given below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2011-24-fig1.png

For simplicity, assume that the binding of these two ligands are independent of each other; i.e. binding of the first ligand does not change the binding constant (complex formation constant) for the second ligand.

a) Equal volumes of $100\,\mathrm{\mu M}$ solutions of ligand $\mathbf{L}$ and protein $\mathbf{P}$ are mixed in a buffer solution of pH 9.50. The formation constant is $K_\mathrm{f}(\mathbf{P\text{-}L}) = 2.22\times10^{4}$. Calculate molar concentration for all the species present in this solution. What percentage of the protein $\mathbf{P}$ is complexed with the ligand $\mathbf{L}$?

b) Ligand $\mathbf{M}$ has a free amine group and only its protonated form, i.e. $\mathbf{MH^+}$, can bind to protein $\mathbf{P}$. What percentage of the ligand $\mathbf{M}$ is protonated at pH 9.50? $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}(\mathbf{MH^+}) = 10.00$.

c) Equal volumes of $100\,\mathrm{\mu M}$ solutions of ligand $\mathbf{M}$ and protein $\mathbf{P}$ are mixed in a buffer solution of pH 9.50. Calculate molar concentration for all the species present in this solution. What percentage of the protein $\mathbf{P}$ is complexed with the ligand $\mathbf{MH^+}$? $K_\mathrm{f}(\mathbf{P\text{-}MH^+}) = 5.26\times10^{5}$.

d) $100\,\mathrm{\mu L}$ of $100\,\mathrm{\mu M}$ protein $\mathbf{P}$, $50\,\mathrm{\mu L}$ of $200\,\mathrm{\mu M}$ of ligand $\mathbf{L}$ and $50\,\mathrm{\mu L}$ of $200\,\mathrm{\mu M}$ of ligand $\mathbf{M}$ are mixed in a buffer solution of pH 9.50. What percentage of the protein $\mathbf{P}$ is bound to (i) only $\mathbf{L}$, (ii) only $\mathbf{MH^+}$ and (iii) both $\mathbf{L}$ and $\mathbf{MH^+}$? Calculate molar concentration for all the species present in this solution.

problems.title: Amides
problems.problem:
Problem 25. Amides

The amide functional group is one of the most fundamental motifs found in chemistry and biology. Typical acyclic amides $\mathbf{1}$ are planar and stable, while the cyclic amides (bridgehead lactams) are unstable.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2011-25-fig1.png

2-Quinuclidone ($\mathbf{2}$), a typical example of bridgehead lactams, is very unstable due to the improper alignment of nitrogen lone pair and carbonyl group for $\pi$-interaction. As a consequence, the amide group resembles an amine as evidenced by the ease of salt formation. The organic synthesis of the tetrafluoroborate salt of 2-quinuclidone ($\mathbf{2}$) is a six-step synthesis starting from norcamphor ($\mathbf{3}$) and the final step being an azide-ketone Schmidt reaction.

a) The reaction of enantiopure norcamphor ($\mathbf{3}$) with m-chloroperbenzoic acid (m-CPBA) gives $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. $\mathbf{A}$ is formed as the major product in 78% yield, whereas the second isomer $\mathbf{B}$ is formed as the minor product. The reaction of $\mathbf{A}$ with lithium aluminum hydride results in the formation of $\mathbf{C}$, whereas the reduction of $\mathbf{B}$ yields optically inactive compound $\mathbf{D}$. Give the structures of the compounds $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$ and determine the absolute configurations (R/S) of the stereogenic carbon atoms in $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2011-25-fig2.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2011-25-fig3.png

b) Treatment of $\mathbf{C}$ with 1 equiv. of tosyl chloride (TsCl) yields the compound $\mathbf{E}$, which is converted into $\mathbf{F}$ by reaction with 1 equiv. of $\ce{NaN3}$ in dimethylformamide. Give the structures of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2011-25-fig4.png

c) $\mathbf{F}$ is subjected to pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) oxidation reaction to form the precursor $\mathbf{G}$ of the target compound. Finally, $\mathbf{G}$ is exposed to tetrafluoroboric acid ($\ce{HBF4}$). The target compound $\mathbf{H}$ is isolated as its tetrafluoroborate salt. Beside this product a second isomer $\mathbf{I}$ is formed as the minor product. Give the structures of $\mathbf{G}$, $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{I}$.

problems.problem:
Problem 26. NMR Spectroscopy

$^1$H-NMR Spectroscopy

The $^1$H-NMR spectroscopy allows the identification of hydrogen atoms in organic molecules. From the position of the signals (chemical shift) and the splitting of the signals, the type and connectivity of the hydrogen atoms can be recognized. Some characteristic hydrogen atom resonances are given below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2011-26-fig1.png

$^1$H-NMR Resonance ranges of typical functional groups in ppm relative to TMS

$^{13}$C-NMR Spectroscopy

The $^{13}$C-NMR is analogous to $^1$H-NMR and allows the identification of carbon atoms in organic molecules. The $^{13}$C-NMR spectrum of a given compound shows as many signals (singlets) as the number of the different carbon atoms. The relative intensities of all kinds of carbon (primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary) signals will be assumed to be equal. Some characteristic carbon resonances are given below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2011-26-fig2.png

$^{13}$C-NMR Resonance ranges of typical functional groups in ppm relative to TMS

Description of six isomeric (constitutional) compounds ($\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$) having the formula $\ce{C5H10O2}$ is as follows

problems.title: Cyclitols
problems.problem:
Problem 27. Cyclitols

Cyclitols have recently attracted a great deal of attention due to their diverse biological activities and their versatilities as synthetic intermediates. Polyhydroxy cyclohexanes, such as inositols, quercitols, and conduritols, belong to the family of cyclitols. These compounds can exist in a number of different stereoisomers; inositols, quercitols, and conduritols have 9, 16, and 6 possible stereoisomers, respectively. Cyclohexa-1,3-diene ($\mathbf{1}$) is an important key compound for the synthesis of versatile cyclitol derivatives. The total synthesis of isomeric cyclitols having the molecular formula $\ce{C6H12O4}$ is shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2011-27-fig1.png

• The reaction of cyclohexa-1,3-diene ($\mathbf{1}$) with singlet oxygen $\ce{O2}(^1\Delta_\mathrm{g})$, generated in situ by irradiation of oxygen molecule in the presence of a sensitizer, yields an unstable bicyclic compound $\mathbf{A}$. The reaction of $\mathbf{A}$ with $\ce{LiAlH4}$ in ether results in the formation of $\mathbf{B}$, whose $^{13}$C-NMR spectrum shows 3 resonances. One of them appears in the $sp^2$ region.

• Osmylation of $\mathbf{B}$ in the presence of an excess of NMO (N-morpholine oxide) (more than 2 equiv.) at room temperature in acetone/$\ce{H2O}$ leads to the isomeric mixture of $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ where the compound $\mathbf{C}$ is formed as the major product.

• Oxidation of $\mathbf{B}$ with m-chloroperbenzoic acid (m-CPBA) gives a diastereomeric mixture of $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$. Treatment of this mixture with $\ce{H2O}$ in the presence of a catalytic amount of $\ce{H2SO4}$ affords only compound $\mathbf{G}$ as a racemic mixture having the molecular formula of $\ce{C6H12O4}$.

a) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathbf{F}$, and $\mathbf{G}$ using dashed-wedged line notation to indicate the relative configurations.

b) Osmylation of $\mathbf{1}$ in the presence of an excess of NMO (N-morpholine oxide) (more than 2 equiv.) at room temperature in acetone/$\ce{H2O}$ leads to the formation of a diastereomeric mixture of $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ where the compound $\mathbf{H}$ is formed as the major product.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2011-27-fig2.png

Draw the structure of $\mathbf{H}$ using dashed-wedged line notation.

c) Reaction of cyclohexa-1,3-diene ($\mathbf{1}$) with 1 equiv. m-chloroperbenzoic acid (m-CPBA) gives a single product $\mathbf{I}$, which is reacted with $\ce{H2O}$ in the presence of a catalytic amount of $\ce{H2SO4}$ to provide $\mathbf{J}$ (There is no rearranged product). Osmylation of $\mathbf{J}$ in the presence of excess of NMO (N-morpholine oxide) (more than 1 equiv.) at room temperature in acetone/$\ce{H2O}$ leads to formation of isomeric $\mathbf{G}$ and $\mathbf{K}$.
