A synthetic polyribonucleotide consisting of only A and C in the ration of 1:5 was used as the messenger RNA (nucleotide residues are arranged randomly in the mRNA).

8. Determine the amino acid composition of the synthesized protein. What are the ratios between the amino acid residues in the protein?

The 3D structure of a tRNA is depicted in Fig. 2. There are two key regions: the CCA3’ terminus which is linked to the amino acid, and the anticodon exactly matching to the mRNA codon.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2013-22-fig2.png

Fig. 2. The 3D structure of a tRNA

9. A mutant $\mathrm{tRNA^{Tyr}}$ with anticodon specific to Ser codon (instead of Tyr codon) was introduced into the synthetic system described in i.8. What would be the resultant protein?

A biochemist specializing in protein chemistry described his discovery of a new mutant protein with Glu to His mutation to a molecular geneticist. The latter was very much surprised and advised the biochemist to do a double check.

10. Why did the geneticist express a doubt concerning the possibility of the above mutation? What mutation is more probable?

problems.title: Intriguing translation
problems.problem:
Problem 23. Intriguing translation

Borrow trouble for yourself, if that’s your nature, but don’t lend it to your neighbours

Joseph Rudyard Kipling

An acyclic oligopeptide $\mathbf{X}$ is composed of residues of two proteinogenic (canonical, encoded) amino acids $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$. The prevalent ionic form of $\mathbf{X}$ in aqueous solution at pH 4.7 consists of 25 atoms.

1. Determine the number of amino acid residues in $\mathbf{X}$. Use the information provided by the Wikipedia at either http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proteinogenic_amino_acid or http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amino_acid (hint: pay attention to the given $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ values of amino acid side groups).

2. How many individual peptides are in agreement with the above information?

Combustion of 1.000 g of $\mathbf{X}$ in an excess of oxygen followed by absorption of the reaction products with an excess of calcium hydroxide solution leads to formation of 3.273 g of precipitate. Quantitative transfer of the filtered precipitate into 10% aqueous hydrochloric acid results in liberation of 0.496 L of gas (STP – standard temperature and pressure).

3. Draw the stereochemical structure of $\mathbf{X}$ supporting it by appropriate calculations. Specify the absolute configuration (R or S) of chiral centers in $\mathbf{X}$.

4. Explain why $\mathbf{A}$, in contrast to $\mathbf{B}$, is not found as a free amino acid in living cells.

Addition of amino acid $\mathbf{A}$ to a growing polypeptide chain during translation is possible only in case of a certain motive ($\mathbf{Element\ X}$) in the secondary structure of messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA). Element $\mathbf{X}$ is a hairpin with two loops composed of approximately 60 nucleotides. Three such motives determining synthesis of glutathione peroxidase fragments in different organisms are schematically given hereunder (left to right: Poxviridae host cell infected with fowlpox, Poxviridae host cell infected with canarypox virus, and human cell).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2013-23-fig1.png

Each square box in the pictures stands for a nucleotide residue with one of the canonical nitrogen bases: adenine (A), guanine (G), uracil (U) or cytosine (C). Hydrogen bonds are formed according to the complementary principle (Chargaff’s rule) between the bases with boxes opposite to each other. The only exceptions are:

• Nucleotides with boxes filled grey: pairs are formed by either two pyrimidines or these are unusual pairs A-C or G-U

• Nucleotides with boxes filled black: pairs are formed by two purines

• Nucleotides located in the middle of the upper loops and visually close to each other due to way of the hairpins representation.

The mRNA triplet (codon) identical for all three sequences is circled.

Fragments of mRNA sequences belonging to different organisms are given in the hereunder Table in an arbitrary order. These sequences contain $\mathbf{Elements\ X}$ depicted in the above images.

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \text{№} & \text{Nucleotide sequence } (5'\rightarrow3') \\ \hline 1 & \text{…GCUGCUAAUGAAGAAAUGACUAUAAAUAGAUGGGUCAUGCCUGACACGCAAAG…} \\ \hline 2 & \text{…AGGCACUCAUGACGGCCUGCCUGCAAACCUGCUGGUGGGGCAGACCCGAAAAUCCCAC…} \\ \hline 3 & \text{…GACGAGAUAAUGAAGAAAUGGUCCUAAACAGAUGGGUCGUUCCUGACACCCCGG…} \end{array}$$

5. Fill the boxes in the images of all three structures, using one-letter symbols for nucleotides, and correlate the images with fragments of mRNA. Note that the sequences in the Table are bit longer than fragments corresponding to Elements X.

6. Draw the unusual base pair guanine-uracil found in the hairpin structure, and show the hydrogen bonds.

7. What is the role of the encircled codon in the case of poxoviruses (but not humans!)? Note that the subsequent triplet determines inclusion of the next amino acid into the growing polypeptide chain. Choose only one answer.

$$\begin{array}{c|l} \text{№} & \text{Answer} \\ \hline 1 & \text{It interacts with transport RNA of amino acid } \mathbf{A} \\ \hline 2 & \text{It determines termination of biosynthesis of the viral polypeptides on ribosome} \\ \hline 3 & \text{It forms a “foot” of the lower loop thus playing a purely structural role} \\ \hline 4 & \text{It is unable to interact with aminoacyl-tRNA. Thus the ribosome ignores it continuing} \\ & \text{addition of amino acids from the next codon} \\ \hline 5 & \text{It is an ordinary codon without any special features} \end{array}$$

RNA-containing viruses are characterized by frequent mutations allowing better adaption to changing environmental conditions.

8. For each of viral sequences, propose a mutation (single nucleotide substitution by another one), which presumably would not affect either translation or glutathione peroxidase functioning. Use the table of codons at http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_code.

problems.title: Unusual amino acids: search for new properties
problems.problem:
Problem 24. Unusual amino acids: search for new properties

If you want it to be done, do yourself

Mr. Zorg, “Fifth Element”

Search for natural compounds with anti-cancer potential is one of rapidly developing branches of modern science. Results of a recent research will be considered below.

$\mathbf{X}$ is a potential antineoplastic drug. In order to study mechanisms of its formation from different precursors, a mixture of three synthesized in the laboratory compounds $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ was administered orally to rats at doses of 63.5, 58.5 and $39.6\,\mathrm{\mu g}$ per kg of body weight, respectively. $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are stable $\alpha$-amino acids found in nature. Residue of one of these compounds is detected in proteins. Information about $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$ is summed up in the table below:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} & \text{Content, mass \%} & & & & \\ \text{Compound} & \text{C} & \text{H} & \text{O} & \text{Number of elements forming the compound} & \text{Number of chiral atoms} \\ \hline \mathbf{A} & 31.09 & 5.74 & 16.57 & 5 & 1 \\ \hline \mathbf{B} & 26.67 & 5.04 & 17.77 & 5 & 1 \\ \hline \mathbf{C} & 9.24 & 3.10 & \text{Is found in } \mathbf{C} & 4 & 0 \end{array}$$

It is also known that:

• $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ have molecular weight of less than 250 g/mole each;

• $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ contain C, H, N and O (not obligatory all these elements) in usual (native) isotopic ratios;

• The number of nitrogen atoms obeys the following inequality: $N_\mathrm{nitrogen}(\mathbf{B}) \ge N_\mathrm{nitrogen}(\mathbf{A})$.

1. Considering all possibilities for the number of nitrogen atoms in $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, determine their elemental composition.

2. If you failed to get the answer in i. 1, take advantage of an additional hint: $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ contain the same number of nitrogen atoms.

3. Draw all possible structures of $\mathbf{B}$ (without stereochemical details).

4. If the provided data is sufficient, indicate the absolute configuration (R or S) at the stereocenters of the structures in i.3.

During the experiment, samples of air exhaled by test animals were collected at definite time intervals. The following substances (in addition to other metabolites) were detected:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Detected gaseous compound} & \text{Density rel. } \ce{H2} & \text{Precursor compound} \\ \hline \mathbf{A1} & 53 & \mathbf{A} \\ \hline \mathbf{B1} & 53.5 & \mathbf{B} \\ \hline \mathbf{C1} & 56 & \mathbf{C} \end{array}$$

5. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{A1}$ and $\mathbf{B1}$, if it is known that $\mathbf{A1}$ has only identical atoms of hydrogen and does not contain $\pi$-bonds.

Formation of $\mathbf{C1}$ from $\mathbf{C}$ in rats proceeds via two enzymatic stages: reduction of $\mathbf{C}$ giving intermediate $\mathbf{X}$ is followed by its transformation into $\mathbf{C1}$.

6. Determine the structures of $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{C1}$, and antineoplastic metabolite $\mathbf{X}$, if it is known that $\mathbf{C}$ does not contain C–O bonds.

Formation of $\mathbf{A1}$ and $\mathbf{B1}$ from $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, respectively, also occurs in two steps, the latter being catalyzed by the same enzyme as was involved in transformation of $\mathbf{X}$ into $\mathbf{C1}$.

7. Determine the structures of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

8. Comment on the choice of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$ masses in the mixture administered to rats.

One of the amino acids discussed above can be found in proteins. It is also know that this amino acid does not have its own transfer RNA (tRNA).

9. Decide the residue of which amino acid ($\mathbf{A}$ or $\mathbf{B}$) can be found in proteins. From the variants listed below, choose one explaining how it appears in proteins.

$$\begin{array}{c|l} \text{№} & \text{Variant} \\ \hline 1 & \mathbf{A}\text{, because it is formed as a result of the one-step post-translational modification of a} \\ & \text{canonical amino acid} \\ \hline 2 & \mathbf{A}\text{, because it is structurally similar to a canonical amino acid, which sometimes leads to} \\ & \text{false insertion during translation} \\ \hline 3 & \mathbf{A}\text{, because it can be involved in protein biosynthesis at ribosomes without pre-formation of} \\ & \text{aminoacyl-tRNA} \\ \hline 4 & \mathbf{B}\text{, because it is structurally similar to a canonical amino acid, which sometimes leads to} \\ & \text{false insertion during translation} \\ \hline 5 & \mathbf{B}\text{, because it can be involved in protein biosynthesis at ribosomes without pre-formation of} \\ & \text{aminoacyl-tRNA} \end{array}$$

problems.title: Specific features of Clostridium metabolism
problems.problem:
Problem 25. Specific features of Clostridium metabolism

Imagination is more important than knowledge

Albert Einstein

As first shown in 1993, a type of acidogenic (producing acid) Clostridium bacteria is capable of glucose fermentation at certain conditions according to the hereunder total reaction equation:

$$\ce{5C6H12O6} + k\,\ce{H2O} \rightarrow l\mathbf{A} + m\mathbf{B} + n\mathbf{C} + 10\mathbf{D} \qquad (1),$$

where $k$, $l$, $m$, $n$ are integers.

$\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ are unbranched saturated carboxylic acids, $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ are gases (at STP) free of C–H bonds. The obtained mixture of $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ has the density rel. $\ce{H2}$ of 10.55.

1. Draw the structural formulae of $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$.

2. Mathematically prove that each of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ is a monocarboxylic acid.

3. Choose the appropriate l:m ratio for the reaction (1) from the variants given below.

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Variant} & l{:}m\ \text{ratios} \\ \hline \text{a.} & 1{:}1 \\ \hline \text{b.} & 1{:}2 \\ \hline \text{c.} & 1{:}3 \\ \hline \text{d.} & 1{:}4 \\ \hline \text{e.} & 1{:}5 \\ \hline \text{f.} & \text{Other ratio} \end{array}$$

Note that the fermentation products contain less carbon atoms than the starting compound.

4. Draw all possible variants of $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

Clostridium is capable of utilizing $\mathbf{D}$ in an unusual synthesis of acetyl-CoA (coenzyme A). This synthetic process is conjugated with cyclic metabolism of a vitamin derivative $\mathbf{Z}$ according to the following scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2013-25-fig1.png

$\mathbf{Z}_\mathbf{start}$ and $\mathbf{Z}_\mathbf{finish}$ contain the same number of nitrogen atoms. Molar fractions ($\chi$) of nitrogen and hydrogen are given below:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Compound} & \chi\,(\mathrm{H}),\% & \chi\,(\mathrm{N}),\% \\ \hline \mathbf{Z}_\mathbf{start} & 43.103 & 12.069 \\ \hline \mathbf{Z}_\mathbf{finish} & 41.818 & 12.727 \end{array}$$

5. Determine the total number of atoms in $\mathbf{Z}_\mathbf{start}$ and $\mathbf{Z}_\mathbf{finish}$, if it is known that these are less than 100 for both compounds.

Back in 1952, it was shown that cultivation of Clostridium thermoaceticum under anaerobic conditions in the presence of only non-radioactive $\mathbf{D}$ isotopologues (compounds $\mathbf{D1}$ and $\mathbf{D2}$) gives rise to formation of acetyl-CoA isotopologues with the equal mass fraction of N (12.08 %). Moreover, no traces of unlabeled acetyl-CoA ($M = 809.6\,\mathrm{g/mol}$) were detected in the experiment.

6. Work out the formulae of $\mathbf{D1}$, $\mathbf{D2}$, and $\mathbf{E}$, if all the coefficients in the reaction equation of acetyl-CoA formation are equal to 1.

Study of Clostridium transcriptome revealed a short (~100 nucleotides) coding sequence composed of only guanine (G) and cytosine (C) present in equimolar quantities and randomly positioned.

7. What is the ratio between the amino acid residues in the olygopeptide encoded by the sequence? Choose only one correct variant.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Variant} & \text{Ratio} & \text{Variant} & \text{Ratio} \\ \hline 1 & 1{:}1{:}2 & 4 & 1{:}1{:}4{:}2 \\ \hline 2 & 1{:}1{:}3 & 5 & 1{:}2{:}2{:}2{:}1 \\ \hline 3 & 1{:}1{:}1{:}1 & 6 & \text{Data insufficient to choose a sole variant} \end{array}$$

One of the proteins synthesized by Clostridium consists of 238 amino acid residues. Positions 230 to 234 (from N-terminus) were identified as Trp-His-Met-Glu-Tyr. A mutation affecting only one nucleotide occurred in the gene region corresponding to the above peptide fragment. As a result, the length of biosynthesized protein decreased up to 234 amino acid residues, whereas the sequence in positions 230 to 234 changed to Trp-Thr-Tyr-Gly-Val.

8. Write down the only possible original (before mutation) mRNA sequence encoding the above peptide fragment.

problems.title: Analysis of complex formation
problems.problem:
Problem 26. Analysis of complex formation

Antibodies $\mathbf{Ab}$ are proteins capable of selective binding with specific antigen $\mathbf{Ag}$ species (usually protein or polysaccharide), thus forming the so-called immune complex $\mathbf{Ab{*}Ag}$. The binding constant of the process $K_\mathrm{b}$ is very high (around $10^9$), however, binding is reversible.

$$\mathbf{Ab} + \mathbf{Ag} \rightleftarrows \mathbf{Ab} * \mathbf{Ag}$$

Despite of seeming complexity of biological objects, their functional features can often be analyzed by simply treating $\mathbf{Ag}$ and $\mathbf{Ab}$ as a ligand and complexing agent, respectively, in a common reaction of the $\mathbf{Ab{*}Ag}$ complex formation. Moreover, specific binding of proteins with other ligands (enzyme inhibitors, lipids, methal ions, etc.) can be analyzed by using the same approach.

1. Express $K_\mathrm{b}$ as a function of equilibrium concentrations [Ab], [Ag], [Ab*Ag] (consider that 1:1 Ab*Ag complex is formed).

Parameter $\bar{\mathbf{n}}$ is an average number of Ag molecules bound to one Ab molecule. In the case of only one binding site in Ab, $\mathbf{0} \le \bar{\mathbf{n}} \le \mathbf{1}$.

2. Express $\bar{\mathbf{n}}$ as a function of $K_\mathrm{b}$ and equilibrium concentration of the unbound ligand [Ag] for this simplest case of a single binding site in Ab molecule. Assume that $K_\mathrm{b}$ remains unchanged in course of the binding process. Draw schematically the $\bar{\mathbf{n}}$ vs [Ag] plot (“titration” curve of Ab with Ag).

For easier and reliable analysis, the titration curve may be linearized in special coordinates.

3. a) Plot the Experimental data A (see the table below) as $\mathbf{[Ab{*}Ag]/[Ag]}$ vs $\mathbf{[Ab{*}Ag]}$.

b) Express $\mathbf{[Ab{*}Ag]/[\ Ag]}$ as a function of $\mathbf{[Ab{*}Ag]}$.

c) One of the data points in the Experimental data A set has been determined incorrectly. Encircle this outlier in the plot.

d) Suggest a way for $K_\mathrm{b}$ determination from the plot analysis.

e) In the same plot, draw schematically a curve for ADP binding with another ligand, if the latter is characterized by a 10 times higher $K_\mathrm{b}$ value (as compared to that for $\mathbf{ADP{*}Mg^{2+}}$ complex formation).

Experimental data set A

ADP protein binds with $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ in 1:1 complex (single binding site, one $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ per site). $K_\mathrm{b}$ is not dependent on $\bar{n}$. ADP total concentration is kept constant at $80\,\mathrm{\mu M}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \ce{Mg^{2+}}\ \text{total concentration, } \mathrm{\mu M} & \text{Bound } \ce{Mg^{2+}}\ \text{concentration, } \mathrm{\mu M} \\ \hline 20.0 & 11.6 \\ \hline 50.0 & 26.0 \\ \hline 100 & 42.7 \\ \hline 150 & 52.8 \\ \hline 200 & 59.0 \\ \hline 300 & 61.1 \\ \hline 400 & 69.5 \end{array}$$

Some antibodies can only bind a single antigen molecule, whereas others bind two (or even more) antigen molecules. Maximal number of $\mathbf{Ag}$ molecules that can be bound to a single $\mathbf{Ab}$ is referred to as the $\mathbf{Ab}$ valence.

4. a) Derive an expression to be used for determination of the $\mathbf{Ab}$ valence from the plot analysis in coordinates $\mathbf{[Ab{*}Ag]/[Ag]}$ vs $\mathbf{[Ab{*}Ag]}$.

b) Plot the Experimental data B using the above coordinates. Determine the enzyme valence.

Experimental data set B

An enzyme binds with its inhibitor $\mathbf{I}$, the binding to different sites is independent, and $K_\mathrm{b}$ is the same. Enzyme total concentration is kept constant at $11\,\mathrm{\mu M}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \mathbf{I}\ \text{total concentration, } \mathrm{\mu M} & \text{Free (unbound) } \mathbf{I}\ \text{concentration, } \mathrm{\mu M} \\ \hline 5.2 & 2.3 \\ \hline 10.4 & 4.95 \\ \hline 15.6 & 7.95 \\ \hline 20.8 & 11.3 \\ \hline 31.2 & 18.9 \\ \hline 41.6 & 27.4 \\ \hline 62.4 & 45.8 \end{array}$$

$\mathbf{Ab}$ specimen often contains admixtures of other proteins not capable of binding with $\mathbf{Ag}$. Thus, a “known” total $\mathbf{Ab}$ concentration includes both functionally active antibodies and unreactive proteins.

5. a) Suggest a way for determination of the actual $\mathbf{Ab}$ concentration from the data analysis in coordinates $\mathbf{[Ab{*}Ag]/[Ag]}$ vs $\mathbf{[Ab{*}Ag]}$.

b) Does the ADP specimen contain any unreactive admixtures (Experimental data A)?

c) Why is it impossible to conclude unambiguously about the presence of unreactive admixtures in the enzyme specimen (Experimental data B)? What helpful (to determine the admixtures concentration) data is missing?

problems.title: Inorganic polymers: polyphosphates and polysilicones
problems.problem:
Problem 27. Inorganic polymers: polyphosphates and polysilicones

There are few elements capable of forming elementary substances with long-chain molecules.

1. Give 3 examples of elements, atoms of which can form elementary substance with linear (or close to linear) chain molecules (longer than 10 atoms).

Such long-chain elementary substances are not very common. However, many elements can form heteroatomic long-chain molecules. High-polymeric inorganic polyphosphates can serve as an example. These compounds are linear polymers composed of orthophosphate residues. The condensation reaction is one of the ways of such polymer formation.

2. Write down the condensation reaction giving diphosphate from the orthophosphate precursor.

3. In general, condensation reactions are reversible. Write down the equilibrium constant of the condensation reaction between phosphate oligomers, provided that polyphosphate species of different polymerization degree (including monomers) are not kinetically distinguishable. Assume that each (poly)phosphate ion present in the system bears only a single bound proton (i.e. may be represented as $\mathrm{P}_i\mathrm{O}_{3i}\mathrm{OH}^{(i+1)-}$).

4. Of the synthetic routes to long-chain polyphosphoric acids listed below, choose the most and the least energetically favorable. Take into account that the P–O bond is macroergic (for instance, $\Delta G^{\circ\prime}$ of adenosine triphosphate hydrolysis into adenosine diphosphate and inorganic phosphate is of about $–31\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$).

i) $\ce{H3PO4}$ condensation in 1 M aqueous solution at room temperature.

ii) $\ce{H3PO4}$ condensation in concentrated solution at room temperature.

iii) $\ce{H3PO4}$ condensation with dichlorophosphoric acid $\ce{HPO2Cl2}$ at elevated temperature.

In many cases, the equilibrium constant of a condensation reaction is too low to provide for high-molecular weight products. Other condensation reactions are too fast, which results in complexity of their control. To overcome these drawbacks, a procedure to form condensing species in situ from corresponding precursor has been developed.

5. Draw the structural formulae of isomeric compounds $\ce{C2Cl3H5Si}$ if none of these contains Si–H bonds. Write down a scheme of condensation of these compounds (in the presence of water) yielding a long-chain molecule. What are the atoms forming the main chain of the product?

6. Which of the isomeric compounds $\ce{C2Cl3H5Si}$ from i. 5 gives the linear condensation product only? Draw the structure of the final condensation product provided all the reactions are by 100% complete. What functional groups may be additionally found in the product due to incomplete hydration or condensation reactions?

7. Write down a reaction scheme illustrating appearance of branching in the main chain during condensation of another isomeric compound $\ce{C2Cl3H5Si}$ from i. 5 (that not chosen in i. 6).

problems.title: Polar and non-polar molecules
problems.problem:
Problem 1. Polar and non-polar molecules

In chemistry, a molecule is considered non-polar when its positive charge center and negative charge center coincide, i.e. the charge distribution is symmetrical in the molecule. On the other hand, when a molecule has two distinct centers for positive and negative charges, it is considered polar.

This charge distribution property is measured by a quantity called the dipole moment which is defined as the magnitude of the charge q and the distance $l$ between the charges:

$$\vec{\mu} = q\vec{l}$$

The dipole moment is a vector pointing from the positive charge center to the negative one.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2014-1-fig1.png

The dipole moment is often expressed in debyes (D). The relationship between debyes (D) and coulomb meters (C·m) in SI units is as follows: $1\,\mathrm{D} = 3.33\times10^{-30}\,\mathrm{C\cdot m}$.

1. The dipole moment is closely related to the molecular geometry. In order to calculate the net dipole moment $\mu$ of multi-atomic molecules, we can add the dipole moment vectors for individual bonds. In this case, an individual bond is considered to have its own dipole moment called the bond moment.

For a non-linear molecule with three atoms, ABC, the net dipole moment $\mu$ can be calculated by adding vectors in which $\vec{\mu}_1$ and $\vec{\mu}_2$ are the bond moments for AB and AC bonds, and $\alpha$ is the bond angle. Determine the general equation for calculating the net dipole moment.

2. The directions of the individual bond moments should be considered.

2.1 The molecule of $\ce{CO2}$ is linear. Calculate the net dipole moment $\mu$ of the molecule.

2.2 A non-linear molecule of $\ce{A2B}$ such as $\ce{H2S}$ has the net dipole moment $\mu \neq 0$. Determine $\mu$ for $\ce{H2S}$ if $\mu_\mathrm{SH} = 2.61\times10^{-30}\,\mathrm{C\cdot m}$ and the bond angle $\alpha = 92.0^\circ$.

3. The bond angle HCH in the formaldehyde molecule is determined experimentally to be approximately $120^\circ$; the bond moments for C-H and C-O bonds are $\mu_\mathrm{C-H} = 0.4\,\mathrm{D}$ and $\mu_\mathrm{C=O} = 2.3\,\mathrm{D}$, respectively.

3.1 Determine the orbital hybridization of C and O atoms, and plot the overlaps of orbitals in the formaldehyde molecule.

3.2 Calculate the net dipole moment ($\mu$) of the formaldehyde (D), given the order of the electronegativity as $\chi_\mathrm{O} > \chi_\mathrm{C} > \chi_\mathrm{H}$. (Hints: Electronegativity is the ability of an atom in a molecule to attract shared electrons to itself).

4. The dipole moments of water and dimethylether in gaseous state are determined as 1.84 D, and 1.29 D, respectively. The bond angle formed by two bond moments of O-H in the water molecule is $105^\circ$. The bond angle formed by two bond moments of O-C in the ether molecule is $110^\circ$.

Estimate the bond angle formed by the bond moments of O-H and C-O in the methanol molecule, given that the dipole moment of methanol molecule is 1.69 D. Assume that individual bond moments are unchanged in different molecules.

problems.title: Calculations of lattice energy of ionic compounds
problems.problem:
Problem 2. Calculations of lattice energy of ionic compounds

1. Lithium is the lightest metal and does not exist in pure form in nature due to its high reactivity to water, moisture, oxygen... Lithium readily forms ion with a 1+ charge when reacting with nonmetals. Write down the following chemical reactions at room temperature:

1.1 Lithium reacts with water.

1.2 Lithium reacts with halogens, e.g. $\ce{Cl2}$.

1.3 Lithium reacts with dilute sulfuric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid.

2. The change in enthalpy of a particular reaction is the same whether it takes place in one step or in a series of steps (Hess's law). Use the following data:

Sublimation enthalpy of $\ce{Li(s)}$, $\Delta_\mathrm{S}H = 159\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

Ionization energy of $\ce{Li(g)}$, $I = 5.40\,\mathrm{eV}$.

Dissociation enthalpy of $\ce{Cl2}$, $\Delta_\mathrm{D}H = 242\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

Electron affinity of $\ce{Cl(g)}$, $E = -3.84\,\mathrm{eV}$.

Formation enthalpy of $\ce{LiCl(s)}$, $\Delta_\mathrm{f}H = -402.3\,\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

$r_{\ce{Li+}} = 0.62\,\mathrm{Å}$; $r_{\ce{Cl-}} = 1.83\,\mathrm{Å}$; $N_\mathrm{A} = 6.02\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$.

2.1 Establish the Born-Haber cycle for lithium chloride crystal.

2.2 Calculate the lattice energy $U_\mathrm{o}$ ($\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$) using the Born-Haber cycle.

3. In practice, experimental data may be employed to calculate lattice energies in addition to the Born-Haber cycle. One of the semi empirical formulae to calculate the lattice energy $U_\mathrm{o}$ for an ionic compound, which was proposed by Kapustinskii, is as follows:

$$U_0 = -287.2\,\frac{Z_+ Z_- \sum \nu}{r_+ + r_-}\left(1 - \frac{0.345}{r_+ + r_-}\right)$$

where: $\nu$ is the number of ions in the empirical formula of ionic compound,

$r_+$ and $r_-$ are the radii of the cation and anion, respectively, in Å,

$Z_+$ and $Z_-$ are cation and anion charges, respectively,

$U_0$ is the lattice energy, in $\mathrm{kcal\cdot mol^{-1}}$.

Use the Kapustinskii empirical formula to calculate $U_\mathrm{o}$ (in $\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$) of LiCl crystal, given that $1\,\mathrm{cal} = 4.184\,\mathrm{J}$.

4. Based on the results of two calculation methods in sections 2 and 3, choose the appropriate box:

• ☐ According to the Born-Haber cycle and Kapustinskii empirical formula for lithium chloride crystal structure, both methods are close to the experimental value.

• ☐ Only the calculated result of the Born-Haber cycle is close to the experimental value.

• ☐ Only the calculated result of the Kapustinskii empirical formula is close to the experimental value.

Data: Given the experimental value of lattice energy for LiCl is $849.04\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

5. In the formation of LiCl crystal, it is found out that the radius of lithium cation is smaller than that of chloride anion. Thus, the lithium ions will occupy the octahedral holes among six surrounding chloride ions. Additionally, the body edge length of LiCl cubic unit cells is 5.14 Å. Assume that $\ce{Li+}$ ions just fit into octahedral holes of the closest packed chloride anions.

5.1 Calculate the ionic radii for the $\ce{Li+}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$ ions.

5.2 Compare the calculated (theoretical) radii with the experimental radii given below, and choose the appropriate box:

• ☐ Both calculated radii of lithium and chloride ions are close to the experimental values.

• ☐ Only the calculated radius of lithium ion is close to the experimental value

• ☐ Only the calculated radius of chloride ion is close to the experimental value.

The experimental radii of $\ce{Li+}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$ are 0.62 Å and 1.83 Å, respectively.

problems.title: A frog in a well
problems.problem:
Problem 3. A frog in a well

The energy levels of an electron in a one-dimensional box are given by:

$$E_\mathrm{n} = n^2\frac{h^2}{8mL^2} \qquad \text{n: 1, 2, 3…}$$

in which $h$ is the Planck's constant, $m$ is the mass of the electron, and L is the length of the box.

1. The $\pi$ electrons in a linear conjugated neutral molecule are treated as individual particles in a one-dimensional box. Assume that the $\pi$ electrons are delocalized in the molecular length with the total number of N $\pi$ electrons and their arrangement is governed by the principles of quantum mechanics.

1.1 Derive the general expression for $\Delta E_\mathrm{LUMO-HOMO}$ when an electron is excited from the HOMO to the LUMO.

1.2 Determine the wavelength $\lambda$ of the absorption from the HOMO to the LUMO.

2. Apply the model of $\pi$ electrons in a one-dimensional box for three dye molecules with the following structures (see the structural formula). Assume that the $\pi$ electrons are delocalized in the space between the two phenyl groups with the length L is approximately equal to $(2k + 1)(0.140)\,\mathrm{nm}$, in which k is the number of the double bonds.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2014-3-fig1.png

2.1 Calculate the box length L (Å) for each of the dyes.

2.2 Determine the wavelength $\lambda$ (nm) of the absorption for the molecules of the investigated dyes.

3. Recalculate the box length L (Å) for the three dye molecules, assuming that the $\pi$ electrons are delocalized over the linear conjugated chain which is presented as a line plotted between the two phenyl groups (see the structural formula). The bond angle C – C – C is $120^\circ$ and the average length of C – C bond is 0.140 nm.

4. Give the following experimental data on the wavelength $\lambda$ of absorption.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Substance} & \textbf{BD} & \textbf{HT} & \textbf{OT} \\ \hline \lambda\ (\mathrm{nm}) & 328.5 & 350.9 & 586.1 \end{array}$$

4.1 Determine the box length L (Å) of the linear conjugated chain for each of the three investigated dyes.

4.2 Tabulate the values of the box length L for the dyes calculated above by the three different methods, denoted as 1, 2, and 3. Choose the method which is the most fit to the experimental data.

problems.title: Particles in 2, 3 - Dimensional Box
problems.problem:
Problem 4. Particles in 2, 3 - Dimensional Box

1. In Problem 3, the energy E of particle in one- dimensional box is calculated as:

$$E = n^2\frac{h^2}{8\,mL^2}$$

where $h$ is Planck's constant; $m$ is the mass of the particle; L is the box length; $n$ is the quantum number, $n$ = 1, 2, 3…

An electron in a 10 nm one-dimensional box is excited from the ground state to a higher energy level by absorbing a photon of the electromagnetic radiation with a wavelength of $1.374\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m}$.

1.1 What is the energy gap ($\Delta E$) of the two mentioned states?

1.2 Determine the final energy state for this transition.

2. The treatment of a particle in a one- dimensional box can be extended to a two-dimensional box of dimensions $L_\mathrm{x}$ and $L_\mathrm{y}$ yielding the following expression for energy:

$$E = \frac{h^2}{8\,m}\left(\frac{n_\mathrm{x}^2}{L_\mathrm{x}^2} + \frac{n_\mathrm{y}^2}{L_\mathrm{y}^2}\right)$$

The two quantum numbers independently can assume only integer values. Consider an electron confined in a two-dimensional box that is $L_\mathrm{x} = 8.00\,\mathrm{nm}$ in the x direction and $L_\mathrm{y} = 5.00\,\mathrm{nm}$ in the y direction.

2.1 What are the quantum numbers for the first three allowed energy levels? Write the first three energy, $E_\mathrm{xy}$, in order of increasing energy?

2.2 Calculate the wavelength of light necessary to move an electron from the first excited state to the second excited one.

3. Similarly, the treatment of a particle in a one-dimensional box can be extended to a rectangular box of dimensions $L_\mathrm{x}$, $L_\mathrm{y}$, and $L_\mathrm{z}$, yielding the following expression for energy:

$$E = \frac{h^2}{8\,m}\left(\frac{n_\mathrm{x}^2}{L_\mathrm{x}^2} + \frac{n_\mathrm{y}^2}{L_\mathrm{y}^2} + \frac{n_\mathrm{z}^2}{L_\mathrm{z}^2}\right)$$

The three quantum numbers $n_\mathrm{x}$, $n_\mathrm{y}$, and $n_\mathrm{z}$ independently can assume only integer values. An oxygen molecule is confined in a cubic box of volume $8.00\,\mathrm{m^3}$. Assume that the molecule has an energy of $6.173\times10^{-21}\,\mathrm{J}$; temperature $T = 298\,\mathrm{K}$.

3.1 What is the value of $n = (n_x^2 + n_y^2 + n_z^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}$ for this molecule?

In a rough approximation to estimate the energy gap of this system, assume that the two closest energy levels correspond to n and n + 1.

3.2 What is the energy separation between the levels n and n + 1?

4. In quantum mechanics, an energy level is said to be degenerate if it corresponds to two or more different measurable states of a quantum system. Consider a particle in a cubic box. What is the degeneracy of the level that has energy 21/3 times that of the lowest level?

problems.title: Tug of war
problems.problem:
Problem 5. Tug of war

"Tug of war is a sport that directly pits two teams against each other in a test of strength. This is also a traditional game of Vietnamese people"

The following table gives the standard molar Gibbs energy at different temperatures for the reaction (1) below:

$$\ce{SO3(g) <=> SO2(g) + 1/2 O2(g)} \qquad (1)$$

$$\begin{array}{l|ccccc} T/^\circ\mathrm{C} & 527 & 552 & 627 & 680 & 727 \\ \hline \Delta_\mathrm{r}G^\circ/\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}} & 21.704 & 20.626 & 14.210 & 9.294 & 4.854 \end{array}$$

1. Use the Van Hoff's equation to estimate the $\ln K_\mathrm{p1}$ at each temperature.

2. Plot $\ln K_\mathrm{p1}$ against $1/T$ to determine the value of $\Delta_\mathrm{r}H^\circ$ in $\mathrm{kJ\cdot mol^{-1}}$ assuming that $\Delta_\mathrm{rnx}H^\circ$ does not vary significantly over the given temperature range.

3. Using the best-fit line to plot a $\ln K_\mathrm{p1}$ versus $1/T$, determine the $K_\mathrm{p2}$ for the following reaction (2) at $651.33\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$:

$$\ce{2SO3(g) <=> 2SO2(g) + O2(g)} \qquad (2)$$

4. An amount of 15.19 g of iron (II) sulfate was heated in an evacuated 1.00 L container to $651.33\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, in which the following reactions take place:

$$\ce{FeSO4(s) <=> Fe2O3(s) + SO3(g) + SO2(g)} \qquad (3)$$

$$\ce{2SO3(g) <=> 2SO2(g) + O2(g)} \qquad (4)$$

When the system has reached equilibrium, the partial pressure of oxygen is of 21.28 mmHg. Calculate the equilibrium pressure of the gases and the value of $K_\mathrm{p3}$ for the reaction (3) at equilibrium.

5. Calculate the percentage of $\ce{FeSO4}$ decomposed?

problems.title: Radiochemistry
problems.problem:
Problem 6. Radiochemistry

Zircon ($\ce{ZrSiO4}$) is a mineral found abundantly in placer deposits located in the central coast of Vietnam. Besides being widely utilized in the ceramic industry, zircon is also used as a raw material for the manufacture of zircaloy which is used to build fuel rods that hold the uranium dioxide ($\ce{UO2}$) fuel pellets in nuclear reactors. Zircon ore contains a trace amount of uranium, and it is not a viable source of uranium in practice. However, zircon crystals make a perfect storage medium to avoid the loss of uranium and lead (Pb) isotopes because of its stable crystal structure. This allows developing uranium-lead dating method.

There are 3 naturally occurring decay series:

• The thorium series begins with $\ce{^{232}Th}$ and ends up with $\ce{^{208}Pb}$.

• The uranium series (also referred to as the uranium-radium series) is headed by $\ce{^{238}U}$. The half-life ($t_{1/2}$) of $\ce{^{238}U}$ is $4.47\times10^{9}$ years.

• The actinium series is headed by $\ce{^{235}U}$ with the half-life of $7.038\times10^{8}$ years.

Four stable isotopes of Pb exist in nature: $\ce{^{204}Pb}$, $\ce{^{206}Pb}$, $\ce{^{207}Pb}$, and $\ce{^{208}Pb}$. The natural abundance of each isotope is shown in the following table.

$$\begin{array}{cccc} \ce{^{204}Pb} & \ce{^{206}Pb} & \ce{^{207}Pb} & \ce{^{208}Pb} \\ \hline 1.4 & 24.1 & 22.1 & 52.4 \end{array}$$

An analysis of a zircon mineral sample gives the following mass ratios of U and Pb isotopes:

$$m(\ce{^{238}U}) : m(\ce{^{235}U}) : m(\ce{^{206}Pb}) : m(\ce{^{204}Pb}) = 99.275 : 0.721 : 14.30 : 0.277$$

1. Indicate the stable isotope of Pb which is not involved in the above decay series.

2. Determine the mass ratio of $\ce{^{238}U}$ to $\ce{^{235}U}$ when the zircon mineral was first formed. Assume that the mineral already contained natural Pb right at the onset of its formation.

3. Production of uranium from low-grade will encounter many difficulties, notably large concentration of impurities and low concentrations of uranium in leach solutions. Various technological advances have been applied to overcome the aforementioned problems; these include fractional precipitation, liquid-liquid extraction, or ion exchange methods.

In an experiment to extract uranium from sample of low uranium content using diluted $\ce{H2SO4}$, in the preliminary treated leach solutions, the concentration of uranyl sulfate ($\ce{UO2SO4}$) is 0.01 M and the concentration of iron(III) sulfate ($\ce{Fe2(SO4)3}$) goes up to 0.05 M. The separation of uranium from iron and other impurities can be carried out by the fractional precipitation method.

Calculate the pH necessary to precipitate 99% of $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ without losing uranium ions. Assume that the adsorption of uranium onto $\ce{Fe(OH)3}$ is negligible. Under the experimental conditions, the solubility product values for $\ce{UO2(OH)2}$ and $\ce{Fe(OH)3}$ are $1.0\times10^{-22}$ and $3.8\times10^{-38}$, respectively.

4. One of the proper methods to obtain a rich uranium solution is the liquid-liquid extraction with the organic phase containing the extracted agent of tributylphosphate (TBP) diluted in kerosene. When extracting uranium in the form of uranyl nitrate ($\ce{UO2(NO3)2}$) under appropriate conditions, the relationship between the concentrations of uranium in water and organic phases is given by:

$$\text{Distribution coefficient: } D = \frac{C_{org.}}{C_{aq}} = 10$$

where: $C_\mathrm{org}$ and $C_\mathrm{aq}$ are the equilibrium concentrations (M) of $\ce{UO2(NO3)2}$ in organic and aqueous phases, respectively.

Calculate the mole percentage (in comparison with the initial concentration) of $\ce{UO2(NO3)2}$ remaining in the aqueous phase after extracting 1.0 L of the solution (with an initial concentration of 0.01 M) with 500 mL of organic solvent.

5. Propose a scheme to extract 96% of $\ce{UO2(NO3)2}$ from 1.0 L of the aqueous phase into 500 mL of the organic phase. Assume that the distribution coefficient remains constant throughout the extraction process (D = 10).

problems.title: Applied thermodynamics
problems.problem:
Problem 7. Applied thermodynamics

1. In applied thermodynamics, Gibbs free energy plays an important role and can be calculated according to the following expression:

$$\Delta G^\circ_{298} = \Delta H^\circ_{298} - T\Delta S^\circ_{298}$$

$\Delta G^\circ_{298}$ - standard free energy change

$\Delta H^\circ_{298}$ - standard enthalpy change

$\Delta S^\circ_{298}$ - standard entropy change

The burning of graphite is represented by two reactions:

$$\ce{C (graphite) + 1/2 O2(g) -> CO(g)} \qquad (1)$$

$$\ce{C (graphite) + O2(g) -> CO2(g)} \qquad (2)$$

The dependence of $\Delta H^\circ$, $\Delta S^\circ$ on temperature is as follows:

Reaction (1): $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{T}(1)\ (\mathrm{J\cdot mol^{-1}}) = -112298.8 + 5.94T$; $\Delta S^\circ_\mathrm{T}(1)\ (\mathrm{J\cdot K^{-1}\cdot mol^{-1}}) = 54.0 + 6.21\ln T$

Reaction (2): $\Delta H^\circ_\mathrm{T}(2)\ (\mathrm{J\cdot mol^{-1}}) = -393740.1 + 0.77T$; $\Delta S^\circ_\mathrm{T}(2)\ (\mathrm{J\cdot K^{-1}\cdot mol^{-1}}) = 1.54 - 0.77\ln T$

Based on the above data:

1.1 Derive the expression for the Gibbs free energy as a function of temperature, $\Delta G^\circ_\mathrm{T} = f(T)$ for each reaction.

1.2 Predict the changes of $\Delta G^\circ_\mathrm{T}$ with an increase in temperature.

2. Assume that at $1400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, during the course of reactions (1) and (2), CO gas might continue to react with $\ce{O2}$ to form the final product $\ce{CO2}$.

2.1 Write down the reaction (3) for the formation of $\ce{CO2}$ from CO gas.

2.2 Calculate $\Delta G^\circ_\mathrm{T}(3)$.

2.3 Determine the equilibrium constant $K_\mathrm{p}$ for reaction (3) at the given temperature.

3. In an experiment, NiO powder and CO gas were placed in a closed container which was then heated up to $1400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. When the system reached equilibrium, there were four species present: $\ce{NiO(s)}$, $\ce{Ni(s)}$, $\ce{CO(g)}$ and $\ce{CO2(g)}$. The mole percentages of CO and $\ce{CO2}$ are 1 % and 99 %, respectively, and the pressure of the system is 1.0 bar ($10^5$ Pa).

3.1 Write down the reactions in the above experiment.

3.2 Based on the experimental results and the above thermodynamic data, calculate the pressure of $\ce{O2}$ in the equilibrium with NiO and Ni at $1400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

problems.title: Complex compounds
problems.problem:
Problem 8. Complex compounds

Ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA) is used as a reagent to titrate the metal ions in the complexometric titration.

EDTA is a tetraprotic acid, abbreviated as $\ce{H4Y}$, with the structure:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2014-8-fig1.png

As EDTA is sparingly soluble in water, a more soluble sodium form, $\ce{Na2H2Y}$, is usually used and $\ce{H2Y^{2-}}$ is commonly known as EDTA. EDTA forms strong 1:1 complexes with most metal ions $\ce{M^{n+}}$.

1. How many atoms of an EDTA molecule are capable of binding with the metal ion upon complexation?

1.1 Check in the appropriate box.

• ☐ 2

• ☐ 4

• ☐ 6

• ☐ 8

1.2 Draw the structure of the complex of a metal ion $\ce{M^{2+}}$ with EDTA.

2. Complexation reaction between $\ce{Y^{4-}}$ form of EDTA and metal ion $\ce{M^{n+}}$ has a large formation constant (stability constant) $\beta$:

$$\ce{M^{n+} + Y^{4-} <=> MY^{(4-n)-}} \qquad \beta = \frac{[\mathrm{MY}^{(4-n)-}]}{[\mathrm{M}^{n+}][\mathrm{Y}^{4-}]}$$

Besides complexation reaction between $\ce{Y^{4-}}$ form of EDTA and metal ion $\ce{M^{n+}}$, other processes in the solution also develop such as formation of hydroxo complexes of the metal ion, acid-base equilibrium of $\ce{H2Y^{2-}}$… To account for such processes conditional formation constant $\beta'$ is used for the calculations. $\beta'$ is determined from $\beta$ as the following expression:

$$\beta' = \beta.\alpha_{\mathrm{M}^{n+}}.\alpha_{\mathrm{Y}^{4-}}$$

where: $\alpha_{\mathrm{Y}^{4-}}$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{M}^{n+}}$ are fractions of $\ce{Y^{4-}}$ ($\alpha_{\mathrm{Y}^{4-}} = \frac{[\mathrm{Y}^{4-}]}{[\mathrm{Y}]'}$) and free metal ion $\ce{M^{n+}}$ ($\alpha_{\mathrm{M}^{n+}} = \frac{[\mathrm{M}]}{[\mathrm{M}]'}$), with $[\mathrm{Y}]'$ and $[\mathrm{M}]'$ being the total concentrations of all forms of $\ce{Y^{4-}}$ and $\ce{M^{n+}}$, excluding $\ce{MY^{(4-n)-}}$. Given that: $\ce{H4Y}$ has $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a1} = 2.00$; $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a2} = 2.67$; $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a3} = 6.16$; and $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a4} = 10.26$ (p$K_\mathrm{a}$ values for $\ce{H5Y+}$ and $\ce{H6Y^{2+}}$ are ignored).

$$\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{s}(\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2})} = 10.95; \quad \log\beta_{\mathrm{MgY}^{2-}} = 8.69$$

$\ce{Mg^{2+} + H2O <=> MgOH+ + H+}$ $\quad {}^{*}\beta = 1.58\times10^{-13}$; ($\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} = -\log K_\mathrm{a}$; $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{s} = -\log K_\mathrm{s}$)

In a typical experiment, 1.00 mL of 0.10 M $\ce{MgCl2}$ solution and 1.00 mL of 0.10 M $\ce{Na2H2Y}$ solution are mixed together. pH of the resulting solution is adjusted to 10.26 by an $\ce{NH3/NH4+}$ buffered solution.

2.1 Calculate conditional formation constant ($\beta'$) of the $\ce{MgY^{2-}}$ complex at pH = 10.26 given that acid-base equilibrium of $\ce{H2Y^{2-}}$ and formation of mononuclear hydroxo complex of $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ occur in the solution.

2.2 Does the $\ce{Mg(OH)2}$ precipitate in this experiment? Check in the appropriate box.

• ☐ Precipitation

• ☐ No precipitation

3. In order to titrate metal ions by EDTA, the conditional formation constant ($\beta'$) of the complex metal – EDTA ($\ce{MY^{(4-n)-}}$) must be large enough, usually $\beta' \geq 1.00\times10^{8}$ - $1.00\times10^{9}$. To determine the concentrations of $\ce{Mn^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Hg^{2+}}$ in an analytical sample, two experiments are carried out.

Experiment 1: Add 25.00 mL of 0.040 M EDTA solution to 20.00 mL of the analytical solution. Adjust the pH of the resulting solution to 10.50. Titrate the excess EDTA with a suitable indicator and 12.00 mL of 0.025 M $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ solution is consumed.

Experiment 2: Dissolve 1.400 gram of KCN into 20.00 mL of the analytical solution (assuming that the volume is unchanged upon dissolution) and then add 25.00 mL of 0.040 M EDTA solution. Titrate the excess EDTA in the resulting mixture at the pH of 10.50; 20.00 mL of 0.025 M $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ solution is consumed.

3.1 Prove that: in the experiment 2, $\ce{Hg^{2+}}$ cannot be determined by titration with EDTA in the presence of KCN in solution (or $\ce{Hg^{2+}}$ is masked in the complex form of $\ce{Hg(CN)4^{2-}}$).

3.2 Write down chemical equations for the reactions in the two experiments and calculate molar concentrations of $\ce{Mn^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Hg^{2+}}$ in the analytical solution. Given that: $\log\beta_{\mathrm{HgY}^{2-}} = 21.80$; $\log\beta_{\mathrm{Hg(CN)}_4^{2-}} = 38.97$; $\mathrm{p}K_{a(\mathrm{HCN})} = 9.35$

(Other processes of $\ce{Hg^{2+}}$ are ignored; the p$K_\mathrm{a}$ values of $\ce{H4Y}$ are provided in question 2).

4. In the titration of polyprotic acids or bases, if the ratios of consecutive dissociation constants exceed $1.00\times10^{4}$, multiple titrations are possible with an error less than 1%. To ensure the allowed error, only acids or bases with equilibrium constants larger than $1.00\times10^{-9}$ can be titrated. To find the end-point, pH range of the indicator must be close to that of the equivalence point ($\mathrm{pH_{EP}}$); the point at which the stoichiometric amounts of analyte and titrant has reacted. Titrate 10.00 mL of 0.25 M $\ce{Na2H2Y}$ solution by 0.20 M NaOH solution in a typical experiment.

4.1 Write down the chemical equation for the titration reaction.

4.2 Determine the value of $\mathrm{pH_{EP}}$.

4.3 Choose the most suitable indicator (check in the appropriate box) for the above titration from the following: bromothymol blue (pH = 7.60); phenol red (pH = 8.20); phenolphtalein (pH = 9.00).

• ☐ Bromothymol blue

• ☐ Phenol red

• ☐ Phenolphtalein

4.4 Titration error $q$ defined as the difference between the titrant amount added and the titrant amount needed to reach the equivalence point is expressed as:

$$q = \frac{C_{NaOH}V_1 - C_{NaOH}V_2}{C_{NaOH}V_2}\times100\% = \frac{V_1 - V_2}{V_2}\times100\%$$

where $C_\mathrm{NaOH}$ is the NaOH concentration; $V_1$: End-point volume of NaOH; $V_2$: equivalence point volume of NaOH.

Calculate the consumed volume of NaOH solution and the titration error if the final pH is 7.60.

problems.title: Lead compounds
problems.problem:
Problem 9. Lead compounds

1. Consider the following nuclide: $\ce{^{209}Bi}$(I), $\ce{^{208}Pb}$(II), $\ce{^{207}Pb}$(III), $\ce{^{206}Pb}$(IV). Which nuclide is the last member of the decay series for $\ce{^{238}U}$? Check in the appropriate box.

• ☐ (I)

• ☐ (II)

• ☐ (III)

• ☐ (IV)

2. There are three natural decay series. They begin with Th-232(I), U-238(II), U-235(III) and end with Pb-208, Pb-206, Pb-207. In which decay chain are there 6 $\alpha$ decays and 4 $\beta$ decays? Choose the correct answer by checking in the appropriate box.

• ☐ (I)

• ☐ (II)

• ☐ (III)

• ☐ None

3. $\ce{Pb(NO3)2}$ solution is slowly added into 20.00 mL of a mixture consisting of 0.020 M $\ce{Na2SO4}$; $5.0\times10^{-3}$ M $\ce{Na2C2O4}$; $9.7\times10^{-3}$ M KI; 0.05 M KCl and 0.0010 M $\ce{KIO3}$. When the bright yellow precipitate of $\ce{PbI2}$ begins to form, 21.60 mL of $\ce{Pb(NO3)2}$ solution is consumed.

3.1 Determine the order of precipitation?

3.2 Calculate the concentration of $\ce{Pb(NO3)2}$ solution?

Given that: $\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{s}(\mathrm{PbSO_4})} = 7.66$; $\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{s}(\mathrm{Pb(IO_3)_2})} = 12.61$; $\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{s}(\mathrm{PbI_2})} = 7.86$; $\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{s}(\mathrm{PbC_2O_4})} = 10.05$; $\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{s}(\mathrm{PbCl_2})} = 4.77$. (Other processes of the ions are ignored).

4. One of the common reagents to detect $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ species is $\ce{K2CrO4}$, giving yellow precipitate $\ce{PbCrO4}$, which is soluble in excess of NaOH. The solubility of $\ce{PbCrO4}$ depends not only on pH but also on the presence of coordinating species... Given that the solubility of $\ce{PbCrO4}$ in 1 M acetic acid solution is $s = 2.9\times10^{-5}$ M, calculate the solubility product $K_\mathrm{sp}$ of $\ce{PbCrO4}$.

$\mathrm{p}K_{a(\mathrm{CH_3COOH})} = 4.76$; $\lg\beta_{\mathrm{Pb(CH_3COO)^+}} = 2.68$; $\lg\beta_{\mathrm{Pb(CH_3COO)_2}} = 4.08$; $\mathrm{p}K_{a(\mathrm{HCrO_4^-})} = 6.5$

$\ce{Pb^{2+} + H2O <=> PbOH+ + H+}$ $\quad {}^{*}\beta = 10^{-7.8}$

$\ce{Cr2O7^{2-} + H2O <=> 2CrO4^{2-} + 2H+}$ $\quad K = 10^{-14,64}$

5. Lead-acid battery, commonly known as lead battery consists of two lead plates a positive electrode covered with a paste of lead dioxide and a negative electrode made of sponge lead. The electrodes are submersed in an electrolyte consisting of water and sulfuric acid $\ce{H2SO4}$. Write the chemical equations for processes on each electrode, overall reaction as the battery discharges and the cell diagram.

Given that: $E^0_{\mathrm{Pb^{2+}/Pb}} = -0.126\,\mathrm{V}$; $E^0_{\mathrm{PbO_2/Pb^{2+}}} = 1.455\,\mathrm{V}$; $\mathrm{p}K_{a(\mathrm{HSO_4^-})} = 2.00$; $\mathrm{p}K_{s(\mathrm{PbSO_4})} = 7.66$; at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$: $2.303\frac{RT}{F} = 0.0592\,\mathrm{V}$

6. Calculate:

6.1 $E^0_{\mathrm{PbSO_4/Pb}}$; $E^0_{\mathrm{PbO_2/PbSO_4}}$

6.2 The potential V of the lead battery if $C_{\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \approx 1.8$ M.

problems.title: Applied electrochemistry
problems.problem:
Problem 10. Applied electrochemistry

1. Reduction-oxidation reactions have played an important role in chemistry due to their potential to be valuable sources of energy for technology and life. Write down chemical equations for the following reactions:

1.1 Oxidation of glucose ($\ce{C6H12O6}$) with $\ce{KMnO4}$ solution in the presence of sulfuric acid to form gaseous $\ce{CO2}$.

1.2 Oxidation of $\ce{FeSO4}$ with $\ce{KMnO4}$ in an acidic medium (sulfuric acid) to form $\ce{Fe2(SO4)3}$.

1.3 Based on the reaction in section 1.2, determine the anodic reaction and cathodic reaction and the relevant cell diagram.

1.4 Derive the expression for electromotive force E of the cell.

2. In the thermodynamics point of view, Gibbs free energy $\Delta G$ at constant P, T condition is closely related to electromotive force E of a redox reaction according to below expression:

$$\Delta G = -nFE \rightarrow E = -\frac{\Delta G}{nF}$$

where: n – number of electrons transferred,

F – Faraday constant.

The correlation of the standard reduction potential between Mn ions in acidic medium is:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2014-10-fig1.png

2.1 Determine the standard reduction potential of the pair $\ce{MnO4^{2-}}/\ce{MnO2}$

2.2 Determine the standard reduction potential of the pair $\ce{MnO2}/\ce{Mn^{3+}}$

3. A process is spontaneous if Gibbs free energy is negative. Based on the thermodynamic data:

3.1 Determine Gibbs free energy of the following reaction:

$$\ce{3MnO4^{2-} + 4H+ <=> 2MnO4- + MnO2 + 2H2O}$$

3.2 Is the reaction spontaneous?

3.3 Calculate $K_\mathrm{c}$ for the reaction.

problems.title: Phosphoric acid
problems.problem:
Problem 11. Phosphoric acid

$\mathbf{A}$ is a solution of $\ce{H3PO4}$ with pH of 1.46.

1. Calculate the molar concentrations of all species in solution $\mathbf{A}$. Given that $K_\mathrm{a}$ values for $\ce{H3PO4}$ are $7.2\times10^{-3}$; $6.3\times10^{-8}$ and $4.2\times10^{-13}$, respectively.

2. Mixing of 50 ml of solution $\mathbf{A}$ and 50 ml of 0.4 M $\ce{NH3}$ solution results in 100 ml of solution $\mathbf{B}$. Calculate pH of solution $\mathbf{B}$ ($\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{NH_4^+}} = 9.24$).

3. 100 ml of solution $\mathbf{B}$ is mixed with 100 ml of 0.2 M $\ce{Mg(NO3)2}$ solution. Determine if precipitate of $\ce{NH4MgPO4}$ forms. The hydrolysis of $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ is ignored and precipitation of $\ce{NH4MgPO4}$ is assumed to be the only reaction, given that $K_\mathrm{sp} = 2.5\times10^{-13}$.

4. Calculate the solubility ($\mathrm{mol\cdot L^{-1}}$) of $\ce{Ca3(PO4)2}$, given $K_\mathrm{sp} = 2.22\times10^{-25}$. (Hint: The hydrolysis of $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ is ignored).

problems.title: Chemical Kinetics
problems.problem:
Problem 12. Chemical Kinetics

Thermal decomposition of dinitrogen pentoxide ($\ce{N2O5}$) in the gas phase has time-independent stoichiometry.

$$\ce{2 N2O5(g) -> 4 NO2(g) + O2(g)} \qquad (1)$$

A kinetic measurement for $\ce{N2O5}$ at $63.3\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is shown in Figure 1 below.

problems.title: Magnetism of transition metal complexes
problems.problem:
Problem 14. Magnetism of transition metal complexes

A transition metal complex containing diamagnetic ligands can be overall diamagnetic (all electrons are paired) or paramagnetic (having unpaired electron(s)) depending on the electronic configuration of the central metal ion, the nature of the ligand, and geometry of the ligand sphere. The magnitude of paramagnetism of a metal complex is commonly reported in terms of the effective magnetic moment ($\mu_\mathrm{eff}$) which can be obtained from the experimental measurement of molar magnetic susceptibility ($\chi_\mathrm{m}$) and is commonly expressed in Bohr magneton (BM).

Theoretically, the magnetic moment is contributed by two components, the spin angular momentum and the orbital angular momentum. For many complexes of first row d-block metal ions, however, the contribution of the second component can be ignored. Thus, the so-called spin only magnetic moment can be determined by the number of unpaired electrons, n:

$$\mu\ (spin\ only) = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ \ (BM)$$

1. The observed effective magnetic moment of two octahedral complexes, $\ce{K4[Mn(CN)6].3H2O}$ and $\ce{K4[Mn(SCN)6]}$ are 2.18 BM and 6.06 BM, respectively.

1.1 Calculate number of unpaired electrons in each complex. Which complex is low spin? Which complex is high spin?

1.2 Rationalize your answers by applying crystal field theory.

2. Calculate the $\mu$ (spin only) of complex $\ce{[Ni(H2O)6]Cl2}$.

3. In practice, the experimentally observed $\mu_\mathrm{eff}$ value of $\ce{[Ni(H2O)6]Cl2}$ is 3.25 BM. This is not surprising due to the fact that magnetic moment of octahedral complexes of $\ce{Ni^{2+}}$ ($\mathrm{d^8}$) usually does not obey the spin only formula. In these cases, the contribution of orbital angular momentum should be taken into account. The simplification of spin-orbit coupling model can be applied to calculate their magnetic moment:

$$\mu_{eff} = \mu(spin\ only)\times\left(1 - \frac{4\lambda}{\Delta_{oct}}\right)$$

where $\lambda$ is spin-orbit coupling constant of $\ce{Ni^{2+}}$ and has the value of $-315\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$

$\Delta_\mathrm{oct}$ is the crystal-field splitting parameter

Calculate the effective magnetic moment of $\ce{[Ni(H2O)6]Cl2}$ taking into account spin–orbit coupling. $\Delta_\mathrm{oct}$ of $\ce{[Ni(H2O)6]^{2+}}$ is $8500\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

4. Dibenzoylmethane (DBM) is a well known chelating κ-O,O-ligand which can form stable complexes with many transition metal ions.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2014-14-fig1.png

Reaction of $\ce{Ni(CH3COO)2.4H2O}$ with DBM in EtOH - $\ce{H2O}$ solution gives light green crystalline complex $\mathbf{A}$ which loses 6.8 % of mass on heating at $210\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in the air to form green solid $\mathbf{B}$. The substance $\mathbf{B}$ is quantitatively converted to brown prismatic crystals $\mathbf{C}$ by re-crystallization in dry toluene. $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are two polymorphic forms and their inter-conversion is reversible. The X-ray single crystal structure of $\mathbf{C}$ shows a square planar geometry with the chemical composition of $\mathrm{[Ni(DBM)_2]}$. While $\mathbf{B}$ is paramagnetic with effective magnetic moment of 3.27 BM, the complex $\mathbf{C}$ is diamagnetic. When $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are kept in the air, they slowly convert to $\mathbf{A}$. This happens much faster in the presence of some organic solvents (Inorg. Chem., 2001, 40, 1626-1636).

4.1 Draw the splitting diagram of the d orbitals of $\ce{Ni^{2+}}$ in $\mathbf{C}$ and confirm its diamagnetic property.

4.2 What is the molecular formula of $\mathbf{A}$? Assume that $\mathbf{A}$ is a mononuclear complex.

4.3 The effective magnetic moment of $\mathbf{A}$ is 3.11 BM (Synth. React. Inorg. Met. Org. Chem., 2009, 39, 694-703). What is the most suitable molecular geometry of $\mathbf{A}$? (Assuming that If A is an octahedral complexes, $\Delta_\mathrm{oct}$ of $\mathbf{A}$ is similar to that of $\ce{[Ni(H2O)6]^{2+}}$).

4.4 Draw all possible isomers of $\mathbf{A}$.

4.5 What do you expect for the molecular geometry of $\mathbf{B}$?

problems.title: Imidazole
problems.problem:
Problem 17. Imidazole

Heterocyclic chemistry is one of the most important fields of organic chemistry and biochemistry. Approximately 55% of publications in organic chemistry are related to the field, and the number of heterocyclic compounds recently found is far more than that of homocyclic compounds. The five-membered ring compounds with two heteroatoms are often present in many substances that are important for life. For example, imidazole ring is present in the essential amino acid, histidine, and its decarboxylation product, histamine. Histidine residues are found at the active sites of ribonuclease and of several other enzymes and play a vital part in the structure and binding functions of hemoglobin. Several drugs are based on the imidazole ring such as nitroimidazole, cimetidine, azomycin, metronidazole, midazolam.

1. Draw the structures of 1,3-diazole (imidazole, $\ce{C3H4N2}$), imidazol-1-ide anion, imidazolium cation, 1,3-oxazole (oxazole, $\ce{C3H3NO}$) and 1,3-thiazole (thiazole, $\ce{C3H3NS}$). Which structure(s) can be considered aromatic?

6. Explain why the C=O IR stretching frequency in 1,1'-carbonyldiimidazole is $100\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ higher than that of 1,1'-carbonyldipyrrolidine ($\ce{CO(C4H8N)2}$).

7. Write down reaction equations for the preparation of CDI (a) using a mixture of 4 mol imidazole and 1 mol phosgene and (b) using a mixture of 2 mol imidazole, 1 mol phosgene, and 2 mol NaOH. Explain why reaction (a) is preferable.

Problem 18. Small heterocycles

Heterocyclic compounds containing the $\ce{CF3}$ group are interesting targets of advanced researches to generate biologically active compounds. It is quite difficult to bring the trifluoromethyl group into saturated heterocyclic structures, especially heterocycles containing nitrogen. However, these heterocycles bearing $\ce{CF3}$ groups have several promising applications. Therefore, studies of such compounds have been carried out by many chemists.

Trifluoroacetaldehyde ($\mathbf{A}$) was treated with ethanol and then refluxed with benzylamine in toluene to afford compound $\mathbf{B}$ ($\ce{C9H8NF3}$). The reaction of compound $\mathbf{B}$ with ethyl diazoacetate in diethyl ether with boron trifluoride etherate ($\ce{BF3.Et2O}$) as a catalyst at $-78\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for 4 hours provided compound $\mathbf{C}$ ($\ce{C13H14NO2F3}$). The reduction of compound $\mathbf{C}$ by $\ce{LiAlH4}$ in THF at room temperature for 2 hours formed compound $\mathbf{D}$. Then, $\mathbf{D}$ reacts with hydrogen in the presence of $\ce{Pd(OH)2}$ as a catalyst in $\ce{CH2Cl2}$ at room temperature for 60 hours to obtain $\mathbf{E}$ ($\ce{C4H6NOF3}$). Compound $\mathbf{E}$ was then allowed to react with 2 equivalents of tosyl chloride (TsCl) in dicloethane with $\ce{Et3N}$ and an amount of 4-dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP) as catalyst. The reaction was carried out at room temperature for 2 hours, then 3 hours of reflux, to furnish compound $\mathbf{F}$. $\mathbf{F}$ reacted with 1.2 equivalents of phenol in the presence of $\ce{K2CO3}$ in DMF to form compound $\mathbf{G}$ ($\ce{C17H16NSO3F3}$).

3. Write reaction mechanisms from $\mathbf{F}$ to $\mathbf{G}$.

problems.title: Vitamin H
problems.problem:
Problem 19. Vitamin H

Vitamin H or biotin is a highly effective growth promoter which plays an important role in many organisms, for instance baker's yeast (Saccharomyces corevisiae). Human beings have different demand in biotin depending on age. Lack of biotin can lead to diseases such as dermatitis, absence of appetite, fatigue, muscular pain and nerve perturbance.

Biotin was first found in 1901 by Wildiers as a growth-promoting vitamin of yeasts. Thereafter, it was found in egg yolk (by Kögl, 1936) and in liver (by Szent-Györgyi, 1936). The absolute configurations of chiral carbons of biotin were established by Trotter and Hamilton in 1966 by the single-crystal X-Ray diffraction. The molecule of biotin has three chiral carbons. Hence, there are theoretically eight diastereomers. Only the (3aS, 4S, 6aR)-(D)-(+)-biotin, however, shows the high bioactivity.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2014-19-fig1.png

In 1982, researchers from Hoffmann-La Roche published an elegant synthesis procedure for (D)-(+)-Biotin from the methyl ester of the amino acid L-Cysteine with the following steps.

1. The thiol group of the methyl ester of L-cysteine was transformed into a disulfide S-S bond (compound $\mathbf{A}$) in an oxidation reaction. $\mathbf{A}$ was then treated with hex-5-inoyl chloride to give compound $\mathbf{B}$ which was subsequently reduced by Zn/$\ce{CH3COOH}$ to afford a thiol. This compound was cyclized by the addition of the –SH group to the terminal alkyne under atmospheric condition, resulting in the formation of $\mathbf{C}$ with a ten-membered ring containing a (Z) C=C double bond. Write down the structural formulae of $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ in the hereunder scheme.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2014-19-fig2.png

2. The reduction of $\mathbf{C}$ by diisobutylaluminium hydride ($(i\text{-Bu})_2\mathrm{AlH}$, DIBAL) resulted in the formation of ($\mathbf{D}$). The condensation reaction between $\mathbf{D}$ and benzylhydroxylamine in dichloromethane produced nitrone $\mathbf{E}$ (a nitrone is an organic compound which contains a $>\mathrm{C{=}N^{+}{-}O^{-}}$ group). $\mathbf{E}$ underwent a 1,3-dipolar intramolecular cyclization reaction to afford polycyclic compound $\mathbf{F}$ of which the two heterocycles, isoxazolidine (1,2-oxazolidine) and tetrahydrothiophene, shared a common bond. The cyclization reaction resulted in the (S) configurations of the two carbons at the common bond and the (R) configuration of the carbon connected to the oxygen. Write down the structural formulae of $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{F}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2014-19-fig3.png

3. When $\mathbf{F}$ was reduced with Zn powder in acetic acid, the N-O bond of the heterocycle isoxazolidine was broken to give compound $\mathbf{G}$. The reaction between $\mathbf{G}$ and chloroformate in the presence of $\ce{Na2CO3}$ in THF resulted in the formation of compound $\mathbf{H}$. The treatment of $\mathbf{H}$ in a hot solution of $\ce{Ba(OH)2}$ in dioxane, followed by an acidic work-up yielded the bicyclic $\delta$-hydroxy acid $\mathbf{I}$ containing all the chiral centers of (D)-(+)-Biotin but with an "excessive" -OH group. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{G}$, $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{I}$ and explain the formation of $\mathbf{I}$ from $\mathbf{H}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2014-19-fig4.png

4. $\mathbf{I}$ was treated with $\ce{SOCl2}$ to yield the corresponding chloride acid $\mathbf{K}$, given that the configuration of the carbon attached to the "excessive" -OH is maintained in $\mathbf{K}$. Ester $\mathbf{L}$ was formed when $\mathbf{K}$ was reacted with methanol. $\mathbf{L}$ was reduced with $\ce{NaBH4}$ in dimethylformamide at $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to give ester $\mathbf{M}$ which was hydrolyzed in aqueous acidic solution of HBr to give optically pure (D)-(+)-Biotin. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{K}$, $\mathbf{L}$ and $\mathbf{M}$ and the intermediates to explain the influence of the sulfur atom on the stereochemical outcome of $\mathbf{K}$.

Problem 20. No perfume without jasmine

The Spanish jasmine originated from the valleys of Himalaya. This so called Jasminum grandiflorum L., which was grafted on the wild Jaminum officinale L, has the possibility to resist against the cold of the mountain climate. In 1962, E. Demole and E. A cyclo-addition reaction, a kind of pericyclic reaction, involves bonding between the termini of two $\pi$ systems to produce a new ring (scheme below). The product has two more $\sigma$ bonds and two less $\pi$ bonds than the reactants. The Diels-Alder reaction, or so called [4+2], is a common thermally activated cycloaddition whose stereoselectivity is syn addition. In this concerted syn addition, the stereochemical relationships among the substituents are retained in the product(s).

Compound $\mathbf{M}$ was separated from the Wittig reaction mixture between $\mathbf{L}$ and the yield $\ce{Ph3P=CHOCH3}$. Draw the structures of the compounds from $\mathbf{G}$ to $\mathbf{L}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2014-20-fig5.png

The hydrolysis of $\mathbf{O}$ in basic solution, followed by a neutralization step and then treatment with diazomethane resulted in the formation of $\mathbf{P}$. In the last step, the target molecule, (Z)-(3R,7S)-methyl jasmonate $\mathbf{Q}$, was obtained in the oxidation reaction of $\mathbf{P}$ with pyridinium dichromate. Problem 1. Brayton cycle

Students have made a device capable to operate in a mode that is close to the ideal Brayton cycle. This thermodynamic cycle has once been proposed for development of internal combustion engines. The device consists of a cylinder with 1 mole of helium fitted with a computer-controlled movable piston. A Peltier element which can heat or cool the gas is mounted in the cylinder wall. The device can operate in the following modes: 1) reversible adiabatic expansion or compression, 2) reversible isobaric cooling or heating.

Through a number of cooling and compression steps, helium is going from the initial state with the pressure of $1\,\mathrm{bar}$ and the temperature of $298\,\mathrm{K}$ into the final state with the pressure of $8\,\mathrm{bar}$ and the temperature of $298\,\mathrm{K}$. (The total number of cooling and compression stages can be from two up to infinity).

1. What is the minimum work that should be done on the gas for this? Compare this value to the work during a reversible isothermal compression.

2. What is the maximum work that can be done on the gas in this process?

3. Let the process be accomplished in three steps. At each step helium is first cooled and then compressed. At the end of each step the pressure increases twice and the temperature returns to the value of $298\,\mathrm{K}$. What is the total heat removed from the gas by a Peltier element?

Once the gas is compressed, it is returned to the initial state ($1\,\mathrm{bar}$ and $298\,\mathrm{K}$) in two stages (heating and expansion).

4. What is the range of possible values of the formal efficiency $\eta$ for the resulting cycle? $\eta$ is the ratio of the useful work done by the gas to the amount of heat given to the gas during the heating stage.

5. In one of the experiments, the gas has been compressed from $1\,\mathrm{bar}$ and $298\,\mathrm{K}$ to $8\,\mathrm{bar}$ and $298\,\mathrm{K}$ in several steps (like in question 3). At the end of each step the pressure is increased by $x$ times and the temperature returns to $298\,\mathrm{K}$. Then helium has been returned to the initial state in two stages – heating and expansion. Theoretical value of $\eta$ for this cycle is 0.379. How many steps were used?

In fact, Peltier elements also consume electric energy during the cooling stage. Assume that they consume as much energy as is removed from the gas.

6. What is the maximum possible efficiency of the considered cycle, taking into account energy consumption during cooling?

Hint: in reversible adiabatic process for helium $pV^{5/3} = \mathrm{const}$. Isochoric molar heat capacity of helium is $3/2R$.

problems.title: Quasi-equilibrium model
problems.problem:
Problem 4. Quasi-equilibrium model

Equilibrium constants are often included into the rate equations for complex chemical reactions. For some rapid reversible steps the ratio of concentration of products to concentration of reactants is assumed to be equal to equilibrium constant, though reaction as a whole still proceeds and chemical equilibrium is not attained. This is quasi-equilibrium approximation. The concept of quasi-equilibrium makes rate equations much simpler which is vitally important for complex reactions.

I. Consider kinetics of a complex reaction

$$\ce{A + B ->[k_\mathrm{eff}] C + D}$$

The following mechanism was proposed

$$\ce{A + B <=>[k_1][k_{-1}] AB ->[k_2] AB^* ->[k_3] C + D}$$

The rates of the forward and reverse reaction of the first step are almost equal,

$$r_1 \approx r_{-1}$$

i.e., quasi-equilibrium is reached.

1. Calculate $k_\mathrm{eff}$, if $k_1 / k_{-1} = 10\,\mathrm{M^{-1}}$, $k_2 = 20\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2015-4-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Gasification of Pt by a flow of atomic fluorine

The ratio $\dfrac{p^2_{\ce{PtF2}}}{p_{\ce{PtF4}}}$ was equal to $10^{-4}\,\mathrm{bar}$ and did not vary with the change of the incident atomic fluorine flow.

2.1. Find the maximum partial pressure of molecular fluorine near the platinum surface under the given experimental conditions. Assume first that gasification does not proceed.

2.3. Make the necessary assumptions and estimate the partial pressure of atomic fluorine in the desorbed flow.

2.4. Put forward the quasi-equilibrium model to account for the rate of gasification of Pt with atomic fluorine,

$$r_\mathrm{Pt} = \frac{dn_\mathrm{Pt}}{dt}\ \ \{\text{mol of Pt / Pt surface area / time}\}$$

Make use of the dimensionless equilibration probability, $\alpha$, which is equal to the fraction of incident fluorine flow involved in gasification. Consider other steps of gasification as quasi-equilibrium. The flow $\rho_i$ of each gaseous species $i$ is related to its partial pressure $p_i$ as

$$\rho_i = c\,\frac{p_i}{(m_i)^{1/2}}$$

where $m_i$ is a molecular mass, $c$ is constant.

2.6. How many grams of Pt will be gasified from $1\,\mathrm{cm^2}$ of the Pt surface in 15 minutes, if the incident flow of atomic fluorine is $2\cdot10^{18}\,\mathrm{atoms/cm^2/s}$?
