problems.title: The Second Law of thermodynamics applied to a chemical reaction
problems.problem:
Problem 5. The Second Law of thermodynamics applied to a chemical reaction

When does chemical reaction proceed spontaneously? The Second Law gives the answer.

Consider a system, a chemical reactor in Fig. 1. Pressure $p$ and temperature $T$ inside the reactor are kept constant. There is no transfer of matter into or out of the system.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2015-5-fig1.png

Fig. 1. Chemical reaction inside a reactor

According to the Second Law, every spontaneous process in such a reactor leads to the decrease of the Gibbs free energy, $G_\mathrm{system}$, i.e. $\Delta G_\mathrm{system} < 0$.

If the chemical reaction, e.g., A + B = C (a), is the only process inside the reactor

$$\begin{aligned} \Delta G_\mathrm{System} &= \Delta G_\mathrm{Reaction}(a)\,\Delta\xi(a) \\ \Delta\xi(a) &= \Delta n_C = -\Delta n_A = -\Delta n_B \end{aligned} \qquad (1)$$

where $\Delta G_\mathrm{Reaction}$ and $\Delta\xi$ are the Gibbs free energy and the extent of reaction (a), respectively, $\Delta n_\mathrm{A}$, $\Delta n_\mathrm{B}$, $\Delta n_\mathrm{C}$ are changes of the numbers of moles of A, B, C in the reaction (a).

1.1. Relate $\Delta\xi$ to $\Delta n_i$ of reactants and products of the following reaction

$$\tfrac{1}{6}\ce{C6H12O6 + O2 = CO2 + H2O} \qquad \text{(b)}$$

1.2. Prove that, according to the Second Law, $\Delta G_\mathrm{Reaction} < 0$ for any single spontaneous chemical reaction in the reactor (Fig.1).

2. The Gibbs free energy of the chemical reaction (a) is:

$$\Delta G_\mathrm{Reaction} = \Delta G^\circ_\mathrm{Reaction} + RT \ln \frac{[\mathrm{C}]}{[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]} < 0 \qquad (2)$$

where [C], [A], [B] are time variant concentrations inside the reactor in the course of spontaneous reaction. Using the law of mass action, relate $\Delta G_\mathrm{Reaction}$ to the ratio of rates of forward $r_1$ and reverse $r_{-1}$ reaction (a). Consider both reactions as elementary ones.

3.1. Derive the expression (2) for $\Delta G_\mathrm{reaction}$ of the following chemical transformations:

(a') $\ce{H2(g) + Br2(g) = 2HBr(g)}$

(a'') $\ce{H(g) + Br2(g) = Br(g) + HBr(g)}$

(a''') $\ce{CaCO3(s) = CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$

3.2. For which of these reactions the relation between $\Delta G_\mathrm{Reaction}$ and $r_1$, $r_{-1}$ derived in Problem 2 is valid?

4. The observed rate of chemical reaction, $r_\mathrm{obs}$, is defined as $r_\mathrm{obs} = r_1 - r_{-1}$.

Let reaction (a) proceed spontaneously. At a certain moment

$$r_\mathrm{obs} / r_1 = 0.5, \qquad [\mathrm{A}] = 0.5\,\mathrm{M},\ [\mathrm{B}] = 1\,\mathrm{M},\ [\mathrm{C}] = 2\,\mathrm{M}.$$

Find the equilibrium constant, $K$, of the reaction (a), $T = 298\,\mathrm{K}$.

5. Plot $r_\mathrm{obs}$ as a function of

a) $r_1$, at $\Delta G_\mathrm{Reaction} = \mathrm{const}$;

b) $r_1$, at $r_{-1} = \mathrm{const}$;

c) $\Delta G_\mathrm{Reaction}$, at $r_1 = \mathrm{const}$.

6. Which thermodynamic and kinetic parameters of a chemical reaction are influenced by a catalyst? Put plus (+) into the cell of the Table if a catalyst may cause a change of the corresponding parameter, (–) otherwise.

Table

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline r_\mathrm{obs} & r_1 & r_1/r_{-1} & \Delta G_\mathrm{Reaction} & r_\mathrm{obs}/r_1 \\ \hline \phantom{+} & & & & \\ \hline \end{array}$$

problems.title: Catalytic transformation of a single molecule on a single nanoparticle
problems.problem:
Problem 6. Catalytic transformation of a single molecule on a single nanoparticle

Use of catalytic nanoparticles opens new ways to study and to understand catalysis. The exiting measurements were performed at Cornell University (NY, USA). The researchers observed the catalytic transformation of single molecules on the surface of a spherical nanoparticle ($d = 6\,\mathrm{nm}$) formed by Au atoms.

The experimental design is shown in Fig.1. The dissolved A was transformed into dissolved B in the presence of Au nanoparticles, adsorbed on the glass slide.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2015-6-fig1.png

Fig.1. The experimental design

The reaction product B is a fluorescent molecule while the reagent A is not. Continuous laser light producing fluorescence was focused within a small surface area containing a single Au nanoparticle. The time dependence of fluorescence on the wavelength characteristic for B, adsorbed on the Au nanoparticle is shown in Fig.2.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2015-6-fig2.png

Fig. 2. Time dependence of intensity of fluorescence coming from a single cluster

The fluorescence of B in the solution could not be detected under the experimental conditions. The same intensity of fluorescence was observed periodically for the time intervals $\tau_2$. The fluorescence disappeared during the time intervals $\tau_1$ between the peaks (see Fig.2). The researchers have performed their measurements for long periods of time and for many different single Au nanoparticles. As a result the averaged values of $[\tau_1]$ and $[\tau_2]$ were obtained.

Answer the following questions about this experiment and the conclusions made by its authors.

1. Estimate the number of the Au atoms in a single nanoparticle if it’s density is equal the bulk density of Au, $19.32\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}$. What fraction of Au atoms is involved in the catalysis if catalytically active is the surface layer with the depth equal to two atomic diameters of Au ($d_\mathrm{Au} = 0.350\,\mathrm{nm}$)?

2. The resolution of the instruments made it possible to measure the fluorescence emitted from $1\,\mathrm{\mu m^2}$ area. The number density of Au nanoparticles on the glass slide was $0.035\,\mathrm{particle\cdot\mu m^{-2}}$. What was the probability (%) of observing fluorescence from a single Au nanoparticle?

3. The authors claimed that each peak in Fig. 2 corresponds to the fluorescence of a single molecule B adsorbed on Au nanoparticle. What was the main argument of the authors?

Consider adsorption of A on Au nanoparticles to be a fast reversible process. Let $m$ catalytic sites exist on the surface of a single nanoparticle. The fraction of catalytic sites occupied by molecules A, is equal to

$$\theta_\mathrm{A} = \frac{K_\mathrm{ads}[\mathrm{A}]}{1 + K_\mathrm{ads}[\mathrm{A}]}$$

4. Relate $[\tau_1]$ and $[\tau_2]$ to the rates of catalytic production/desorption of a single molecule B on/from a single Au nanoparticles.

5. Plot $[\tau_1]^{-1}$ and $[\tau_2]^{-1}$ as a function of concentration of A in the solution.

6. How will $[\tau_1]^{-1}$ and $[\tau_2]^{-1}$ change with the increase of nanoparticle diameter from 6 to $12\,\mathrm{nm}$?

problems.title: Esterification of a dicarboxylic acid

2. Find the maximum yield.

3. Answer the questions 1 and 2 at arbitrary $K_1$ and $K_2$.

problems.title: Three elements

Three elements – $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}$, and $\mathbf{C}$ form three binary compounds. Each element has the same valence in these compounds. The mass fraction of $\mathbf{A}$ in the compound with $\mathbf{B}$ is 75%, and the mass fraction of $\mathbf{B}$ in the compound with $\mathbf{C}$ is 7,8%. problems.title: Simple experiments with copper(II) chloride
problems.problem:

2. Draw the structure of at least three copper containing species that can be present in the solution.

3. To the aliquots of the copper chloride(II) solution in the test tubes (a) zinc powder and the solutions of (b) sodium iodide, (c) sodium nitrate, (d) sodium sulfide were added dropwise. What changes happen if they are? Provide equations. In what cases copper is completely or partly reduced?

problems.title: An element typical for Azerbaijan mud volcanoes expelled water
problems.problem:
Problem 10. An element typical for Azerbaijan mud volcanoes expelled water

Azerbaijan is famous for mud volcanoes. About 400 active mud volcanoes are present in this region, both onshore and offshore - more than half the total throughout the world. Mud volcanoes come in a variety of shapes and sizes, but those most common in Azerbaijan have several small cones, or vents, up to about four meters in height. Mud volcanic eruptions in Azerbaijan normally last for less than a few hours, and are characterized by vigorous extrusion of mud breccias, hydrocarbon gases, and waters. Bakhar is a mud volcano with a high seep activity in the dormant period. The reservoirs formed by the volcanoes’ activity contain the expelled waters. Those of Bakhar volcano have a composition with Na and Cl as dominant ions. The analyzed waters are enriched in metals and in an element $\mathbf{X}$ that causes flame coloration. Its’ concentration in seeping water of 250 ppm represents a 55-fold enrichment in comparison to seawater. Being concentrated, the expelled water gives the white crystals, among them the compound $\mathbf{Y}$, one of the main sources of $\mathbf{X}$. The common oxide of $\mathbf{X}$ contains 31.0% of the element, whereas the compound $\mathbf{Y}$ – 11.3% only.

1. What are the element $\mathbf{X}$ and the compound $\mathbf{Y}$?

2. Calculate the mass of $\mathbf{Y}$ that can be obtained from 1 L of expelled water.

3. The mass loss under gentle heating of $\mathbf{Y}$ is 37.8%. Draw a possible structure of anion in $\mathbf{Y}$, knowing that it contains two different types of $\mathbf{X}$ atoms (three- and four-coordinated).

problems.title: The Prussian blue
problems.problem:

The Prussian blue is a component of black and bluish inks for printing. The precipitate formed upon the dropwise addition of potassium ferrocyanide to the ferric chloride solution contains 34.9% (mass) of iron.

1. Give a formulae of the precipitate and write the chemical equation. (Use 55.8 for atomic mass of iron).

2. Using the crystal field theory show the $d$-orbital splitting pattern for all Fe atoms in the Prussian blue.

3. What causes the intense color of the pigment?

4. What product initially forms from potassium ferrocyanide and ferric chloride solution in the inverse-mixing-order route? Give the equation.

For platinum (II) and (IV) a large number of complexes is known. For most of them the isomers were isolated.

1. Explain what is the reason for the existence of different isomers and draw the structures for all $\ce{Pt(NH3)2Cl2Br2}$ species.

2. The reaction of thiourea with $\ce{[Pt(amine)2Cl2]}$ isomers results in different products. Explain this fact and give the reaction scheme.

3. Give an example of $\ce{PtX(amine)Cl2}$ isomeric complexes reacting with thiourea with the formation of one and the same product.

4. Explain why do the reactions of $\ce{[PtCl4]^{2-}}$ and $\ce{[AuCl4]^-}$ with iodide result in different products.

problems.title: Redox equilibria in aqueous solutions
problems.problem:
Problem 13. Redox equilibria in aqueous solutions

Using the Latimer diagrams (pH = 0):

$$\ce{[Au(H2O)6]^{3+}} \xrightarrow{\ 1.401\,\mathrm{V}\ } \ce{[Au(H2O)6]^+} \xrightarrow{\ 1.692\,\mathrm{V}\ } \ce{Au}$$

$$\ce{[AuCl4]^-} \xrightarrow{\ 0.926\,\mathrm{V}\ } \ce{[AuCl2]^-} \xrightarrow{\ 1.154\,\mathrm{V}\ } \ce{Au}$$

$$\ce{[AuBr4]^-} \xrightarrow{\ 0.810\,\mathrm{V}\ } \ce{[AuBr2]^-} \xrightarrow{\ 0.960\,\mathrm{V}\ } \ce{Au}$$

answer the following questions:

1. Is Au(I) stable to disproportionation in aqueous solutions in the absence and in the presence of chloride and bromide ions? Support your answer by calculations.

3. At what pH interval is it possible to oxidize gold powder by hydrogen peroxide ($E^\circ_{\ce{H2O2,H+/H2O}} = 1.763\,\mathrm{V}$) in the presence of chloride-ions? Assume that the activities of all ions in the solution except $\ce{H+}$ are 1.

problems.title: Determination of acetylsalicylic acid purity
problems.problem:
Problem 14. Determination of acetylsalicylic acid purity

Aspirin – acetylsalicylic acid – is used to treat pain and to reduce fever, at low doses, to prevent heart attacks, strokes, and blood clot formation. It is one of the most widely used medications in the world, with an estimated 80 billion of tablets of it being consumed each year. Aspirin tablets can be contaminated with salicylic acid – the reagent for synthesis of acetylsalicylic acid. The content of salicylic acid is controlled in accordance with national pharmacopoeias. It must not exceed 0.1–0.3 %. Redox titration using bromine as an oxidation agent is one of the possible techniques to determine salicylic acid in aspirin.

$4.4035\,\mathrm{g}$ portion of powdered aspirin tablets was dissolved in $250.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ volumetric flask. For redox titration, reagent (bromine) was generated in situ (in the same titration flask). Bromide-bromate mixture was made of potassium bromide ($0.5950\,\mathrm{g}$) and potassium bromate ($0.1670\,\mathrm{g}$) in $100\,\mathrm{mL}$ of water. $25.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ aliquot was transferred to a titration flask, also sulfuric acid and $20.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the above mixture was added. The volume was made up to $50.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ with water. Flask was corked up and stirred for 10 min.

1. Write the balanced equations of the reactions described.

2. At what maximal pH bromide will react with bromate? The standard redox potentials are:

$$E^\circ_{\ce{2BrO3^-,H+/Br2}} = 1.52\,\mathrm{V}, \quad E^\circ_{\ce{Br2/2Br^-}} = 1.09\,\mathrm{V}.$$

Solution obtained after filtration of the reaction mixture was titrated against a $0.02015\,\mathrm{M}$ solution of $\ce{NaAsO2}$ and a mean titre of $9.93\,\mathrm{mL}$ was obtained.

3. Write the balanced equations of the reactions described.

4. Calculate the percentage of salicylic acid in tablets by mass.

5. Do the tablets meet the regulatory requirements?

problems.title: Chemical dosimeter
problems.problem:
Problem 15. Chemical dosimeter

Chemical dosimeters are widely used for remote determination of high-level doses of radiation. Most common type of dosimeter is a ferrous-ferric sulfate dosimeter. When ionizing radiation passes through the solution, lots of products (radicals, ions, and molecules) are formed. Most of them can oxidize $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ into $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$.

1.1. Choose the electronic configuration of $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ cation:

A) $3d^64s^0$ $\quad$ B) $3d^54s^0$ $\quad$ C) $3d^44s^2$ $\quad$ D) $3d^54s^1$

1.2. Write the balanced equations for oxidation of $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ with the following particles:

A) $\ce{H2O+}$ $\quad$ B) $\ce{OH^.}$ $\quad$ C) $\ce{H2O2}$

The resulting solution is then titrated and the amounts of Fe(II) and Fe(III) are calculated. For these purpose, permanganatometric and iodometric titrations can be used.

2.1. Write down the balanced redox equation for the reaction between:

a) iron(II) sulfate and potassium permanganate in acidic media;

b) iron(III) sulfate and potassium iodide;

c) sodium thiosulfate and iodine.

2.2. Calculate concentrations of cations $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ and/or $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ in each of the following cases:

a) To titrate $20.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of Fe(II) solution, $12.30\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $0.1000\,\mathrm{M}$ potassium permanganate solution was spent.

b) $1.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of solution containing Fe(III) was diluted up to $20.00\,\mathrm{mL}$, to resulted solution an excess of potassium iodide solution was then added. The iodine formed was titrated with $4.60\,\mathrm{mL}$ sodium thiosulfate solution ($0.0888\,\mathrm{M}$).

c) An aliquot $5.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ was titrated with $0.1000\,\mathrm{M}$ potassium permanganate solution, the average volume being equal $7.15\,\mathrm{mL}$. After that, an excess of potassium iodine solution was added to the flask. Titration of the resulting solution required $13.70\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $0.4150\,\mathrm{M}$ sodium thiosulfate.

Frequently, chemical dosimeters are used for measuring doses near nuclear reactors where large amounts of various radionuclides are accumulated.

3.1. Match mother and daughter radionuclide, indicate the type of decay ($\alpha$ or $\beta^-$) in each case:

Mother radionuclide:

a) $\ce{^{60}Co}$ $\quad$ b) $\ce{^{90}Sr}$ $\quad$ c) $\ce{^{226}Ra}$ $\quad$ d) $\ce{^{137}Cs}$ $\quad$ e) $\ce{^{212}Po}$

Daughter radionuclide:

1) $\ce{^{90}Zr}$ $\quad$ 2) $\ce{^{137}Xe}$ $\quad$ 3) $\ce{^{214}Rn}$ $\quad$ 4) $\ce{^{222}Rn}$ $\quad$ 5) $\ce{^{137}Ba}$ $\quad$ 6) $\ce{^{60}Ni}$ $\quad$ 7) $\ce{^{60}Fe}$ $\quad$ 8) $\ce{^{208}Pb}$ $\quad$ 9) $\ce{^{90}Y}$

Radioactivity $A$ is directly proportional to the number of particles $N$ of a substance ($A = \lambda N$), where $\lambda$ is the decay constant related to half-life by the equation $\lambda = \ln 2 / T_{1/2}$. Radioactivity is measured in becquerel (symbol Bq) units: 1 Bq is one decay per second.

3.2. Using values of half-lives, calculate (in GBq) radioactivity of samples containing:

a) $1.3141\,\mathrm{g}$ $\ce{^{226}RaCl2}$

b) $1.0\,\mathrm{mg}$ $\ce{^{90}Sr(NO3)2}$ and $0.5\,\mathrm{mg}$ $\ce{^{137}CsNO3}$

$T_{1/2}(\ce{^{226}Ra}) = 1612$ years, $T_{1/2}(\ce{^{90}Sr}) = 29$ years, $T_{1/2}(\ce{^{137}Cs}) = 30$ years.

3.3. Explain why $\ce{^{226}Ra}$ is dangerous for humans?

3.4. It is well known that radionuclide $\ce{^{64}Cu}$ decays to $\ce{^{64}Ni}$ (this is attributed to electron capture, process when nuclei absorb inner electron) and $\ce{^{64}Zn}$ ($\beta^-$ decay). Half-life for electron capture is 20.8 hours, for $\beta^-$ decay is 32.6 hours.

a) Calculate the average half-life of $\ce{^{64}Cu}$.

b) How much time is required for radioactivity of a $\ce{^{64}Cu}$ sample to decrease by 10 times?

problems.title: Determination of water in oil
problems.problem:
Problem 16. Determination of water in oil

Oil is the most important mineral for Azerbaijan. From chemist’s point of view it is a mixture of a great number of substances of different nature – both organic and inorganic. At all stages of petroleum refining, it is important to control the content of inorganic impurities, including water, in oil. One of the popular chemical methods for the determination of water in various organic matrices is named Karl Fischer titration. The method is based on the reaction described by R. Bunsen:

$$\ce{I2 + SO2 + H2O -> HI + H2SO4}$$

1.1. Indicate the oxidant and reductant in the reaction.

1.2. Put the coefficients in this reaction. Sum of the least integer coefficients is

A) 14 $\quad$ B) 9 $\quad$ C) 7 $\quad$ D) 10

Reagent which was proposed by the German chemist Karl Fischer is a mixture of pyridine, sulfur dioxide, iodine, and methanol. In this case, the following reactions occur during titration:

$$\ce{SO2 + CH3OH + H2O + I2 -> 2HI + CH3OSO3H}$$

$$\ce{Py + HI -> PyH+I-}$$

$$\ce{Py + CH3OSO3H -> PyH+ CH3OSO3-}$$

2.1. What is the role of pyridine in the composition of Fisher reagent?

2.2. What substance(s) could be used instead of pyridine?

A) Imidazole $\quad$ B) Pyrrol $\quad$ C) Hydrazine $\quad$ D) Butylamine

2.3. However, the above composition of titrant may lead to various side reactions. Write the possible reactions taking place between the components of the Fisher reagent and the following substances:

a) Aldehydes, RC(O)H

b) Ketones, RC(O)R

c) Mercaptans, RSH

d) Organic peroxides, ROOH

Indicate if an overestimation or underestimation of the water content is observed in each case.

3.1. Fischer reagent is to be standardized prior to use, i.e. it is necessary to set amount of water corresponding to one volume of a titrant. The reagent was prepared by the following procedure: 49 g of iodine were dissolved in 158 g of pyridine, then 38.5 g of liquid sulfur dioxide was introduced while cooling. Thereafter, mixture was diluted up with methanol to 1 liter.

a) Using the above data, calculate the theoretical titre of the Fischer reagent (in mg/mL).

b) Calculate the practical titre (in mg/mL) of Fischer reagent, if to reach the endpoint for the titration of 5 g of a mixture of methanol and water (water content of 1% by volume), 19 mL of titrant was spent.

c) Why do the results obtained differ?

d) Calculate the water content (in %) in the sample of sour oil, if the content of mercaptan in sulfur recalculation is 1 wt.% and titration of 1.00-g sample of sour oil dissolved in methanol required 7.5 mL of titrant.

3.2. The modern version of water determination in different samples is coulometric Karl Fischer titration. During the titration iodine is generated electrochemically and the water content is defined as the total amount of current passing through the coulometer. Titration is stopped when the generation of iodide stops in the system.

a) Using Faraday's law, calculate the mass fraction of water in the oil sample (10.0 g), if 375.3 Coulombs passed through a coulometer.

b) 1.000 g portion of sugar was dissolved in 15 mL of methanol and chloroform mixture. Calculate the molar and mass fractions of water and sugar, if for a coulometric titration of sugar a total charge of 567.2 Coulombs was required, while 31.1 Coulombs were required to titrate solvent.

problems.title: Oxidation and inspiration
problems.problem:
Problem 17. Oxidation and inspiration

[Epigraph:] With every breath, I breathe in so much of inspiration. I feel if there is one thing as free and as important as oxygen, it's inspiration. (Sharad Sagar)

Oxygen is not only chemical element but also the essential element of life. Its most stable form, dioxygen, $\ce{O2}$, constitutes 20.8% of the volume of the Earth’s atmosphere. All forms of oxygen are able to oxidize various compounds, especially organic ones. The type of oxygen-containing functionalities in organic compounds could be efficiently determined by IR spectroscopy. Thus, C=O groups are characterized by intense absorption at $1750\text{–}1660\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and O–H group is characterized by absorption in the region of $3600\text{–}3000\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

The most typical oxidation of saturated hydrocarbons with $\ce{O2}$ is the burning process. However, some reaction have been developed producing various oxygenated products. For example, Gif reaction (which received this name in honor of Gif-sur-Yvette where Prof. Derek Barton was working when he disclosed this transformation) represents the oxidation of saturated hydrocarbons with air oxygen at room temperature. Thus, the oxidation of adamantane leads to three products:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2015-17-fig1.png

Products $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are isomers. The compound $\mathbf{Y}$ can be easily transformed to $\mathbf{Z}$. IR spectra of the compounds $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ contain a band around $3300\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, while IR spectrum of compound $\mathbf{Z}$ contains band $1720\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$.

1. Write down the structural formulae of compounds $\mathbf{X}$–$\mathbf{Z}$.

Without catalysts $\ce{O2}$ has, fortunately, very low reactivity. Otherwise, all living organisms should be oxidized by air. A wide variety of oxidizing reagents have been developed for selective or undiscriminating oxidation of various functional groups in high yield. Below 7 organic molecules are given. They were synthesized by oxidation with 7 indicated reagents.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2015-17-fig2.png

These oxidation reactions proceed without C–C cleavage.

2. Put the correspondence between the products and the oxidants and determine the starting organic compounds.

Examples of the chemoselective oxidation of the same substrate with different oxidants affording different reaction products are given below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2015-17-fig3.png

Compounds $\mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{J}$, and $\mathbf{K}$ react with $\ce{Ag(NH3)2OH}$ solution producing the metallic silver precipitation. Compound $\mathbf{H}$ could be formed by oxidation of $\mathbf{J}$. The treatment of 1.44 g of $\mathbf{L}$ with metallic sodium produces 0.224 L ($P = 1\,\mathrm{atm}$, $T = 273\,\mathrm{K}$) of hydrogen gas.

3. Write down the structural formulae of compounds $\mathbf{H}$–$\mathbf{L}$.

For many people the taste and odor of truffles are so delightful that truffles cost more than their weight in gold. The compound $\mathbf{X}$ is responsible for the divine smell of the black truffle. The treatment of 0.108 g of compound $\mathbf{X}$ with the acidified solution of $\ce{HgSO4}$ leads to the formation of some precipitate $\mathbf{Z}$. problems.title: Synthesis of large rings. The magic or routine work?
problems.problem:
Problem 23. Synthesis of large rings. The magic or routine work?

The synthesis of large rings is a challenging problem of the synthetic organic chemistry. On the contrary, Nature solves this problem efficiently. Thus, various fungus produce macrolactone polyketides. One of them, Macrosphelide A, attracts attention as potent, orally bioavailable inhibitor of the interaction between cancer and endothelial cells. A number of syntheses of this molecule was reported. One of them was based on the utilization of lactic (2-hydroxypropionic) acid derivative according to Scheme below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2015-23-fig1.png

1. Decipher this scheme. Write down the structural formulae of compounds $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{L}$.

2. Write down the IUPAC name of compound $\mathbf{E}$.

problems.title: What Time is it in Baku or Cheating the Death
problems.problem:
Problem 24. What Time is it in Baku or Cheating the Death

[Epigraph:] One looking at the puddle, sees in her dirt, and another – reflected in her star (Immanuel Kant)

People use acronyms for convenience sake. Still, sometimes the meanings are not absolutely unambiguous. Thus, AZT generally standing for Azerbaijan time has acquired an alternative meaning in pharmacology denoting one of the most usable anti-HIV drugs. Nucleoside $\mathbf{A1}$, a major component of nucleic acids, was used as a starting material in AZT synthesis. Under complete combustion with subsequent condensation of water $\mathbf{A1}$ gives a gas undergoing an 11-fold volume decrease when bubbled through the 1 M KOH solution.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2015-24-fig1.png

1. What are the building blocks of nucleosides?

2. Deduce the structures of all of $\mathbf{A1}$ to $\mathbf{A4}$. Note that:

• When arranged in any order the numbers of atoms in $\mathbf{A1}$ are not described by either arithmetic or geometric progression

• all the synthetic steps are $\mathrm{S_N}$-type reactions

• $\mathbf{A4}$ is a binary compound (85.8 % N by mass)

• O is the heaviest element in both $\mathbf{A3}$ and AZT

3. How many stereoisomers of AZT do exist?

4. Give the full wording for the pharmaceutical AZT acronym.

5. Propose the mechanism of AZT antiviral action.

Metabolism of AZT is diverse and includes several pathways (X, Y, and Z) shown in the hereunder scheme (all balanced equations). X, the major of these, leads to a higher soluble product $\mathbf{B1}$ excreted with urine. Y provides the cytotoxic product $\mathbf{B2}$ with the same number of atoms as that in AZT. Z is found in patients infected with a specific bacteria, the product $\mathbf{B4}$ retaining the AZT-type activity.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2015-24-fig2.png

6. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{B1}$-$\mathbf{B4}$.

"Dallas Buyers Club", a movie from 2013, received numerous awards including three Oscars. It is based on a true story describing ambiguous results of the first clinical AZT trials. The protagonist suffering from AIDS lacks a positive effect from AZT and switches over to drugs unauthorized by US FDA. One of the latter is based on the substance $\mathbf{D}$.

$\mathbf{D}$ (51.17 % C by weight) and nucleoside $\mathbf{N}$ (a major component of nucleic acids; 47.57 % C by weight) differ by one atom only. Under complete combustion with subsequent condensation of water, the mixture of $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{N}$ of any composition gives gaseous products undergoing a 7-fold decrease of their total volume when bubbled through the 1 M KOH solution. It was found that $\mathbf{D}$ imitates AZT with respect to the mechanism of its action.

7. Calculate the number of C and N atoms in $\mathbf{D}$ without deciphering its structure.

8. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{N}$.

9. Do you support the “Dallas Buyers Club” principal character in his belief that $\mathbf{D}$ possesses a major clinical advantage over AZT? Comment why physicians used to administer AZT and $\mathbf{D}$ in a combination.

The compound $\mathbf{D}$ turns out to be a prodrug. Its active metabolite $\mathbf{M}$ (17.23 % P and 35.62 % O by mass) is produced by a number of manufacturers for research (non-clinical) purposes only.

10. Draw the structure of $\mathbf{M}$.

Note: If you feel like watching the above movie, check the film rating system accepted in your country.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2015-24-fig3.png

problems.title: Number One Enzyme
problems.problem:
Problem 25. Number One Enzyme

Enzymes rule over in biochemical processes. Enzyme Commission (EC) numbers have been proposed in order not to be lost in the vast variety of biocatalysts. This is a four-level classification based on the types of enzymatic reactions, each specific reaction being described by four numbers separated by periods. Number 1 of 6 top-level EC numbers is attributed to oxidoreductases, enzymes catalyzing oxidation/reduction reactions (transfer of H and O atoms or electrons from one substance to another). These reactions are of a great importance for both energy transformation and xenobiotic metabolism.

Changes of the oxidation state of a molecule can be achieved in different ways, which makes possible a more detailed classification of oxidoreductases. Many of these require a cofactor or coenzyme. Thus, dehydrogenases remove two hydrogen atoms from an organic substrate and pass them over to a suitable acceptor like nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide {phosphate} ($\ce{NAD+}$ {$\ce{NADP+}$}) or flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2015-25-fig1.png

1. Write down the equation of ethanol oxidation involving $\ce{NAD+}$ as the coenzyme. Show the changes in the nicotinamide moiety.

2. Sometimes the route of dehydrogenase reaction is determined by the coenzyme/cofactor involved. Predict the structures of $\mathbf{A1}$–$\mathbf{A3}$ in the following scheme if it is known that 1.00 g of $\mathbf{A3}$ gives 7.52 g of silver precipitate under Tollens’ reagent treatment.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2015-25-fig2.png

Oxygenases catalyze direct addition of oxygen atoms originating from $\ce{O2}$ to an organic substrate. These enzymes are further subdivided into mono- and di-oxygenases depending on the number of incorporated atoms (one and two, respectively). In the case of monooxygenases the other oxygen atom is reduced to water by an appropriate reactant. Cytochrome P-450-dependent monooxygenase is an exceptionally important representative of the class.

An aromatic compound $\mathbf{B1}$ contains 77.75% C and 14.80% O by mass. $\mathbf{B1}$ metabolism in rat liver microsomes develops in two ways (see on the hereunder scheme). $\mathbf{B2}$ reveals 4 signals in $^1$H-NMR spectrum. $\mathbf{B2}$ and $\mathbf{B3}$ undergo color changes when added to 1% $\ce{FeCl3}$ solution, whereas the $\mathbf{B1}$ color is unaffected by such treatment. All of $\mathbf{B1}$ to $\mathbf{B4}$ are composed of the same elements. $\mathbf{B4}$ is a gas under STP.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2015-25-fig3.png

3. Decipher $\mathbf{B1}$ to $\mathbf{B4}$. Write down the balanced equations.

Under oxygen deficiency $\mathbf{B1}$ partially converts into $\mathbf{B5}$, an isomer of $\mathbf{B2}$. This transformation requires a vitamin as the oxygen acceptor. Further oxidation of $\mathbf{B5}$ leads to $\mathbf{B6}$ characterized by 2 signals in $^1$H-NMR spectrum.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2015-25-fig4.png

4. Draw the structures of $\mathbf{B5}$ and $\mathbf{B6}$ as well as of both forms of the vitamin.

Like dehydrogenases, oxidases remove hydrogen atoms from an organic substrate transferring these either to the molecular oxygen or $\mathbf{X}$, which finally results in water formation in both cases. The phenol oxidation can be described by the following equation:

$$2\,\text{Phenol} + \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{Y} + \ce{2H2O}$$

The reaction develops via a free radical intermediate and leads to a mixture of isomers of $\mathbf{Y}$ (77.4 % C by mass).

5. Decipher $\mathbf{X}$. Draw the isomers of $\mathbf{Y}$ that show a sole peak in the phenolic region of $^1$H-NMR spectra at low temperatures.

problems.title: Holy War against Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse
problems.problem:
Problem 26. Holy War against Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse

For centuries the Caspian Sea is widely known for its oil fields. Nowadays it attracts ever increasing attention of researches as a treasury of biological resources, in particular, of algae which can be considered as virtually inexhaustible source of unique chemicals. These studies are in line with the global fight of Enlightened Humanity against the four Horsemen of the Apocalypse – Conquest, War, Famine, and Death.

Substances $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ have been isolated from red algae Asparagopsis armata. These substances are rarely found in nature and belong to the same class of organic compounds. A sample of 1.000 g of $\mathbf{Y}$ was combusted in an excess of oxygen at high temperature followed by complete absorption of colorless gaseous ($25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, 1 atm) mixture of products with an excess of aqueous calcium hydroxide solution leading to 1.620 g of a white precipitate. Addition of the supernatant to an excess of silver nitrate solution provided 1.786 g of a colored precipitate.

It is also known that:

• cooling of $\mathbf{Y}$ combustion products from 150 down to $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ does not result in any condensed phase;

• white precipitate is an individual compound;

• the molar masses of each of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are less than 275 g/mol;

• the number of atoms of any element in the molecules of $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ does not exceed 3.

1. Without revealing the molecular formula, deduce which elements may be found in $\mathbf{Y}$.

2. Without revealing the molecular formula of $\mathbf{Y}$, write down the equation that includes numbers of atoms in the molecule as unknowns. Can this equation be of help in establishing the $\mathbf{Y}$ composition?

3. Determine the molecular formula of $\mathbf{Y}$ using all the data provided.

4. Will the substitution of silver nitrate by silver oxide in ammonia solution in the above experiment change the weight and color of the precipitate? To support the answer, calculate the solubility of AgBr ($K_\mathrm{sp} = 5.4\cdot10^{-13}$) in 1.0 M $\ce{NH3}$ taking into account that the two first stepwise formation constants of silver-ammonia complexes are $10^{3.32}$ and $10^{3.92}$, respectively.

Subjecting 1.000 g of $\mathbf{X}$ to the described above analysis sequence results in a colored gaseous ($250\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, 1 atm) mixture of products leading to 0.756 g of a white individual precipitate after passing the mixture through an excess of aqueous calcium hydroxide solution. Addition of silver nitrate solution to the supernatant also provides a colored precipitate.

It is known that molecules of $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{X}$ differ by one element, $\mathbf{Y}$ having one atom more. $\mathbf{X}$ can exist as a mixture of enantiomers, whereas $\mathbf{Y}$ reveals geometric isomerism. Furthermore, $\mathbf{Y}$ reacts with 0.1 M aqueous KOH solution at room temperature.

5. Deduce the molecular formula and draw the structure of $\mathbf{X}$.

6. Draw all possible geometric isomers of $\mathbf{Y}$.

7. Based on theoretical considerations decide which of the Horsemen of the Apocalypse can be potentially defeated by $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$?

Substance $\mathbf{Z}$ (41.00% O by weight) belongs to the same class of compounds as $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$. However, $\mathbf{Z}$ has been only detected in leaves of some plants, and never in algae.

Combustion of a 1.000-g sample of $\mathbf{Z}$ in a large excess of oxygen followed by complete absorption of colorless gaseous ($25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, 1 atm) products with an excess of aqueous calcium hydroxide solution leads to 3.065 g of a white precipitate. By contrast, no precipitate formed when the supernatant from the previous test was added to an excess of silver oxide in ammonia solution.

It is also known that:

• one of the gaseous products of $\mathbf{Z}$ combustion has the density of 1.43 g/L (measured at $34\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, 750 Torr);

• the number of atoms of any element in the molecule of $\mathbf{Z}$ does not exceed 3.

8. Find the molecular and structural formulae of $\mathbf{Z}$.

Both $\mathbf{Z}$ and its sodium salt are highly toxic to all mammals.

9. Knowledge of the area of organisms producing $\mathbf{Z}$ as well as of its metabolic pathway in mammals can be considered as a weapon against some of the Horsemen of the Apocalypse. Comment which of these, in your mind.

problems.title: Dimerization of Acetic Acid
problems.problem:
Problem 1. Dimerization of Acetic Acid

Ethanoic acid or acetic acid ($\ce{CH3COOH}$) is partially dimerized into dimers in the vapor phase. At a total pressure of $0.200\,\mathrm{atm}$, ethanoic acid is 92.0% dimerized at $298\,\mathrm{K}$. By increasing the temperature to $318\,\mathrm{K}$, the degree of dimerization is lowered, with $K_p = 37.3$.

1.1) Calculate the enthalpy and the entropy changes for the reaction, assuming that $\Delta H^\circ$ and $\Delta S^\circ$ do not vary with temperature.

1.2) Applying the Le Chatelier's principle, an increase of pressure should (select one correct answer)

• ◯ favor the dimerization.
• ◯ not favor the dimerization.

1.3) Continued from question 1.2, the extent of dimerization (select one correct answer)

• ◯ decreases with increasing the temperature.
• ◯ increases with increasing the temperature.

problems.title: Solubility of Calcite
problems.problem:
Problem 2. Solubility of Calcite

Calcite is a stable form of calcium carbonate ($\ce{CaCO3}$). The solubility product ($K_{sp}$) is decreased with increasing temperature; $K_{sp}$ are $9.50\times10^{-9}$ and $2.30\times10^{-9}$ at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, respectively. Estimate the enthalpy change for the solubility process of calcite.

problems.title: Expansion of Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics of Liquid Mixing
problems.problem:
Problem 3. Expansion of Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics of Liquid Mixing

3.1) A quantity of $0.10\,\mathrm{mol}$ of an ideal gas $\mathbf{A}$ initially at $22.2\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is expanded from $0.200\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ to $2.42\,\mathrm{dm^3}$. Calculate the values of work ($w$), heat ($q$), internal energy change ($\Delta U$), entropy change of the system ($\Delta S_{sys}$), entropy change of the surroundings ($\Delta S_{surr}$), and total entropy change ($\Delta S_{univ}$) if the process is carried out isothermally and irreversibly against an external pressure of $1.00\,\mathrm{atm}$.

3.2) If $3.00\,\mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathbf{A}$ is condensed into liquid state and is mixed with $5.00\,\mathrm{mol}$ of liquid $\mathbf{B}$, calculate the changes in entropy and Gibbs free energy upon such mixing at $25.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. This mixture can be assumed to be ideal.

problems.title: Vibrational Frequency of a Diatomic Molecule
problems.problem:
Problem 4. Vibrational Frequency of a Diatomic Molecule

For the vibrational motion of a diatomic molecule using a harmonic oscillator model, the allowed vibrational energy levels can be described as

$$E_\upsilon = \left(\upsilon + \frac{1}{2}\right)h\nu \qquad ;\ \upsilon = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$

where $\upsilon$ is the vibrational quantum number and $\nu$ is the vibrational frequency. The vibrational frequency represented by the harmonic oscillator model is

$$\nu = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}}\,,\ \text{where } k \text{ is the force constant and } \mu \text{ is the reduced mass.}$$

For molecule CX, where X is an unknown atom, the vibrational absorption energy from vibrational ground state to the first vibrational excited state is $2170.0\,\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and the force constant is $1.903\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg\,s^{-2}}$.

4.1) Find the reduced mass of CX in amu.

4.2) What is atom X?

problems.title: Water-gas-shift Reaction
problems.problem:
Problem 5. Water-gas-shift Reaction

In a drive toward cleaner energy production, fuel cell holds great promise because of its capability of generating electricity directly from chemical reactions with environmentally-benign byproducts. In particular, for hydrogen fuel cell, the only waste produced by the device is just water.

In order to use fuel cell at an industrial scale, continuous production of hydrogen that directly feeds into a fuel cell module is required. One option to mass produce hydrogen for this purpose is the conversion of hydrocarbon fuel using hot steam. However, this kind of reaction often leads to mixed products that consist of $\ce{H2}$, $\ce{CO2}$, and $\ce{CO}$. Moreover, $\ce{CO}$ is not only hazardous to human health, but it also degrades fuel cell's active material. The reversible water-gas-shift (WGS) reaction, $\ce{CO + H2O <=> CO2 + H2}$, provides one method of converting toxic $\ce{CO}$ into $\ce{CO2}$ and useful $\ce{H2}$. The efficiency of this reaction strongly depends on the solid catalyst used.

5.1) In one process, an equimolar mixture of $\ce{CO}$ and steam is continuously passed to a WGS reactor containing catalyst at atmospheric pressure and $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Assuming that the catalyst is 95.0% efficient in converting the reactants into the products and that the reaction in the reactor is approximately at equilibrium in this condition, estimate the free energy change for this reaction?

5.2) Now assume that a large surface of catalyst is initially available to reacting molecules, and the rate of reaction is measured immediately at the onset of the reaction. Below are the initial rates measured at different initial pressures of $\ce{CO}$ and $\ce{H2O}$.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Trial} & P_{CO},\ \mathrm{atm} & P_{H_2O},\ \mathrm{atm} & dP_{H_2}/dt,\ \mathrm{atm\,s^{-1}} \\ \hline 1 & 0.10 & 0.90 & 4.0\times10^{-4} \\ 2 & 0.15 & 0.85 & 5.6\times10^{-4} \\ 3 & 0.25 & 0.75 & 8.2\times10^{-4} \\ 4 & 0.28 & 0.72 & \text{X} \end{array}$$

What is X?

5.3) In another condition where the pressure of hydrogen is found to be $0.50\,\mathrm{atm}$, $-dP_{H_2}/dt = 3.0\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{atm\,s^{-1}}$. According to the information given in questions 5.1, 5.2, and this question, estimate the rate of hydrogen production when the pressures in the reactor of $\ce{CO}$, $\ce{H2O}$, $\ce{CO2}$, and $\ce{H2}$ are 0.14, 0.14, 0.36, and $0.36\,\mathrm{atm}$, respectively. (Give your answer to three significant figures.)

5.4) Calculate the Gibbs free energy change for the conditions described in question 5.3.

5.5) Surface coverage, $\theta$, is an important kinetics parameter, especially for reactions on solid surfaces. It can be defined as the number of adsorbed molecules on a surface divided by the total number of adsorbing sites on that surface. For WGS, after the adsorption of $\ce{CO}$ and $\ce{H2O}$ on the catalyst's surface, a carbonyl intermediate can be formed, which then dissociates to give surface-bound $\ce{CO2}$ and H atom. If the carbon dioxide is produced at a rate of $1.0\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{molecules\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$ with associated rate constant of $2.0\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{molecules\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$, what is the value of $\theta$ for this intermediate?

problems.title: Camphor in Benzene
problems.problem:
Problem 6. Camphor in Benzene

The vapor pressure of pure benzene ($\ce{C6H6}$) is $100\,\mathrm{torr}$ at $26.1\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Calculate the vapor pressure and the freezing point of a solution containing $24.6\,\mathrm{g}$ of camphor ($\ce{C10H16O}$) dissolved in $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of benzene. The density of benzene is $0.877\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. The freezing point and the cryoscopic constant ($K_f$) of pure benzene are $5.50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $5.12\,^\circ\mathrm{C\,kg\,mol^{-1}}$, respectively.

problems.title: Gas and Liquid
problems.problem:
Problem 7. Gas and Liquid

7.1) At temperatures above the boiling point, $\mathbf{A}$ behaves like an ideal gas. In a hypothetical situation, Jacques Charles performed an experiment about the volume-temperature relationship and obtained the following result (which is not necessarily drawn to scale):

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2017-7-fig1.png

What is the volume of $\mathbf{A}$ at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$?

7.2) At equilibrium, the vapor pressures above liquids $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are $100.1\,\mathrm{kPa}$ and $60.4\,\mathrm{kPa}$, respectively. The two liquids $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ are mixed thoroughly at $298\,\mathrm{K}$. What is the vapor pressure above a mixture containing $3\,\mathrm{mol}$ $\mathbf{B}$ and $4\,\mathrm{mol}$ $\mathbf{C}$?

7.3) What are the mole fractions of $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$ above the mixture explained in question 7.2?

problems.title: Decomposition of Nitrous Oxide
problems.problem:
Problem 8. Decomposition of Nitrous Oxide

Nitrous oxide decomposes exothermically into nitrogen and oxygen, at a temperature of approximately $565\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

$$\ce{2N2O -> 2N2(g) + O2(g)}$$

This reaction follows the second-order kinetics when carried out entirely in the gas phase.

8.1) If the reaction is initiated with $[\ce{N2O}]$ equal to $0.108\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$, what will its concentration be after $1250\,\mathrm{s}$ have elapsed at $565\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$? The rate constant for the second order decomposition of $\ce{N2O}$ is $1.10\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$ at this temperature.

8.2) The activation energy for the second order reaction at $565\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is $234\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. What is the rate constant for the reaction at $600\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$?

problems.title: Avogadro's Number
problems.problem:
Problem 9. Avogadro's Number

An internationally accepted procedure is as follows.

We start with a "perfect" sphere of pure $\ce{^{28}Si}$ isotope. The weight of this sphere is W g. The volume V of the sphere is found from the accurate measurement of the diameter of the sphere. The unit cell of a crystal of silicon is a "diamond cubic lattice", i.e. a face-centered unit cell but with 4 Si atoms inside the cube. The length of the unit cell can be determined precisely from X-ray crystallographic measurements of a single crystal of $\ce{^{28}Si}$ isotope.

The experimental data are as follow:

Weight of sphere, W: $1000.064\,543(15)\,\mathrm{g}$

Volume of sphere: $431.049\,110(10)\,\mathrm{cm^3}$

Length of unit cell, $\alpha$: $543.099\,619(20)\,\mathrm{pm}$

Atomic weight of $\ce{^{28}Si}$, A: $27.976\,970\,029(23)\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$

Number of Si atoms in unit cell, n:

9.1) Write down the equation for calculating Avogadro's number $N_\mathrm{A}$ in terms of the parameters.

9.2) How many silicon atoms are in the unit cell?

9.3) Calculate Avogadro's number using the above data. Give answer to 7 significant figures.

Acid Dissociation Constants

10.1)

problems.title: Amperometric Titration: Titration of Pb²⁺ with Cr₂O₇²⁻
problems.problem:
Problem 11. Amperometric Titration: Titration of $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ with $\ce{Cr2O7^{2-}}$

Amperometry is one of the sensitive electroanalytical methods used for quantitative determination of electroactive species. A working electrode is held at a certain voltage (vs reference electrode) that is suitable for oxidation or reduction of an analyte. The analyte will be oxidized or reduced at the surface of the working electrode and the current passing through this electrode is measured. This current is directly proportional to the concentration of analyte and is used for quantitative purpose. It can be used for detection of titration end-point. In this example amperometric detection was used for monitoring a titration progress. $20\text{-}\mathrm{cm^3}$ of lead (II) ion solution was titrated with $0.0020\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ potassium dichromate solution. A dropping mercury electrode (DME) was used as a working electrode and the potential of $-0.8\,\mathrm{V}$ (vs SCE, saturated calomel electrode) was applied to this electrode for enabling the reduction of lead (II) ion and dichromate ion with potassium nitrate as supporting electrolyte. The current-volume of titrant data are shown in Table 1.

Reference: Vogel's Textbook of Quantitative Chemical Analysis, 5th edition, John Wiley & Sons, New York, pp630.

Table 1. Titration data

$$\begin{array}{c|c} \text{Volume of } 0.0020\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}} \text{ dichromate } (\mathrm{cm^3}) & \text{Current (microampere)} \\ \hline 0.00 & 9.8 \\ 2.00 & 8.0 \\ 4.00 & 6.0 \\ 6.00 & 4.0 \\ 8.00 & 2.2 \\ 10.00 & 3.5 \\ 12.00 & 5.5 \\ 14.00 & 7.6 \\ 16.00 & 9.5 \end{array}$$

11.2) Write the titration reaction.

11.3) Calculate the concentration of lead (II).

problems.title: Conductometric Titration
problems.problem:
Problem 12. Conductometric Titration

Conductivity detector is an electrochemical technique which applies alternating current (AC) signal to two identical electrodes. The applied AC signal induces ions to move in solution and switching of polarity of the AC voltage avoids electrolytic reaction at the electrode. As a result, the mobility of ions in solution relates to the conductivity of ions in solution. Conductivity probe was used in acid-base titration of $25.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ $\ce{HCl}$ vs $0.100\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ $\ce{NaOH}$. The conductivity signal was recorded during $\ce{NaOH}$ addition. The conductometric titration setup is shown in Fig 1. When standard $\ce{NaOH}$ solution was dropped under gravity force to the titration cell at 3 drops per second and the conductivity value from conductometer recorded, the plot of conductivity of solution vs titration time is shown in Fig 2.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2017-12-fig1.png

Fig 1. Conductometric titration setup.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2017-12-fig2.png

Fig 2. Plot of conductivity of an initial $25.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ $\ce{HCl}$ vs titration time.

12.1) Explain why the slope of titration curve before and after the turning point is different.

12.2) Calculate the concentration of $\ce{HCl}$, if the volume of $\ce{NaOH}$ of each drop is $0.029\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ and the turning point is at 108 second.

problems.title: Titration of Cu and Zn in Metal Alloy
problems.problem:
Problem 13. Titration of Cu and Zn in Metal Alloy

A metal alloy which contains mainly Cu and Zn was analyzed for its metal content. An alloy sample of $2.300\,\mathrm{g}$ was placed in a $250\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ erlenmeyer flask. To this flask, $5.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of mixed acid (concentrated nitric acid and concentrated hydrochloric acid) was added in a fume hood for dissolution of the alloy. The resulting solution was transferred quantitatively into $250\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask and adjusted to volume with deionized water.

A $25.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquot of sample solution was adjusted to pH 5.5 and titrated with $0.100\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ EDTA solution using 1-(2-pyridinezao)-2-naphthol or PAN as indicator. Problem 14. Spectrophotometric Determination of Iron

To study in vitro gastric digestion of iron, the following procedure is carried out. Dried and homogeneously ground supplement tablet of $0.4215\,\mathrm{g}$ is accurately weighed, mixed with $10\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of water, adjusted to pH 2.0 with $6\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ $\ce{HCl}$, $0.375\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of pepsin solution (16% w/v) added, and adjusted to $12.50\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ with $0.01\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ $\ce{HCl}$. This mixture was quantitatively transferred into a dialysis bag of a fixed volume, which is further immersed for 2 hours in a $20.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ solution containing $0.01\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ $\ce{HCl}$. Iron released by gastric digestion is dialyzed until the concentration of iron inside and outside the dialysis bag are equal.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2017-14-fig1.png

To determine the gastric digestible iron from the supplement tablet, colorimetric measurement after complex formation between ferrous ion (M) and complexing agent (L) is carried out at pH 5.0. The resulting $\mathrm{ML_3}$ complex exhibits light absorption at $520\,\mathrm{nm}$, whereas M and L do not absorb light at this particular wavelength. Within the visible wavelength region, ferrous ion (M) does not absorb light, the complex ML absorbs light at X nm with the molar absorptivity of $50\,\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$, and the complex $\mathrm{ML_2}$ absorbs light at Y nm with the molar absorptivity of $200\,\mathrm{L\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$.

14.1) The stepwise constants, $K_1$, $K_2$ and $K_3$, refer to the formation of the complexes one step at a time.

(i) At equilibrium, the absorbance of the solution (in 1.0-cm cuvette) at X nm is 0.400. This solution also contains $1\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ of M and $2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ of L. Calculate the stepwise formation constant of ML ($K_1$).

(ii) Then, L is added into the solution. At equilibrium, the absorbance of the solution (in 1.0-cm cuvette) at Y nm is 0.400. This solution also contains $2\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ of ML and $2\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ of L. Calculate the stepwise formation constant of $\mathrm{ML_2}$ ($K_2$).

(iii) In an excess of L, all of iron is in the form of $\mathrm{ML_3}$.

Consider the following table:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} [\mathrm{M}],\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}} & [\mathrm{L}],\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}} & \text{Abs (at 520 nm), pathlength (b) = 1 cm} \\ \hline 6.25\times10^{-5} & 2.20\times10^{-2} & 0.750 \\ 3.25\times10^{-5} & 9.25\times10^{-5} & 0.360 \end{array}$$

a) Calculate the molar absorptivity ($\varepsilon$) of $\mathrm{ML_3}$ complex

b) Calculate the overall formation constant ($K_f$) of $\mathrm{ML_3}$ complex

c) Calculate the stepwise formation constant ($K_3$) of the complex

14.2) The CHN analysis shows that the complexing agent (L) contains 80% C, 4.44% H, and 15.56% N. The molar mass of this compound is $180\,\mathrm{g}$. Determine the molecular formula of L.

14.3) The $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ complexes, ML, $\mathrm{ML_2}$ and $\mathrm{ML_3}$, adopt the octahedral structure (assume perfect octahedral geometry for each isomer of these three complexes). Sketch the d-orbital splitting diagram for $\mathrm{ML_3}$. Draw all possible isomers of $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ complexes. Order the magnitudes of $\Delta_\mathrm{o}$ (crystal field splitting) of these three complexes and explain. (Spectrochemical series: $\ce{I-} < \ce{Br-} < \ce{Cl-} \approx \ce{SCN-} < \ce{F-} \approx \text{urea} < \ce{ONO-} \approx \ce{OH-} < \ce{H2O} < \ce{NCS-} < \text{pyridine} \approx \ce{NH3} < \text{en} < \text{bipy} < o\text{-phen} < \ce{NO2-} < \ce{CN-} \approx \ce{CO}$)

14.4) To determine the dialyzable iron concentration (iron outside the dialysis bag), $5.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the solution outside the dialysis bag is added with a reducing agent to ensure that all of dissolved iron is in the ferrous ion form. Then, the solution is adjusted to the suitable pH, followed by addition of excess amount of complexing agent (L) and deionized water added to make up the volume to $50.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ in a volumetric flask. The absorbance measured at $520\,\mathrm{nm}$ is 0.550. Calculate the concentration of dialyzable iron (in unit of $\mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}$).

14.5) Presume all of the iron in the supplement tablet is completely digestible in the gastric condition. Determine in mg the iron in $1.0000\,\mathrm{g}$ of supplement tablet.

problems.title: Natural Chelator from Shrimp Shell

Problem 23. Natural Chelator from Shrimp Shell

Chitosan is a linear polysaccharide composed of $\beta$-(1-4)-linked D-glucosamine (deacetylated unit) and N-acetyl-D-glucosamine (acetylated unit). It is made by treating the chitin shells of shrimp or other crustaceans with a strong base, like sodium hydroxide. The deacetylation of chitin by a strong base yields partially-acetylated chitosan as shown below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2017-23-fig1.png

Chitosan can be used for a variety of purposes like helping plants to fight off fungal infections, preventing spoilage in wine, helping deliver drugs through the skin, being applied to reduce bleeding, and as an antibacterial agent. In the environmental aspect, chitosan can be used as an effective metal ion adsorbent. The adsorption capacities of chitosan for Cu(II), Hg(II), Pb(II) and Zn(II) are 79.94, 109.55, 37.2, $47.15\,\mathrm{mg\,(g\ chitosan)^{-1}}$, respectively.

23.1) Suggest the preferred binding sites in completely-deacetylated chitosan for metal ion.

The selectivity of chitosan towards $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ can be increased by modification with $\ce{CS2}$ yielding partially modified chitosan (PMCS) as in the structure below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2017-23-fig2.png

The absorption capacity toward $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ was increased from 37.2 to $156.0\,\mathrm{mg\,g^{-1}}$ chitosan (Wang, N.; Zheng, P.; Ma, X. Powder Technol. 2016, 301, 1-9.)

23.2) Suggest the most preferred site(s) in chitosan for $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$ and draw the bond(s) between that preferred site(s) and $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$. Explain the increase in absorption capacity of PMCS toward $\ce{Pb^{2+}}$.

To increase the sensitivity of the chitosan toward metal ion, the dye like meso-tetra(p-carboxyphenyl)porphyrin is chemically bonded with chitosan matrix. After the two acidic protons are removed, the four nitrogen atoms will bind with metal ion. The two axial sites of the metal ion normally bind with water molecules yielding the octahedral complex. Each metal ion gives characteristic absorption maximum in the visible range.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2017-23-fig3.png

23.3) Suggest the bonds between meso-tetra(p-carboxyphenyl)porphyrin and chitosan if a weak protonic acid is used as a catalyst.

23.4) If $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ is being adsorbed by the chitosan-porphyrin adsorbent, draw the structure of the complex and predict the approximate $d$-orbital splitting in the proposed complex.

Problem 33. Stereoisomers without Stereocenter

Axial chirality refers to stereoisomerism of a special case of chirality in which a molecule does not possess a stereogenic center but an axis of chirality. An axis of chirality is defined as an axis about which a set of substituents is held in a spatial arrangement that is not superimposable on its mirror image.

Two necessary preconditions for axial chirality are:

i. A rotationally stable axis

ii. Presence of different substituents on both sides of the axis

Axial chirality is most commonly observed in atropisomeric biaryl compounds wherein the rotation about the aryl-aryl bond is restricted, for example, biphenyl, binaphthyls. Certain allene compounds also display axial chirality.
