Problem 28. Polymers

Polymerization processes play a crucial role in the petrochemical and manufacturing industries, allowing the creation of complex polymers that were previously inaccessible, thanks to techniques like olefin metathesis.

28.1. For each polymerization reaction below, draw the draw the repeating units of the resulting polymers. In addition, classify each polymerization as step growth, chain growth, or living polymerization.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-28-fig1.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-28-fig2.png

You have a mixture of polystyrenes with three different architectures (linear, cyclic, and graft). Suppose that, despite the different architectures, these polystyrenes have exactly the same overall number- and weight-average molecular weights.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-28-fig3.png

28.2. What do you expect the gel-permeation chromatography (GPC) data to look like? Draw the expected concentration signal and explain.

problems.title: Polymer functionalization
problems.problem:
Problem 29. Polymer functionalization

The term "click chemistry" is a collective name for organic chemical reactions that allow the linking of two molecules with high specificity and efficiency under relatively mild reaction conditions. One of the most characteristic examples of this reaction family is the Cu(I)-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition. In this process, an azide group and a carbon-carbon triple bond form a 1,2,3-triazole ring, covalently linking species carrying two different functional groups.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-29-fig1.png

In the following, we utilize this reaction for the functionalization of poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC). This is achieved by replacing some of the Cl atoms with azide groups, followed by quantitatively introducing them into azide-alkyne cycloaddition with a slight excess of added propargyl-poly(dimethylsiloxane)-monomethyl ether. The reaction sequence is illustrated in the scheme below:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-29-fig2.png

29.1. Draw the polymer structures P1 and P2 using the notations provided in the scheme.

The propargyl-poly(dimethylsiloxane)-monomethyl ether, the substantially higher molecular weight partially azidated PVC, the cycloaddition reaction mixture at the end of the reaction, and the purified P2 product were all examined using gel permeation chromatography. The obtained chromatograms are presented below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2024-29-fig3.png

29.2. Match the measured samples with the obtained gel permeation chromatography curves.

29.3. Estimate the average number of poly(dimethylsiloxane) side chains per PVC molecule in the purified P2 product.

29.4. Calculate the excess (in mol%) of propargyl-poly(dimethylsiloxane)-monomethyl ether that was added to the azidated PVC in the functionalization reaction.

problems.title: Polyurethane network
problems.problem:
Problem 30. Polyurethane network

We aim to create a novel polyurethane network using hexamethylene diisocyanate (HDI, $\ce{OCN-(CH2)6-NCO}$), poly(ethylene glycol) ($\ce{HO-(CH2CH2O)_{$n$}-H}$, $M_\mathrm{n} = 500\,\mathrm{g/mol}$), and a "homemade" polyol crosslinker. Initially, we convert the hydroxyl groups of the cross-linking polyol into acetates using acetic anhydride. Subsequently, the obtained product, i.e., the acetylated polyol, along with the initial polyol, undergoes gel permeation chromatography. The results are as follows:

$$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|} \hline & M_\mathrm{n}\ /\ \mathrm{g/mol} & M_\mathrm{w}\ /\ \mathrm{g/mol} & I_\mathrm{p} \\ \hline \text{Sample 1} & 1383 & 2531 & 1.83 \\ \hline \text{Sample 2} & 1240 & 2232 & 1.80 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

For the polyurethane synthesis, we mix $1.6820\,\mathrm{g}$ of HDI, $4.0000\,\mathrm{g}$ of poly(ethylene glycol), and a sufficient amount of cross-linking polyol to ensure an equal number of hydroxyl and isocyanate groups.

30.1. Determine the average number of hydroxyl groups per molecule in the cross-linking polyol.

30.2. Calculate the mass of cross-linking polyol required for the polyurethane synthesis?

The reaction between isocyanate and hydroxyl groups is modeled by the following equation. Moving forward, we disregard changes in volume and temperature, and assume equal reactivity between identical groups in different chemical environments:

$$\sim\!\sim\!\sim\mathrm{NCO} + \mathrm{HO}\!\sim\!\sim\!\sim\ \rightarrow\ \sim\!\sim\!\sim\mathrm{NHCOO}\!\sim\!\sim\!\sim$$

You can model the time evolution of the process using a simple kinetic law with an order of 1 for each reactant.

After 3 hours of the reaction, a sample was withdrawn, and the subsequent GPC result is as follows:

$$\begin{array}{|l|c|c|c|} \hline & M_\mathrm{n}\ /\ \mathrm{g/mol} & M_\mathrm{w}\ /\ \mathrm{g/mol} & I_\mathrm{p} \\ \hline \text{Sample 3} & 1227 & 3288 & 2.68 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

30.3. Calculate the conversion after 3 hours?

Crosslinking polymers leads to gelation, a sudden increase in viscosity. A simple model predicts that this gel point occurs when $M_\mathrm{n}$ becomes infinitely high.

30.4. Identify the conversion corresponding to the gel point in this model.

30.5. Determine the reaction time at which the reaction reaches the gel point.

problems.title: Stereocamelstry
problems.problem:
Problem 1. Stereocamelstry

The UAE is well known for its camel shows, where camels stand in a line one after another and don't really do anything else. This arrangement of camels is called a train of camels, or a caravan of camels, and the camels are tied head to tail. This is the most convenient way of arranging camels when moving across the desert.

For this problem we shall approximate a normal camel as having a plane of symmetry along its body; its left side is the same as its right side. However, the two ends of a camel are different; a camel has a head end (H) and a tail end (T).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-1-fig1.png

Colin was trying to tie lots of camels up into trains of camels that were two camels long, but was a bit forgetful and didn't think to look at which way around the camels were when he was tying them up. This resulted in three different arrangements of camels in the train being possible.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-1-fig2.png

The three arrangements possible when viewed from overhead are shown above. We could call these three arrangements HH, HT, and TH respectively, based on whether the head or the tail of the camel comes first as we look from top to bottom. We might at first think that there is a fourth possible arrangement of camels (TT). However, this arrangement is not unique. If we were to view the TT arrangement from the other end, it is the same as HH.

This question requires you to draw various arrangements of camels. If your artistic skills have deserted you somewhat, then you may approximate a camel to something simpler in your drawings such as an arrow. It is important to remember though that camels are three dimensional objects.

(a) Draw all possible arrangements of camels in a camel train that is three camels long.

(b) Draw all possible arrangements of camels in a camel train that is four camels long.

When camels are tied up for the night, they are sometimes arranged side by side. Let's first consider a parking arrangement where two camels are side by side. Again, Colin was a bit forgetful and didn't pay attention to which way round he was tying the camels. There are three possible side by side arrangements of two camels.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-1-fig3.png

When viewed from overhead, and described going left to right, we can call these arrangements HH, HT, and TH respectively. Again, we might think there is a fourth possible arrangement of camels (TT), but this is the same as HH if viewed from the other side. The HT and TH arrangements are also interesting, as they are chiral arrangements of camels. Even though an individual camel is achiral, these two arrangements of camels are chiral overall, and they are enantiomers of each other.

(c) Draw all possible arrangements of camels when three camels are tied side by side, indicating which arrangements are achiral and which arrangements are chiral.

(d) Draw all possible arrangements of camels when four camels are tied side by side, indicating which arrangements are achiral and which arrangements are chiral.

Although camels are famous for going for long periods without water, they do sometimes need to drink. A particular well has space for four camels to stand around it and drink water. To do this, the camels should be arranged around the well as shown.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-1-fig4.png

However, Colin was forgetful again and did not pay attention to which was the head end, and which was the tail end, when tying them up.

(e) Draw all possible arrangements of camels around the well, indicating which arrangements are achiral and which arrangements are chiral.

Carrying people across the desert is an arduous task for camels. Camels bend their front legs to sit down when carrying a rider and sometimes this leads to them injuring a leg. An individual camel who has injured one leg is no longer achiral and becomes a chiral camel. We will call chiral camels who have injured their front right leg as $R$ camels and camels who have injured their front left leg as $S$ camels.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-1-fig5.png

(f) Draw all possible arrangements of camels when two chiral camels are tied side by side, indicating which arrangements are achiral and which arrangements are chiral. Assume camels were picked randomly from a herd containing both $R$ and $S$ camels and then were parked randomly with no attention paid to which way around they were parked.

Fortunately, the UAE have just opened a Care Centre for Chiral Camels. To maximise efficiency, Carol the surgeon operates on two camels at once. The camels are lying down during their operation and there are three possible operation layouts: (i) feet-to-feet, (ii) hump-to-hump, and (iii) feet-to-hump. Note in the cartoon below only the top leg is visible.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-1-fig6.png

(g) Draw all possible arrangements of two chiral camels on the operating table in a feet-to-feet layout, indicating which arrangements are achiral and which arrangements are chiral. Just consider the position of the two camels relative to each other.

(h) Draw all possible arrangements of two chiral camels on the operating table in a hump-to-hump layout, indicating which arrangements are achiral and which arrangements are chiral. Just consider the position of the two camels relative to each other.

(i) Draw all possible arrangements of two chiral camels on the operating table in a feet-to-hump layout, indicating which arrangements are achiral and which arrangements are chiral. Just consider the position of the two camels relative to each other.

No camels were harmed in the making of this question.

problems.title: Mirror, mirror plane on the wall, who's the deadliest of them all?
problems.problem:
Problem 2. Mirror, mirror plane on the wall, who's the deadliest of them all?

In the fairy tale $\textit{Snow White}$, the evil queen looks at her reflection in the mirror and asks, "Mirror mirror on the wall, who is the fairest one of all?" The queen assumes she sees her exact self in the mirror; however, this is not always true. The reflection of a chiral object in a mirror gives its enantiomer. Sadly, for us chemists, this book from 1812 does not specify whether the queen was a chiral object or not.

Some compounds are formed as mixtures of many isomers, some of which are chiral, and some are not. Different isomers often have different chemical properties including how toxic they are. This is problematic if the synthesis leads to a mixture of isomers, but not all isomers are useful.

2025 is the 200th anniversary of the discovery of one of these compounds, 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane ($\mathbf{HCH}$), where many isomers turned out to be very toxic.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-2-fig1.png

In 1825, British scientist Michael Faraday reported the discovery of benzene, which he had extracted from products of the pyrolysis of sperm oil. Through a series of meticulous experiments, he identified the accurate mass percentage of carbon and hydrogen in benzene. However, due to the concept of "proportionals" in use in science at the time, Faraday called this molecule the "bi-carburet of hydrogen" as 11.44 was close to 12, which was two "proportionals" of carbon.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-2-fig2.png

Figure 1: Left. Faraday's sample of the bi-carburet of hydrogen which is kept at the Royal Institution. Right. Faraday's determination of the mass percentages in benzene.

Faraday also reported the reaction of benzene with various other chemicals including chlorine gas.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-2-fig3.png

Figure 2: Faraday's description of the reaction of benzene and chlorine under sunlight.

Several different equations could be written to describe his observations, likely due to the presence of impurities in the sample. However, the "solid crystalline body" produced was the first synthesis of $\mathbf{HCH}$. Faraday correctly deduced that this compound contained carbon, hydrogen, and chlorine, but was unable to identify it further or know that it contained a mixture of isomers.

A modern synthesis of $\mathbf{HCH}$ involves the treatment of benzene with chlorine gas under UV light. The reaction is a free-radical addition.

(a) Write an equation for this reaction.

$\mathbf{HCH}$ exists as nine stereoisomers. For the purposes of parts (b) and (c) consider the cyclohexane ring to be flat.

(b) Draw all the stereoisomers of $\mathbf{HCH}$.

The nine stereoisomers of $\mathbf{HCH}$ are named with the following Greek letters.

$$\begin{array}{ccc} \alpha+ & \alpha- & \beta \\ \gamma & \delta & \varepsilon \\ \zeta & \eta & \theta \end{array}$$

(c) Using the following clues, as far as possible, assign the Greek letters to each of the isomers.

• The $\beta$ and $\varepsilon$ isomers contain centres of inversion.

• The $\zeta$ isomer is not an epimer of the $\alpha+$ isomer.

• The $\theta$ isomer is an epimer of the $\eta$ isomer.

• The $\gamma$ isomer has more planes of symmetry than the $\delta$ isomer.

• The $\eta$ isomer does not possess a plane of symmetry through any of the atoms.

• The + and – refer to dextrorotatory and levorotatory respectively.

• The $\beta$ isomer has by far the lowest chemical reactivity.

(d) Explain why the $\beta$ isomer has by far the lowest chemical reactivity.

Many years later, the mixture of isomers of $\mathbf{HCH}$ was found to have potent insecticidal activity. Dutch chemist Teunis van der Linden was the first to isolate and describe $\gamma$-$\mathbf{HCH}$ in 1912 and this isomer was named "lindane" after him. By 1942, it was realised that lindane ($\gamma$-$\mathbf{HCH}$) was the isomer responsible for the potency of the insecticide and $\gamma$-$\mathbf{HCH}$ went on sale as a seed treatment in 1949 called $\textit{Mergamma A}$, which contained 1% mercury and 20% lindane. The mercury was removed later for safety reasons, but lindane products remained on sale for over 50 years.

Whilst the $\gamma$-isomer of $\mathbf{HCH}$ was available in >98% purity by this point, this was achieved through purification; the synthesis of $\mathbf{HCH}$ always gave a complex mixture composed of 65-70% $\alpha$-$\mathbf{HCH}$, 7-10% $\beta$-$\mathbf{HCH}$, 14-15% $\gamma$-$\mathbf{HCH}$, 7% $\delta$-$\mathbf{HCH}$, 1-2% $\varepsilon$-$\mathbf{HCH}$, and 1-2% of the other isomers. Once separated, the remaining isomers were dumped creating huge chemical waste problems.

(e) Suggest why very little of the $\zeta$-$\mathbf{HCH}$, $\eta$-$\mathbf{HCH}$, and $\theta$-$\mathbf{HCH}$ isomers are formed during synthesis.

Over time the toxicity of $\gamma$-$\mathbf{HCH}$ itself became apparent. The $\gamma$-isomer is now classified by the World Health Organisation as acutely toxic. Prolonged exposure leads to various symptoms including headaches, dizziness, seizures, convulsions, and even death in extreme cases. An international ban on the use of $\gamma$-$\mathbf{HCH}$ in agriculture came into effect in 2009. The $\alpha$-$\mathbf{HCH}$ and $\beta$-$\mathbf{HCH}$ isomers, which were dumped as chemical waste, proved to be even more toxic. All isomers show long term persistence in the environment and hence still cause problems today.

In 2021, a research team led by Swiss chemist Bill Morandi developed a new way to clean up $\mathbf{HCH}$ waste through electrolysis. His reaction reverses the reaction performed two centuries earlier by Faraday, as $\gamma$-$\mathbf{HCH}$ is converted back to benzene. However, rather than produce toxic chlorine gas, the chlorine atoms are transferred to another readily available non-cyclic alkene starting material $\mathbf{A}$, giving chloroalkane $\mathbf{B}$ as a by-product. This makes the transformation overall redox neutral. This process is highly synthetically useful as it removes toxic $\mathbf{HCH}$ waste and produces two valuable chemical products: benzene and chloroalkane $\mathbf{B}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-2-fig4.png

The mass spectrum of compound $\mathbf{B}$ gave the following ions: m/z 238.125 (100.0%); 239.128 (13.0%); 240.122 (63.9%); 241.125 (8.3%); 242.119 (10.2%); 243.122 (1.3%). Percentages listed show the relative amounts with the most intense peak set at 100%.

(f) Determine the formula for $\mathbf{B}$.

Compound $\mathbf{B}$ is produced as a racemic mixture of two enantiomers. As this process was designed to potentially be run on a large scale, compound $\mathbf{A}$ was chosen to be as simple/cheap as possible.

(g) Propose structures for compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

The compound 1,2,5,6,9,10-hexabromocyclododecane ($\mathbf{HBCD}$) has a lot of structural similarity to $\mathbf{HCH}$. It also exists as multiple different stereoisomers; many of which are produced during its synthesis.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-2-fig5.png

Dubai is famous for skyscrapers and high-rise buildings. Although not an issue in the UAE, many tall buildings in colder climates use polystyrene foam for thermal insulation. This insulation is very flammable, and due to the fire risks in tall buildings, flame retardants are put on this polystyrene foam. $\mathbf{HBCD}$ is used as one such flame retardant.

(h) Draw all the stereoisomers of $\mathbf{HBCD}$, indicating which ones are chiral and which ones are achiral.

$\mathbf{HBCD}$ is also now known to have significant toxicity problems and be long lived in the environment. Assessing overall toxicity is complicated because the different isomers have different toxicities and break down at different rates.

Unlike $\mathbf{HCH}$, the $\mathbf{HBCD}$ commercial product is used as a mixture of isomers. $\mathbf{HBCD}$ is produced from the bromination of cyclododeca-1,5,9-triene. Four isomers of cyclododeca-1,5,9-triene are possible: (i) all-$\textit{cis}$; (ii) $\textit{cis,cis,trans}$; (iii) $\textit{cis,trans,trans}$; and (iv) all-$\textit{trans}$.

(i) Assuming the standard mechanism of alkene bromination, determine which $\mathbf{HBCD}$ isomers are produced from each of the four possible starting materials.

(j) Given the commercial $\mathbf{HBCD}$ product is quoted as containing "three major diastereoisomers", is it possible to determine which isomer of cyclododeca-1,5,9-triene is used as the starting material for the commercial synthesis?

problems.title: Cedrene
problems.problem:
Problem 4. Cedrene

Sesquiterpenes are a class of organic structures that contain three isoprene units and often have the molecular formula $\ce{C15H24}$. Cedrene is one such compound that is found in the essential oil of cedar. There are two types of cedrene, $\alpha$ and $\beta$, which differ in the position of the double bond.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-4-fig1.png

(a) Circle the stereocentres in $\alpha$-cedrene and assign them as $R$ or $S$.

There are various ways to synthesise cedrene. In this exercise we look at two of these methods.

In 1955 Stork $\textit{et al.}$ used an eight step synthesis to make cedrol, a precursor to cedrene. It is possible to convert cedrol to cedrene by adding a sulfate salt. The synthesis of cedrene starts from compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

Method 1: Synthesis of $\alpha$-cedrene by Stork et al. (1955)

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-4-fig2.png

Additional hints:

• Pyr=pyridine;

• $\ce{(COCl)2}$ works similar to $\ce{SOCl2}$;

• $\ce{CrO3}$, Pyr converts alcohols to ketones;

• Organocadmium reagents work similar to Grignard reagents;

• Cedrol can be converted to cedrene via an elimination reaction in which water is removed;

• $\ce{LiAlH4}$ performs a reaction similar to the one shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-4-fig3.png

(b) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{C}$, $\mathbf{G}$, $\mathbf{I}$, and $\textbf{cedrol}$ that are obtained after work-up. You do not need to show stereochemistry.

Method 2: Cyclisation of nerolidol

It is also possible to isomerise the structure of nerolidol to both $\alpha$-, and $\beta$-cedrene by adding acid. This will remove the alcohol group and start a cyclisation reaction. The conversion takes place via multiple intermediate structures. Incomplete structures of three of these intermediates are shown.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-4-fig4.png

Intermediates $\mathbf{1}$ and $\mathbf{3}$ are charged. Intermediate $\mathbf{2}$ is neutral.

(d) Complete the structure of intermediates $\mathbf{1}$, $\mathbf{2}$, and $\mathbf{3}$ by adding double bonds and charges in the correct places.

Four carbon atoms are circled in nerolidol. Through understanding the mechanism we can determine where these four carbon atoms end up in cedrine.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-4-fig5.png

problems.title: Stereochemical models
problems.problem:
Problem 5. Stereochemical models

Stereochemistry is abundant in the natural world, with most molecular building blocks of life being chiral. While the origin of homochirality is still a subject of much debate, there is no doubt about the importance of stereochemistry in biological systems. The famous thalidomide tragedy occurred due to one stereoisomer having therapeutic effects while the other stereoisomer was teratogenic. Since then, synthetic chemists have focussed efforts on developing methods to make molecules in a stereoselective way. In this question, we will explore different aspects of stereochemical control.

One of the simplest ways to perform a stereoselective reaction is through the use of a chiral reagent.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-5-fig1.png

(a) By considering the transition state for the hydroboration reaction across the double bond, draw the structure of the major stereoisomer $\mathbf{A}$.

Instead of using a chiral reagent, the presence of a stereocentre nearby can also help to control the stereochemical outcome of a reaction. Imagine you want to synthesise product $\mathbf{A}$ starting from a carbonyl group. You could come up with two methods to do this (Reaction $\mathbf{B}$ and Reaction $\mathbf{C}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-5-fig2.png

The stereochemical outcome of the reactions can be predicted using the Felkin-Anh model.

(b) For each reaction, draw a Newman projection showing the ideal approach of the nucleophile. Use the labels =O, –H, –Ph, –Me and –$i$Pr. Show the structure of the nucleophile in full.

(c) Draw the structures of compounds $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$, indicating the stereochemistry clearly.

(d) Which reaction should you use to synthesise product $\mathbf{A}$?

☐ $\mathbf{B}$ ☐ $\mathbf{C}$ ☐ Either $\mathbf{B}$ or $\mathbf{C}$ ☐ Neither $\mathbf{B}$ nor $\mathbf{C}$

Often, the stereochemical outcome can be influenced by a small change in the reagent. Let's predict the stereoselectivity of the following reaction using the Felkin-Anh model:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-5-fig3.png

(e) Draw a Newman projection showing the ideal approach of the nucleophile. Use the labels =O, –H, –Me, –$\ce{CH2}$OTBS and Nu.

(f) Draw the structure of compound $\mathbf{D}$, indicating the stereochemistry clearly.

The stereochemical outcome of the reaction can be changed by using a different alcohol protecting group.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-5-fig4.png

(g) Draw a diagram of the transition state in this reaction. $\textit{Hint:}$ It involves the formation of a six-membered ring adopting a half-chair conformation.

(h) Draw the structure of compound $\mathbf{E}$, indicating the stereochemistry clearly.

(i) Why does the Felkin-Anh model not predict the correct stereoisomer in this example?

Six-membered rings are highly favoured thermodynamically, and many organic reactions go through transition states that involve six-membered rings. One example is the aldol reaction, which goes through a six-membered ring Zimmerman-Traxler transition state.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-5-fig5.png

(j) Determine the geometry of the boron enolate formed.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-5-fig6.png

(k) Using the Zimmerman-Traxler model, draw the arrangement of the reactants as they come together to form the six-membered ring transition state in the reaction to form $\mathbf{F}$. $\textit{Hint:}$ The Houk model predicts that stereocentre next to an alkene favours a geometry with the smallest group eclipsing the double bond. However, in this case, the smallest group should be facing the large Boron substituents to minimise steric strain.

(l) Draw the structure of compound $\mathbf{F}$, indicating the stereochemistry clearly.

Once again, changing the reaction conditions can lead to the formation of a different stereoisomer.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-5-fig7.png

(m) Using the Zimmerman-Traxler model, draw the arrangement of the reactants as they come together to form the six-membered ring transition state in the reaction to form $\mathbf{G}$. $\textit{Hint:}$ Carefully consider the geometry of the enolate. You should have two six-membered rings in this transition state.

(n) Draw the structure of $\mathbf{G}$, indicating the stereochemistry clearly.

In fact, using a chiral reagent, yet another stereoisomer can be formed selectively.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-5-fig8.png

Rationalising the stereoselectivity of this reaction is beyond the syllabus of IChO2025 and left as a challenge to the enthusiastic student!

problems.title: Stereocontrol in the synthesis of FR66979
problems.problem:
Problem 6. Stereocontrol in the synthesis of FR66979

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-6-fig1.png

FR66979 was isolated from the bacterium $\textit{Streptomyces sandaensis}$ in 1987. It was first identified as a promising antibiotic, but subsequently found to also possess potent antitumour activity by forming interstrand cross-links in duplex DNA. problems.title: Coenzyme A and anaplerotic reactions
problems.problem:
Problem 7. Coenzyme A and anaplerotic reactions

Glycolysis is one of the most important catabolic transformations. It affords pyruvate, which is further subjected to oxidative decarboxylation under aerobic conditions entering the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle in the form of acetyl-coenzyme A (CoA), which reacts with oxaloacetate to produce citrate.

CoA is composed of three blocks, which are residues of phosphorylated ADP, pantothenic acid (vitamin $\mathrm{B_5}$), and thioethanolamine:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-7-fig1.png

During CoA biosynthesis, vitamin $\mathrm{B_5}$ is modified from both sides.

(a) Suggest the canonical amino acid $\mathbf{X1}$, from which the thioethanolamine residue originates. Draw the structure of the L-isomer of $\mathbf{X1}$ with stereochemical details. What is the absolute configuration ($R$ or $S$) of the stereocentre?

Vitamin $\mathrm{B_5}$ is produced in most bacteria by combination of pantoate and a non-canonical amino acid $\mathbf{X2}$, which is a nearest homologue of the canonical amino acid $\mathbf{X3}$ and a structural isomer of the canonical amino acid $\mathbf{X4}$.

(b) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{X2}$-$\mathbf{X4}$ and pantoate.

CoA is a universal carrier of acyl groups in numerous metabolic processes including degradation and biosynthesis of fatty acids. The $\beta$-oxidation of fatty acids takes place in the mitochondrial matrix through a series of four reactions collectively referred to as $\beta$-oxidation. This process is named for the successive oxidations occurring at the $\beta$-carbon, which lead to the stepwise removal of two carbon atoms from the carboxyl end of the fatty acyl-CoA molecule.

Four enzymes are involved in this process and their functions are shown in the table.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{Abbreviation} & \textbf{Name} & \textbf{Function} \\ \hline \text{EH} & \text{Enoyl-CoA Hydratase} & \text{Forms a }\beta\text{-hydroxyl carbonyl (aldol) from an }\alpha,\beta\text{-unsaturated carbonyl} \\ \hline \text{KT} & \beta\text{-ketothiolase} & \text{Cleaves the bond between the }\alpha\text{ and }\beta\text{-carbons in a }\beta\text{-ketothioester} \\ \hline \text{HD} & \text{3-L-hydroxyacyl-CoA Dehydrogenase} & \text{Oxidises a hydroxyl group to a carbonyl group} \\ \hline \text{AD} & \text{Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase} & \text{Removes hydrogen atoms from the }\alpha\text{ and }\beta\text{ positions of a carbonyl to form an }\alpha,\beta\text{-unsaturated carbonyl} \end{array}$$

The process of the $\beta$-oxidation of fatty acids is shown underneath with blanks.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-7-fig2.png

(c) Fill in the circles with the abbreviations of the enzymes needed. Each enzyme should be used once.

(d) Draw in the hexagons the structure(s) of the substrate(s) needed by the enzyme at each point.

(e) Complete the rectangles with the structures of the intermediates.

Recently CoA was found to play an important protective role in preserving a particular functional group in various enzymes from irreversible oxidation. This reaction is referred to as CoAlation.

(f) From the following functional groups, choose the most probable one that is being protected:

–OH –C=O –COOH –C(O)$\ce{NH2}$ –$\ce{NH2}$ NH-C$\ce{(NH2)2+}$ –SH -S-$\ce{CH3}$

During the periods of rest, organisms synthesise various important molecules including storage compounds, mostly using TCA cycle intermediates as starting substrates, thus depleting the pool of cycle intermediates. As a result, glycolytic overproduction of pyruvate and phosphoenolpyruvate as well as that of acetyl-CoA is observed when energy is required again. This happens because of a diminished concentration of oxaloacetate, which slows down the initial reaction of the TCA cycle.

Most organisms can overcome this potentially dangerous situation due to four different reactions catalysed by enzymes $\mathrm{E_1}$-$\mathrm{E_4}$ belonging to three different classes.

Enzymes catalyse diverse reactions and can be grouped into six classes:

i) Oxidoreductases – Oxidation/reduction reactions.

ii) Transferases – Transfer of a methyl-, acyl-, amino- or phosphate group from one substance to another; kinases forming a subclass catalyse the transfer of phosphate group(s) from high-energy phosphorylated species to accepting substrate(s).

iii) Hydrolases – Hydrolytic formation of two products from a substrate.

iv) Lyases – Non-hydrolytic addition or removal of groups from substrates, with C-C, C-N, C-O, or C-S bonds cleavage in the latter case.

v) Isomerases – Intramolecular rearrangement.

vi) Ligases – Joining together two molecules by formation of new C-O, C-S, C-N, or C-C bonds with simultaneous breakdown of ATP.

$\textit{Hint:}$ enzymes catalyse both forward and reverse reactions.

A very important reaction occurring in mammalian livers and kidneys is catalysed by $\mathrm{E_1}$:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-7-fig3.png

Biotin (see below) covalently bound to a lysine (Lys) residue is the co-factor found in the active site of $\mathrm{E_1}$. The reaction develops in two subsites, one being responsible for the biotin carboxylation ($\textbf{Scheme 1}$) and the other for $\ce{CO2}$ attachment to pyruvate.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-7-fig4.png

After being transferred to the second subunit, $\ce{CO2}$ leaves the biotin residue, the enol form of which further activates pyruvate by removing one of its protons to facilitate its reaction with $\ce{CO2}$ ($\textbf{Scheme 2}$):

$\mathrm{E_2}$ catalyses a reversible reaction which involves (along with other reaction participants) GTP, oxaloacetate, and phosphoenolpyruvate, the latter containing nearly twice as much energy as in ATP.

(k) Write down the $\mathrm{E_2}$ catalysed reaction.

(l) What class does $\mathrm{E_2}$ belong to?

$\mathrm{E_2}$ plays an important role in the process of gluconeogenesis where it catalyses one of the bypass steps given in $\textbf{Scheme 3}$ (phosphorylated nucleosides and inorganic phosphate are not shown).

$\ce{CO2}$ (in the form of the hydrogencarbonate anion) is attached to pyruvate in mitochondria and is released as a result of decomposition of $\mathbf{F}$ in the cytoplasm. Studies show that this is the same species. Thus, one should not expect any label in newly formed glucose if $\ce{^{14}CO2}$ enters the carboxylation reaction instead of $\ce{^{12}CO2}$. However, some trace amount of labelled glucose is detected in actual experiments with $\ce{^{14}CO2}$.

People who smoke have an increased chance of getting lung cancer; there are multiple reasons for this. Problem 9. Determining the stereochemistry of enzymatic reactions

In 1975, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Sir John Warcup Cornforth for his work on the stereochemistry of enzyme-catalysed reactions. Enzymes are nature's chiral catalysts that perform thousands of reactions in our bodies every day, and elucidating the stereochemical result of enzymatic reactions was a huge challenge to biochemists at that time.

In this question, we will focus on one particular enzymatic transformation: the isomerisation of isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) to dimethylallylpyrophosphate (DMAPP), by the enzyme isopentenyl pyrophosphate isomerase.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-9-fig1.png

We can break down the mechanism of the reaction into two separate steps: The removal of a proton from carbon $\mathbf{c}$, and the addition of a proton to carbon $\mathbf{a}$. In this question, we will focus on the addition of a proton to carbon $\mathbf{a}$.

To determine the stereochemistry of the addition of a proton to carbon $\mathbf{a}$, one of the protons on carbon $\mathbf{a}$ in IPP was labelled with tritium ($\ce{^3H}$, T). The isomerase reaction was carried out in $\ce{D2O}$, such that a deuterium ($\ce{^2H}$, D) would be added to carbon $\mathbf{a}$. The final product is chiral due to the modified methyl group (a $\ce{CH3}$ group with three different isotopes of H). In order to trap the product, another enzyme was added to catalyse the irreversible condensation of two molecules of IPP with DMAPP to form product $\mathbf{A}$.

How can we determine the chirality of such a methyl group? To do this, an ingenious method was devised. First, chiral product $\mathbf{A}$ containing the labelled methyl group was converted to chiral acetic acid through two steps.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-9-fig2.png

(a) Suggest a suitable two-step sequence of reactions that can convert chiral product $\mathbf{A}$ to chiral acetic acid $\mathbf{B}$.

Chiral acetic acid was then subjected to a few more enzymatic transformations. For the purpose of the next part, we will consider the transformation to have been performed on the ($S$)-isomer.

(b) Draw the structure of ($S$)-$\mathbf{B}$.

($S$)-$\mathbf{B}$ was converted into chiral acetyl CoA which then reacted with glyoxylic acid to form malic acid. The second step is catalysed by malate synthase and proceeds through an attack into the glyoxylic acid (forming a new chiral centre with ($S$) configuration) with inversion of configuration at the original chiral centre. Two products are formed in a 4:1 ratio ($\textit{Hint:}$ kinetic isotope effect). Fumarase catalyses the anti-periplanar elimination of water from the mixture of $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ to give $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$ respectively.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-9-fig3.png

(c) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$, clearly showing the stereochemistry.

(d) Draw the Newman projections of the most stable conformation of both $\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$.

(e) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{G}$, clearly showing the stereochemistry.

The amount of tritium can be determined by measuring the radioactive activity. A ratio $Z$ is defined as:

$$\boldsymbol{Z} = \frac{\text{T activity after fumarase}}{\text{T activity before fumarase}}$$

(f) For ($S$)-$\mathbf{B}$, determine the value of $\boldsymbol{Z}$.

(g) Similarly, determine the value of $\boldsymbol{Z}$ for ($R$)-$\mathbf{B}$.

Thus, new methods have been developed to synthesise chiral acetic acid. One such method is described below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-9-fig4.png

Partial synthesis of a natural product

Total syntheses of natural products are rarely performed to acquire a commercial route to a physiologically active compound of value. Rather, total syntheses are often carried out to show that they can be done or they are carried out to prove the structure of the natural product, especially its stereochemistry, when spectroscopic methods give ambiguous results. A synthesis of the latter was carried out to obtain a bicyclic hexapeptide, which had been isolated from $\textit{Aspergillus flavus}$, and for which structure $\mathbf{1}$ had been assigned through complex spectroscopic studies. Problem 12. Imine`s guide to the biochemical galaxy

Imines are abundant chemicals both in the laboratory and in nature. Numerous organic reactions have been developed that utilise imines. One example is reaction X, for which the simplified mechanism is shown below (reaction X is the same reaction throughout this task). It is initiated by formation of $\mathbf{3}$, which is followed by protonation. Cation $\mathbf{4^+}$ can cyclise to $\mathbf{5^+}$, which yields $\mathbf{6^+}$ after 1,2-migration. Alternatively, cation $\mathbf{4^+}$ can directly undergo a 1,6-cyclisation to produce intermediate $\mathbf{6^+}$. The process is terminated by deprotonation, which yields product $\mathbf{7}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-12-fig1.png

(a) Draw the structures of compound $\mathbf{3}$ and intermediates $\mathbf{4^+}$-$\mathbf{6^+}$.

(b) Draw the most stable resonance form of $\mathbf{5^+}$ and of $\mathbf{6^+}$, which demonstrate cation stabilisation.

Reaction X is robust which enables its use in total syntheses. Intermediates similar to $\mathbf{5^+}$ can be trapped depending on their structure and other things present in the reaction. A part of a total synthesis is presented below as an example, where such an intermediate was stable. In this case, the tosyl group (Ts) was used as an electrophile instead of $\ce{H+}$ to initiate reaction X.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-12-fig2.png

(c) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{9}$, $\mathbf{10}$, and $\mathbf{12}$-$\mathbf{14}$. Stereochemistry is not important in this part of the task. $\textit{Hint:}$ substituent R is a disubstituted aromatic ring.

(d) Choose the reason(s) why compound $\mathbf{14}$ is a final product. Circle the correct answer(s).

A. Aromatisation is favourable.

B. Aromatisation is unfavourable.

G. Steric hindrance enhances the rate of six-membered ring formation.

H. Steric hindrance decreases the rate of six-membered ring formation.

(e) How many stereoisomers does compound $\mathbf{15}$ have?

The hypothesis that six-membered products were obtained by migration was confirmed by many experiments. For example, compound $\mathbf{17}$ can be synthesised from $\mathbf{16}$ (the stereochemistry of the migrated fragment was retained). The mechanism of this transformation is presented below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-12-fig3.png

(f) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{17}$, $\mathbf{18^+}$-$\mathbf{20^+}$. $\mathbf{18^+}$ and $\mathbf{19^+}$ are resonance structures. Specify the absolute stereochemistry where necessary.

As previously mentioned, reaction X occurs naturally in some organisms. Compounds $\mathbf{21}$ and $\mathbf{22}$ can be synthesised from amino acids through a series of enzymatic transformations. A single enzyme catalyses two sequential final steps: imine formation and reaction X.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-12-fig4.png

(g) Suggest a biochemical pathway for the syntheses of both $\mathbf{21}$ and $\mathbf{22}$ using a pair of starting materials from those listed below: choose one amino acid and one aldehyde. The pathway should not exceed four steps; consider imine formation and reaction X as two separate steps.

Specify the enzyme for each step using the following abbreviations:

Amino acids:

problems.title: Schiff bases, the Universe, and biochemistry
problems.problem:
Problem 13. Schiff bases, the Universe, and biochemistry

Schiff bases are imines with an alkyl or aryl substituent on the nitrogen atom. They play an important role in many biochemical and biotechnological processes. Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, $\mathbf{1}$), an enzymatic cofactor derived from vitamin $\mathrm{B_6}$, is one of the biologically important compounds that readily forms Schiff bases. A reaction cascade with an amine leads to PLP being transformed into pyridoxamine phosphate (PAP, $\mathbf{2}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-13-fig1.png

In many enzymes, the reactive aldehyde group of PLP does not exist in the free form. Instead, it forms a Schiff base product ($\mathbf{4}$) with a specific lysine residue of an enzyme.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-13-fig2.png

(a) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{4}$ and $\mathbf{5}$ using the lysine residue abbreviation $\mathbf{3}$.

Transaminases (also referred to as aminotransferases) catalyse reactions between an $\alpha$-amino acid and an $\alpha$-ketocarboxylic acid. In the case of the enzyme $\mathrm{E_1}$, the process starts with transamination of the PLP-lysine adduct $\mathbf{4}$ in the active site by alanine. The end of the catalytic cycle is given below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-13-fig3.png

(b) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{6}$, $\mathbf{10}$, and quinoid intermediate $\mathbf{8}$.

(c) Propose the missing part of the $\mathrm{E_1}$ catalytic cycle, clearly showing the reactants, intermediates, and the cofactor structure.

Beside transamination, amino acid racemisation and decarboxylation can be induced by PLP depending on the nature of the enzyme. All these processes start with Schiff base formation. Then the quinoid intermediate is obtained due to elimination of one of substituents at the $\alpha$-carbon atom.

(d) What is/are the reason(s) that may cause elimination of a substituent? Circle the correct answer(s).

a. Steric hindrance due to the tetrahedral environment of the $\alpha$-carbon atom.

b. Steric hindrance due to the planar geometry of the quinoid intermediate.

c. Being electron deficient, the pyridinium ring withdraws electron density from the $\alpha$-carbon atom.

d. Being a strong nucleophile, the pyridinium ring attacks the carbonyl atom of the amino acid.

e. Being a strong electrophile, the pyridine nitrogen atom attacks the carbonyl carbon of PLP.

f. Being a strong nucleophile, the pyridine nitrogen atom attacks the carbonyl carbon of PLP.

(e) Draw the structures of the starting Schiff bases, quinoid intermediates, and the product(s) for:

• racemisation of L-alanine,

• decarboxylation of L-alanine.

Show the absolute stereochemistry where necessary.

Schiff bases are involved in inter- and intramolecular cross-linking of extracellular matrix proteins such as collagen and elastin. The carbonyl group necessary for the reaction with the amine group appears in an allysine residue due to oxidative deamination of the lysine residue during a post-translational modification. The latter process is catalysed by the enzyme $\mathrm{E_2}$. Its cofactor (quinone $\mathbf{11}$) is formed inside the active site of the enzyme from residues of two amino acids as shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-13-fig4.png

(f) Select which amino acid residues were used in the biosynthesis of $\mathbf{11}$.

a. Alanine

b. Arginine

c. Asparagine

d. Glycine

e. Methionine

f. Tyrosine

g. Tryptophan

h. Lysine

(g) Circle the most electrophilic carbonyl group in $\mathbf{11}$. Draw the resonance structure that confirms your hypothesis. Use the simplified structure of $\mathbf{11}$ shown above.

The catalytic cycle of $\mathrm{E_2}$ for the transformation of lysine $\mathbf{3}$ to allysine $\mathbf{14}$ is shown below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-13-fig5.png

(h) Draw the structures of $\mathbf{12}$, $\mathbf{13}$, $\mathbf{14}$, and $\mathbf{16}$. Use the simplified formulae of $\mathbf{3}$ and $\mathbf{11}$ given above.

Isotope labelling is a method that allows us to track the origin of certain fragments after a chemical reaction. It is used extensively in biochemistry to study mechanisms of reactions.

Different versions of labelled lysine were prepared, and mass spectra (MS) were recorded for them using electrospray ionization in positive mode. The results of the analysis are presented below in the table.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \textbf{Spectrum number} & \textbf{Ion }[\mathrm{M+H}]^+ & \textbf{Compound} \\ \hline 1 & 145 & \\ \hline 2 & 146 & \\ \hline 3 & 147 & \\ \hline 4 & 148 & \\ \hline 5 & 149 & \\ \hline 6 & 150 & \end{array}$$

(i) The mass spectra do not change for any of the labelled lysines after the samples are dissolved in methanol. Choose which of the labelled lysine compounds $\mathbf{17}$-$\mathbf{31}$ could correspond to the given molecular ions in the table above.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-13-fig6.png

Desmosine $\mathbf{32}$ and isodesmosine $\mathbf{33}$ are two essential components of elastin. To biosynthesise them, one lysine and three allysine residues are needed to link four polypeptide fragments. One lysine residue and one allysine residue form Schiff base $\mathbf{34}$, whereas the other two allysine residues undergo an aldol condensation that produces $\mathbf{35}$. The two intermediates $\mathbf{34}$ and $\mathbf{35}$ finally react to give either $\mathbf{32}$ or $\mathbf{33}$.

(j) Draw the structures of intermediates $\mathbf{34}$ and $\mathbf{35}$.

To reveal the mechanism of the biosynthesis of $\mathbf{32}$ and of $\mathbf{33}$, lysine labelled on the $\varepsilon$-carbon atoms was prepared. Then a sample of elastin was biosynthesised from it and then subjected to post-translational modification.

(k) Circle the labelled carbon atom in allysine which originated from $\varepsilon$-labelled lysine.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icp-2025-13-fig7.png
